ideaData.title: Rotor excitation winding rewound for 48 V: four times the turns, quarter current
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (general practice, not attributed to a named supplier): a 48 V wound-rotor belt machine often inherits its rotor from the 12 V alternator family, so the field coil is a ~12 V-class winding of roughly 2.0-2.6 Ω hot (about 350-450 turns of Ø0.7-0.8 mm wire) that needs 5-7 A for full excitation. Fed from the 48 V bus through the excitation H-bridge that TI describes as standard for this machine type, it runs at only ~15-25 % duty, so the field switches, the brushes and the slip rings carry the full 5-7 A DC plus PWM ripple, and the brush voltage drop (~1-2 V per pair) is the dominant loss in the field circuit. Proposal: rewind the coil for 48 V: four times the turns (≈1,500-1,700 turns of Ø0.36-0.40 mm IEC 60317-13 Grade 2 wire) in the same coil window, so the same ampere-turns need one quarter of the current (≈1.3-1.8 A). Copper mass and I²R loss are unchanged at equal fill (R rises 16×, I² falls 16×), and the field time constant L/R is unchanged because L and R both scale with N². What changes is everything that carries current: brushes, brush shunts, slip-ring width, field MOSFETs, current-sense shunt and the field-path EMC filter all drop a size. Benchmark: series 48 V belt machines with slip-ring excitation exist (see sources); the specific coil design of any production unit could not be confirmed, so this idea applies wherever a 12 V-class winding has been carried over.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Money comes from downsizing every current-carrying element of the field path by 4×: smaller brushes and holder, 2 A-class instead of 10 A-class field switches, a cheaper shunt and a smaller field-path EMC filter. The finer wire costs slightly more per kg and takes longer to wind, which is booked as an added cost.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Field-coil winding moves from Ø0.75 mm to Ø0.38 mm wire: the flyer winder needs a finer nozzle, a low-tension dancer and a turn counter; cycle rises from ~9 s to ~14 s per coil (about 0.6 extra winder-hours per shift at 50,000/yr). No new presses; brush-holder mould inserts are re-cut; inverter PCB keeps its footprint.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count is unchanged, but the field-lead termination to the slip ring must cope with a finer wire: specify resistance-fusing with a sleeve or a doubled lead end to avoid neck breakage. Poka-yoke: the 48 V coil carries a different bobbin colour so a 12 V-class rotor cannot enter the 48 V line.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — small euros per part, but every field-path component drops a size with no performance change
costSavingPotential.percentage: 4-6 % of the field-circuit (rotor coil + brushes + field driver) cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate, one machine per vehicle. Cost-bridge lines: Field switches in excitation bridge €1.10→€0.55 (+0.55); Brushes, shunts and brush-holder €0.95→€0.70 (+0.25); Field current-sense shunt and filter €0.45→€0.25 (+0.20); Field coil wire and winding time €1.60→€1.75 (-0.15); Field-path PCB copper / connector pin rating €0.25→€0.15 (+0.10). Net €0.95 per vehicle; range €0.90-€1.30 reflects supplier quote spread; × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €45K-€65K. Payback = (tooling €60000 + capex €40000 + validation €180000) ÷ (mid annual €55K ÷ 12) ≈ 61 months.

ideaData.riskNotes: Finer wire is more fragile in winding and at the lead-out; enamel pinholes over 1,600 turns raise inter-turn short risk — 100 % surge test of the coil. Inductive kick on switch-off is now up to ~4× the voltage in the field path, so the de-excitation path must be clamped below the MOSFET rating. Validate with ISO 16750-2 / LV 148 supply tests, brush wear endurance and thermal cycling per ISO 16750-4.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Valeo 48V iBSG (series claw-pole BSG); TI 48 V starter-generator architecture note — Claw-pole 48 V P0 machine with integrated electronics; field excited through slip rings from a standard H-bridge on the machine electronics. How this differs: Neither source states the field-coil voltage class; this idea is a general-practice proposal to design the coil for the 48 V bus and size brushes and switches to one quarter of the current.

engineering.mechanism: Field MMF = N·I. At equal coil window and fill factor, quadrupling N quarters the wire cross-section, so R scales with N² (×16) while the required current falls to I/4: I²R = (I/4)²·16R = I²R — copper loss in the rotor is unchanged (~60-90 W at full field). Inductance L ∝ N² also rises 16×, so τ = L/R is unchanged (~0.1-0.2 s for this class of rotor) and torque response is not affected. The brush pair drop (~1.5 V at 6 A) is 12 % of a 12 V field supply but only ~3 % of 48 V, and brush I²R + contact loss falls from ~9 W to ~2.5 W. Switch conduction loss in the excitation bridge falls 16× at the same RDS(on).
engineering.specDeltas: Rotor drawing: coil spec changes from ~400 turns Ø0.75 mm to ~1,600 turns Ø0.38 mm IEC 60317-13 Grade 2 (class 200), hot resistance 32-42 Ω at 150 °C (was 2.0-2.6 Ω), coil window unchanged. Brush spec: section 5×6.5 mm → 4×5 mm, shunt 0.75 mm² → 0.35 mm². Field bridge: 80 V MOSFETs rated ≥5 A continuous, clamp/de-excitation path rated ≥90 V. Software: field-current controller gains rescaled for the new R and L; current-sense range 0-8 A → 0-2.5 A.
engineering.validationPlan: Rotor DV: 100 % surge (impulse winding) test at 1.5 kV on the coil, IEC 60317 enamel continuity on wire lots, thermal cycling −40/+180 °C 500 cycles on 6 rotors, overspeed 22,000 rpm × 2 min. System: ISO 16750-2 and LV 148 supply-voltage profiles incl. 58 V/70 V transients on 3 machines; brush wear endurance 1,500 h equivalent (start-stop + generation duty) on 6 machines, wear <60 % of allowance; ISO 16750-4 thermal shock. PPAP: rotor and brush holder re-submission (PSW level 3).
engineering.dfmImplications: Winder: finer nozzle, dancer and turn counter (≈€40k across two spindles); +5 s cycle. Lead termination by resistance fusing with a sleeve to protect the 0.38 mm wire. Brush-holder mould inserts re-cut (≈€25k). Poka-yoke by coloured bobbin and rotor laser code; no change to stator, end shields or EOL fixtures.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline field path (switches, brushes/holder, shunt/filter, coil, PCB rating) ≈ €4.35 per vehicle. Proposed ≈ €3.40 (net of the coil premium): switches −€0.55, brushes −€0.25, shunt/filter −€0.20, PCB rating −€0.10, coil +€0.15 added cost. Net ≈ €0.95 per vehicle. Not included: any efficiency gain from lower brush loss (~6 W, too small to price), re-tooling of the winder spindles beyond the stated tooling.

title: Two-switch asymmetric field bridge with forced de-excitation deletes 48 V load-dump clamp
description: [MHEV] Deletes two of four field MOSFETs and two gate-driver channels, and the external 48 V TVS clamp array with its mounting; adds two fast diodes. Firmware gains a de-excitation state; no new sensors. Baseline (general practice): a 48 V claw-pole BSG drives its rotor field from a full four-switch H-bridge, as TI describes as standard, and the 48 V bus in addition carries a high-energy TVS clamp array at the machine B+ terminal (or relies on a prolonged active short circuit of the stator) to absorb a load dump — the 48 V battery disconnecting while the machine is generating. The reason is the field time constant: with the field current left to free-wheel at ~1 V the excitation decays over 0.3-0.5 s, and a load dump lasts up to 400 ms (Analog Devices), so the machine keeps generating into an unloaded bus. ideaData.title: Two-switch asymmetric field bridge with forced de-excitation deletes 48 V load-dump clamp
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (general practice): a 48 V claw-pole BSG drives its rotor field from a full four-switch H-bridge, as TI describes as standard, and the 48 V bus in addition carries a high-energy TVS clamp array at the machine B+ terminal (or relies on a prolonged active short circuit of the stator) to absorb a load dump — the 48 V battery disconnecting while the machine is generating. The reason is the field time constant: with the field current left to free-wheel at ~1 V the excitation decays over 0.3-0.5 s, and a load dump lasts up to 400 ms (Analog Devices), so the machine keeps generating into an unloaded bus. Proposal: a two-switch asymmetric half-bridge (one high-side and one low-side MOSFET plus two fast diodes). Field current in a claw-pole machine is unipolar, so the second leg of a full H-bridge is not needed for control; turning both switches off forces the field current back into the DC link through the diodes, applying −Vbus (≈ −48 to −58 V) across the coil, exactly the forced de-excitation path described in US 8487592. Decay time falls from ~300 ms to ~25-40 ms; combined with a short (≤50 ms) active short circuit of the stator phases, the generated energy stays inside the DC-link capacitor and MOSFET avalanche capability, so the external TVS array is deleted.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Two fewer power devices and one fewer bolted component on the B+ path; one fewer screw joint and torque check. Board area freed (~4 cm²). Diode orientation is checked by AOI; no service impact.

ideaData.riskNotes: If the de-excitation path fails open the coil energy has nowhere to go: the diodes must be rated for the full field current and the inductive energy (½LI² ≈ 2-4 J). engineering.mechanism: Coil current decay follows L·di/dt = −V. With free-wheeling at ~1 V and L ≈ 0.4 H, R ≈ 2.5 Ω, decay is governed by τ = L/R ≈ 0.16 s, i.e. ~0.35-0.5 s to 10 %. Applying −48 V instead makes the decay a linear ramp: Δt = L·I/V = 0.4 × 6 / 48 ≈ 50 ms to zero (≈25-40 ms for the smaller rotors). Load-dump energy into the bus is roughly P_gen × t: 12 kW × 0.4 s = 4.8 kJ unchecked versus ~12 kW × 0.04 s ≈ 0.5 kJ, of which an active short circuit diverts most; the DC-link (≈3-5 mF) absorbs ½C(60²−48²) ≈ 2.6-4 J only when generation stops within milliseconds — hence ASC + fast de-excitation together.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: external TVS clamp array part number and its M6 fixing; delete MOSFETs Q3/Q4 and two gate-driver channels. Add: two 100 V / ≥10 A fast diodes (AEC-Q101). Spec: field current to <10 % within 50 ms after fault flag; bus peak ≤ 60 V for ≥ 40 ms load dump at 18,000 rpm full field; ASC entry ≤ 2 ms. Software: new fault state "forced de-excitation + timed ASC" in the machine controller; DTC unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Bench: load-dump injection (battery disconnect while generating) at 3,000/10,000/18,000 rpm, full field, −40/25/125 °C, 5 machines × 50 events, pass = bus ≤60 V and no MOSFET avalanche beyond rating. LV 148 E48-xx over-voltage tests; ISO 16750-2 supply tests; AEC-Q101 qualified diodes; 1,000 h HTOL on 3 boards. Vehicle: battery-contactor-open events on 2 cars. PPAP: electronics re-PSW, software release; FMEDA update for ISO 26262 safety goal on over-voltage.
engineering.dfmImplications: Two fewer power devices to place and inspect; one fewer screw joint and torque check on the B+ path; AOI checks diode polarity. New SMT stencil (~€5k) and ICT fixture update (~€25k). EOL adds a 0.3 s de-excitation-time measurement on the existing tester.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline field switching + protection ≈ €2.55 per vehicle (4 MOSFETs, 4 driver channels, TVS array, board area). Proposed ≈ €0.97: MOSFETs −€0.45, driver −€0.20, TVS −€0.95, PCB −€0.10, diodes +€0.12. Net ≈ €1.58 per vehicle. Not included: any reduction of DC-link capacitance (kept as is), software engineering hours (in validation figure).

title: Field-coil resistance doubles as rotor thermometer; one stator NTC replaces two
description: [MHEV] Deletes one NTC, its leads, sleeving and placement in the end winding, one termination and one ADC channel; measured rather than worst-case rotor temperature trims field-coil copper by about 5 %. Baseline (general practice): a 48 V BSG carries two stator NTC thermistors embedded in the end winding — one for the derating model and one as a plausibility/redundant channel — each with sleeved leads routed to the electronics, two connector or solder positions and two ADC channels. Rotor temperature is not measured; the field coil is protected by a conservative current limit assuming worst-case 180-200 °C, which drives the coil copper size. Proposal: the controller already measures field voltage (duty × bus voltage) and field current, so R_field = V/I is available every PWM cycle; copper's +0.393 %/K coefficient turns it into a rotor thermometer with ±5-8 K accuracy after a brush-drop correction. US 9048766 describes exactly this field-resistance/temperature relationship for wound-rotor machines. The rotor estimate becomes the plausibility partner of the one remaining stator NTC (rotor and stator temperatures are coupled through the air gap with a known thermal model), so the second NTC, its leads and its ADC channel are deleted, and the field current limit becomes temperature-based, letting the coil be sized ~5 % leaner in copper.

engineering.mechanism: Copper resistivity rises 0.393 %/K: R(T) = R25·[1 + 0.00393·(T − 25)]. A 2.4 Ω coil at 25 °C reads 3.58 Ω at 150 °C; a ±1 % measurement error (current shunt + duty) maps to ±2.5 K, and an uncorrected 0.3 V brush-drop error at 5 A (≈0.06 Ω) maps to ±6 K — hence the brush-drop model. With a worst-case assumption the field current limit must hold the coil below 200 °C at 140 °C under-bonnet ambient; with measurement the limit is applied only when the coil is actually hot, which allows ~5 % less copper cross-section for the same duty-cycle protection.
engineering.specDeltas: Stator drawing: delete NTC #2 (part number, lead routing, sleeving PET Ø2 mm, lacing note). Electronics: delete ADC channel and termination TP for NTC #2. Rotor drawing: field-coil wire Ø0.75 → Ø0.73 mm, same turns. Software: rotor-temperature estimator with brush-drop correction, update gate I_field >1 A, filter 1 s; plausibility |T_rotor_est − T_model| < 25 K else derate. EOL: store R_field@25 °C ±0.5 %.
engineering.validationPlan: Dyno correlation: 3 machines with slip-ring telemetry thermocouples in the field coil; WLTP, hill-tow 3,500 kg and repeated-boost cycles at −20/25/45 °C ambient; requirement ±8 K over 40-200 °C. Fault injection: NTC open/short, brush wear 80 %, slip-ring contamination; diagnostic coverage per ISO 26262-5. ISO 16750-4 thermal durability unchanged. PPAP: stator and rotor drawing change, software release, DFMEA/FMEDA update.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes one lacing step and one fragile lead from the impregnated end winding — the NTC lead is a known breakage point during lacing and impregnation handling. EOL adds a 1 s reference-resistance write. Zero tooling; stator fixture loses one sensor nest.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline sensing + field copper ≈ €4.33 per vehicle (two NTCs €1.10, placement €0.60, termination €0.25, copper €2.38). Proposed ≈ €3.23 including a €0.03 EOL step. Net ≈ €1.10-1.20 per vehicle. Not included: any warranty benefit from fewer NTC lead breaks, and the software engineering effort (in the validation figure).

engineering.mechanism: Open-circuit phase EMF of a wound-field machine is E = k·ω·Φ(I_f), where Φ(I_f) is set by the claw-pole magnetic circuit. Shorted field turns lower I_f-per-volt and shift the curve right; an oversized air gap or wrong stack height lowers the slope in the linear region; saturation of claws or yoke shows as early knee. Four points on the curve at 6,000 rpm resolve these within ±1 %. Loaded output current is a function of the same E, the phase impedance (R measured directly, L from the PWM ripple) and the inverter, so a machine passing E(I_f), R, insulation and inverter motoring checks predicts loaded output to about ±3 % — verified by the correlation study.
engineering.specDeltas: Control plan: delete loaded-generator characteristic at 1,800/3,000/6,000 rpm and motoring torque point from 100 % EOL; add E(I_f) at 1,500 and 6,000 rpm, 4 field steps, limit ±2.5 % of golden curve; stator surge 1.0 kV, waveform-area difference <8 %; insulation ≥100 MΩ at 500 V DC; phase-lead joint resistance ≤ +5 % of nominal by 4-wire; position-sensor offset ±1.5° el. Audit: 1/50 machines on loaded dyno, full curve. Fixture: polygon chuck replaces spline/pulley adaptors.
engineering.validationPlan: Correlation: 600 machines tested both ways across 3 rotor lots and 3 stator lots; seeded-defect set (shorted field turns, wrong stack, cracked phase weld, misplaced sensor, magnetically damaged claw) 30 parts, detection 100 %. Gauge R&R <10 % on E and R. Run-at-rate 2 shifts. PPAP: process flow, PFMEA, control plan resubmission; customer approval of audit frequency. Ongoing: monthly audit-dyno capability (Cpk ≥1.33 on output current).
engineering.dfmImplications: One universal polygon chuck replaces 4 pulley/spline adaptors; no torque coupling alignment. Cell footprint 25 → 10 m². Test cycle 80 → 38 s. Lab audit dyno shared with PPAP/requalification. Operator role: load/unload only; automatic lot hold on SPC drift.

title: Claw rotor balanced once to G2.5 with fans fitted; complete-machine trim balance deleted
description: [MHEV] Deletes the complete-machine trim-balance station (cycle, operator, rework); tighter rotor balancing and a pulley runout gate cost a little more. Baseline (general practice for high-speed belt machines): the claw-pole rotor is balanced as a sub-assembly by drilling the claw outer periphery (the method in US 5229672), then the complete machine — rotor in its bearings, with pulley and nut — is spun again and trim-balanced (pulley drilling or claw spot drilling through windows) because pulley eccentricity, bearing runout and end-shield bore misalignment add unbalance. engineering.mechanism: Permissible residual unbalance U = 9549·G·m/n (g·mm, m in kg, n in rpm). For a 2.2 kg claw rotor at 18,000 rpm: G6.3 → 7.4 g·mm, G2.5 → 2.9 g·mm. Pulley eccentricity adds U = m·e: a 0.25 kg pulley with 0.03 mm runout (e = 0.015 mm) adds 3.75 g·mm; bearing-seat eccentricity of 0.005 mm on 2.2 kg adds 11 g·mm unless seats are ground with the balance datum. With one-clamp grinding (≤0.01 mm coaxiality) and pulley runout ≤0.03 mm, the RSS stack is ≈ √(2.9² + 3.75² + 5²) ≈ 7 g·mm, inside the G6.3 complete-machine limit without trimming.
engineering.specDeltas: Rotor drawing: balance grade G6.3 → G2.5 (ISO 21940-11) at 2 planes, measured with fans, slip-ring assembly and bearing inner rings fitted; drill Ø6 mm max, depth ≤4 mm in claw periphery, ≥3 mm from claw tip. Shaft: bearing seats ground in one clamping, coaxiality 0.01 mm to A-B. End shields: bore positions to common datum, 0.02 mm. Pulley: radial runout 0.03 mm TIR, 100 % gauged. Delete machine trim-balance operation and its work instruction.
engineering.validationPlan: Capability: 300 machines measured at EOL vibration (no correction) — residual ≤ G6.3 at 99.73 % (Cpk ≥1.33). NVH: 1st-order vibration and whine on 3 vehicles, acceleration ≤ baseline +1 dB. Durability: bearing endurance 1,000 h at max belt load on 6 machines; overspeed 22,000 rpm × 2 min. PPAP: process change notification, PFMEA and control plan update; rotor drawing change.
engineering.dfmImplications: One station and one handling of the finished machine removed; no drilling on a finished machine, no swarf behind fans. Balancer upgrade (two-plane, auto-drill, re-check) ≈€120k; runout gauge ≈€20k fixture. Grinder program change only. Serial-linked balance record gates assembly.

title: Zoned sealing on the BSG: sealed slip-ring and electronics chamber, drained active part

engineering.mechanism: Water damages a wound machine by three mechanisms: (1) conductive contamination of the brush track (brush dust + water → tracking and galvanic slip-ring corrosion), (2) insulation resistance loss through unimpregnated paths, (3) bearing ingress. An impregnated stator with class-200 enamel and full resin coverage keeps insulation resistance >100 MΩ after soak; the rotor field coil is resin-bonded inside the claws. Water entering an open active part is centrifuged outward at 18,000 rpm (ω²r ≈ 1,885² × 0.05 m ≈ 1.8×10⁵ m/s², about 18,000 g at the ~100 mm claw OD) and leaves through drains; drag torque of a thin film is <0.1 Nm. The brush chamber, separated by an FKM double-lip seal (surface speed ~13 m/s at Ø14 mm shaft), keeps IP6K9K.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: O-ring P/N ×2 at front/rear end-shield spigots, ePTFE vent P/N on active part, splash shield P/N + 3 clips from engine dress BOM. Add: cast drain ports 2× Ø5 mm per shield with 3 mm labyrinth lip at 6 o'clock; FKM double-lip seal Ø14 × 24 × 5 at slip-ring chamber. Spec: active part IPX4K/IPX9K splash; chamber + electronics IP6K9K and IPX7; insulation resistance ≥100 MΩ @500 V after 24 h soak; leak test chamber 300 mbar, decay <2 mbar/10 s.
engineering.validationPlan: Machine: ISO 20653 IPX4K/IPX9K (active part), IP6K9K + IPX7 (chamber), dust IP5K on 3 machines each; ISO 16750-4 damp heat cyclic 21 days and salt spray 96 h; slurry ingress test. Vehicle: wading trough 900 mm × 50 crossings at 7 km/h, hot engine, on 2 SUVs; insulation and brush-track inspection afterwards. Durability: 1,000 h with 20 wet/dry cycles. PPAP: end-shield die change, BOM deletions, engine dress change.
engineering.dfmImplications: Three fewer seals fitted and no O-ring pinch risk at spigot assembly; one engine-dress part and 3 clips gone. engineering.mechanism: Brush current is 2-7 A DC; a press-fit eye-of-needle pin has a contact resistance of ~0.1-0.3 mΩ, giving <15 mW per pin — far below a screw joint's thermal limit. Brush positioning tolerance governs spring force and wear: a moulded PPS guide holds ±0.05 mm and the brush clearance 0.1-0.2 mm, equal to riveted boxes. Resistance welding the Cu shunt to a CuSn6 tab forms a solid-state joint with no solder phase, so there is no Sn-based creep or thermal-cycle fatigue at 150 °C ambient, which is the classic weak point of soldered shunts.

title: Slip rings overmoulded on the BSG rotor shaft with weld tabs for field leads
description: [MHEV] Removes the bought-in module (with supplier margin and logistics), the press-fit and knurl, and most of the OD turning stock; soldering becomes resistance welding. Adds an overmoulding step in-house. Baseline (alternator practice): a bought-in slip-ring module — two copper rings moulded into a phenolic or PBT body with two internal lead wires ending in hooks — is pressed onto a knurl at the shaft end after the claw halves are assembled; the field-coil ends are routed along the claw and soldered or hot-staked to the hooks; then the ring OD is finish-turned for runout. Proposal: overmould the two Cu rings (Cu-ETP or CuAg0.1) directly onto the shaft at the shaft machining stage in a thermoset (phenolic PF or BMC) or PA46-GF30, with the lead conductors formed as stiff CuSn6 tabs that stand proud at the claw side. After claw and coil assembly, the coil ends are resistance-welded (fused) to the tabs. The press-fit operation and its knurl are deleted, the bought module margin disappears, and because rings are moulded concentric to the shaft centres the finish turning stock drops to ~0.1 mm (light skim only). Slip-ring and brush construction follow the generic Lundell rotor (EEP description: copper slip rings and carbon brushes feed the field coil).

engineering.mechanism: Slip-ring surface speed at Ø14-16 mm and 20,000 rpm is 15-17 m/s; ring runout must stay <0.03 mm or brush bounce raises wear and arcing. A press-fitted module adds the knurl-to-body tolerance (≈0.05 mm) to the moulding tolerance, hence the turning stock; overmoulding on the shaft between centres removes the press interface. Hoop stress in a Cu ring of mean radius 7.5 mm at 20,000 rpm: σ = ρω²r² = 8,900 × 2,094² × 0.0075² ≈ 2.2 MPa — negligible; the critical load is differential thermal expansion between Cu (17 ppm/K) and resin (PF ~20-30 ppm/K), managed by undercut anchors.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: slip-ring module P/N, knurl Ø15 h11 on shaft, press-fit work instruction. Add: overmould drawing — two Cu-ETP rings 3.5 mm wide, 1.0 mm radial, dovetail anchors; resin PF (glass/mineral filled) or PA46-GF30; insulation ≥100 MΩ at 500 V ring-to-ring and ring-to-shaft; tabs CuSn6 0.6 mm. Ring OD runout 0.02 mm after 0.1 mm skim, Ra 0.4-0.8 µm. Field-lead joint: resistance fusing, pull ≥30 N.

title: BSG stator stack held by in-die interlocks plus two weld seams instead of six
description: [MHEV] Welding station cycle and its fixture wear drop to two tacks; the separate stacking/counting operation disappears into the press; stack-height scrap falls with in-die control. The die gains an interlock station, booked as added tooling cost per part. Baseline (general practice where the BSG stator uses stamped ring laminations, e.g. M330-35A): loose laminations are counted off the press, stacked on a mandrel, compressed and joined by six full-length laser (or TIG) weld seams on the yoke OD, each ~32-40 mm long. Welding is a separate station with fixture, laser source and seam inspection, and every seam shorts the laminations at the OD. ideaData.title: BSG stator stack held by in-die interlocks plus two weld seams instead of six
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (general practice where the BSG stator uses stamped ring laminations, e.g. M330-35A): loose laminations are counted off the press, stacked on a mandrel, compressed and joined by six full-length laser (or TIG) weld seams on the yoke OD, each ~32-40 mm long. Welding is a separate station with fixture, laser source and seam inspection, and every seam shorts the laminations at the OD. Proposal: stack in the die — each lamination carries 6-8 V-shaped interlock dimples in the low-flux outer yoke, the last station punches through to separate stacks at a programmed count (auto-stack-height control), and two short (10-15 mm) laser tack seams at 180° remain only for handling stiffness during winding insertion and impregnation. The joining review in PMC7602500 reports that both interlocking and welding raise eddy loss, with loss rising linearly with the number of interlocks — so the interlocks are placed in the outer yoke where flux density is lowest, the count is minimised, and the weld seams that short the full stack length are mostly removed, keeping iron loss roughly neutral. Bonding (15-44 % lower loss per Charged EVs/Eurogroup) is the premium alternative; at BSG frequencies the interlock route is the cheaper choice.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Stacks leave the press as a handled unit — no loose-lamination counting errors (wrong stack height is a known cause of output-current failure at EOL). Interlocks give inherent angular alignment, so no keyway mandrel. Poka-yoke: stack-height verification in-die.

engineering.mechanism: Eddy loss rises when laminations are electrically connected over a closed path. A full-length OD weld seam connects all N laminations and, with seams on both sides of a flux path, closes loops that carry circulating currents at the stator frequency (BSG: 16 poles × 18,000 rpm / 120 → 2.4 kHz). An interlock connects only adjacent laminations at a point in the outer yoke where B ≈ 0.4-0.8 T versus 1.5-1.7 T in the teeth; loss rises per interlock (linear, PMC7602500) but the loop area is small. Removing four of six seams and placing 6-8 interlocks at the yoke OD keeps total iron loss within about ±3 % of the welded baseline — to be confirmed by ring tests.
engineering.specDeltas: Stator core drawing: joining note "6 × laser seam 36 mm" → "6-8 interlock dimples, depth 0.5 × t (0.17 mm), at Ø_OD − 2 mm, + 2 × laser tack 12 mm at 0°/180°"; stack push-off force ≥ 600 N; stack height tolerance ±0.15 mm (in-die). Die: add interlock form and separation stations, stack counter/height controller. Delete: stacking station, keyway mandrel, 4 weld programs.
engineering.validationPlan: Iron loss: 10 stacks each route, ring test 1.0-1.5 T at 400/1,000/2,000 Hz, acceptance ≤ +3 % vs welded. Mechanical: push-off ≥600 N before/after impregnation and after 500 thermal cycles −40/+180 °C. Machine: output current map and efficiency at 6 points on 3 machines; NVH whine order check; ISO 16750-3 vibration 22 h/axis. PPAP: die change, process flow, core drawing change.
engineering.dfmImplications: Stacks come off the press as handled units, deleting the stacking station and counting errors. Laser cycle 22 s → 6 s. Die gains two stations and needs ~10 % more maintenance; interlock punch wear monitored by push-off audit. No new fixtures; keyway mandrel retired.

title: BSG stator phase ends welded to inverter busbars, deleting lugs and terminal block
description: [MHEV] Deletes six ring lugs, crimping, six screws and torque checks, and the insert-moulded terminal block; adds a welding operation. Lower joint resistance also reduces hot-spot related warranty. Baseline (general practice where the machine and its electronics are built as separable modules): the 48 V BSG stator has six phase-end leads (three phases, start and finish, or two three-phase systems) gathered from the end winding, sleeved in glass-fibre/silicone tubing, crimped into tinned Cu ring lugs and bolted with M5 screws onto a terminal block with brass inserts on the electronics side; each joint carries 150-300 A rms in boost. Proposal: the stripped phase-end bundles are TIG-fused or resistance-brazed into a short Cu-ETP sleeve that is laser-welded (or resistance-welded) to the inverter AC busbar tabs, which are part of a stamped CuSn0.15 comb moulded into the electronics carrier. The terminal block, six lugs, six screws and the crimp and torque operations disappear; joint resistance falls because a welded joint has no contact interface. The machine and electronics are then serviced as one unit, which is already the case for integrated-electronics BSGs such as the Valeo iBSG.

ideaData.riskNotes: Welding enamelled multi-strand bundles needs complete enamel removal; incomplete fusion gives high resistance and heating at 300 A boost. Copper spatter into the machine must be avoided. Validate: joint micro-sections, 4-wire resistance ≤ 50 µΩ, power cycling 300 A × 30 s on/off 50,000 cycles, ISO 16750-3 vibration, thermal shock, and EOL resistance gate.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Valeo 48V iBSG (claw-pole BSG with integrated electronics) — Machine and electronics integrated in one belt starter-generator unit. How this differs: The iBSG phase-connection method was not found; this idea is a general-practice proposal to weld phase ends to the inverter busbars where the baseline still uses lugs and a bolted terminal block.

ideaData.materialGrade: Tinned Cu-ETP ring lugs + M5 screws + PA66-GF30 terminal block with brass inserts → Cu-ETP fusing sleeves welded to CuSn0.15 busbar tabs
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Crimp + bolt (6 joints, torque-checked) → TIG fusing / resistance brazing + laser welding (6 joints, resistance-checked)
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: A bolted lug joint has two contact interfaces (lug-to-insert and screw clamp) of 20-50 µΩ each when new, rising as tin creeps and preload relaxes under −40/+150 °C cycling. At 250 A rms boost the loss per joint is I²R = 250² × 80 µΩ ≈ 5 W, concentrated at the interface; six joints dissipate ~30 W during boost. A metallurgical (fused/welded) joint is ≤20 µΩ and does not relax: ~1.3 W per joint. Preload loss in an M5 joint through a PA66 block also needs metallic inserts — which the weld removes.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete P/Ns: ring lug ×6, M5×10 screw ×6, terminal block (PA66-GF30 + 6 brass inserts). Add: Cu-ETP fusing sleeve ×6 (Ø6 × 8 mm), busbar comb tab length +6 mm. Process: enamel stripping by laser on bundle ends, TIG fusing 2.5 kA class, laser weld tab-to-sleeve 3 kW, weld depth ≥0.8 mm. Spec: joint resistance ≤50 µΩ by 4-wire, no spatter beyond shield, micro-section voids <10 %.
engineering.validationPlan: DV: 30 joints micro-sectioned per parameter window; power cycling 300 A, 30 s on / 60 s off, 50,000 cycles on 6 machines (ΔR ≤10 %); ISO 16750-3 engine vibration; ISO 16750-4 thermal shock 500 cycles; salt spray on exposed joints. PV: 3 machines full EOL + boost endurance. PPAP: new process (welding), BOM deletions, service concept change (unit replacement) agreed with aftersales.
engineering.dfmImplications: Part count −13; screwdriving station and crimp press retired; one welding cell with spatter shield and 4-wire test (≈€150k). Length-coded tabs give phase poka-yoke. Repair: no re-work of welded joints in plant except scrap of the unit — mitigated by first-time-right monitoring.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline phase connection ≈ €2.71 per machine (lugs/crimp €0.90, block €1.10, screws/torque €0.36, sleeving €0.20, warranty €0.15). Proposed ≈ €0.75 (busbar tab extension €0.30, sleeves/welding €0.35, sleeving €0.05, warranty €0.05). Net ≈ €1.96 per vehicle. Not included: efficiency gain from ~25 W lower joint loss in boost, aftersales cost of unit replacement.

title: Water-jacketed BSG keeps one rear internal fan with uneven blade pitch; front fan deleted
description: [MHEV] Deletes the front fan stamping and its projection-weld cycle; the rear fan becomes a slightly more expensive progressive-die part with modulated pitch. Less fan mass also means less balancing correction. Baseline (alternator heritage, general practice): the claw-pole rotor carries two stamped DC01 steel internal fans projection-welded to the claw faces — a front fan (~10 blades) and a larger rear fan (~12 blades) — because an air-cooled alternator must pull air across both end windings. When the stator sits in a water jacket, as on Audi's water-cooled 48 V belt alternator-starter, most of the stator copper and iron loss leaves through the jacket, and the fans only need to cool the field coil, the rear end winding near the brushes and the bearing. When the stator sits in a water jacket, as on Audi's water-cooled 48 V belt alternator-starter, most of the stator copper and iron loss leaves through the jacket, and the fans only need to cool the field coil, the rear end winding near the brushes and the bearing. Proposal: delete the front fan; keep one rear fan redesigned for the reduced airflow, with blades at unequal pitch (e.g., 11 blades, angular spacing modulated ±8°, mass centre kept on the axis) and a blade count that is not a multiple or sub-multiple of the claw count (8 claws per half on a 16-pole rotor). ideaData.dfmDfa: One fewer part and weld per rotor; rear fan orientation keyed by a pilot hole to one claw so the modulated pitch is always indexed the same way to the claws (consistent balance and noise). No service impact.

ideaData.materialGrade: Two DC01 (EN 10130) 1.2 mm fans → one DC01 1.5 mm rear fan with modulated pitch
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Two progressive-die fans + two projection welds → one progressive-die fan + one projection weld
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Fan affinity laws: flow ∝ n, pressure ∝ n², power ∝ n³. At 18,000 rpm two alternator fans absorb ~0.3-0.6 kW; one smaller-duty fan roughly halves that. Heat balance: at 10 kW generation and ~85 % efficiency the machine loses ~1.8 kW; with a jacket, stator copper and iron (≈70 %) go to coolant, leaving ~0.4-0.5 kW (field coil ~80 W, rear end winding, bearings, brushes) for air. A fan tone at blade-pass f = z·n/60 = 11 × 300 = 3.3 kHz with ±8° pitch modulation spreads its energy over side-bands, and z = 11 avoids coincidence with the 8th claw order (2.4 kHz).
engineering.specDeltas: Delete front fan P/N and its weld program. Rear fan: DC01 1.2 mm → 1.5 mm, 12 equal blades → 11 blades at pitches 30.4°/33.5°/36.7° sequence (mass centre on axis, ≤0.5 g·mm), outer Ø as before, pilot hole indexed to claw #1. Front end shield: add 6 axial inflow windows 8 × 20 mm. Thermal spec: field coil ≤185 °C at 140 °C inlet air, max continuous generation.
engineering.validationPlan: Thermal: 3 machines with telemetry thermocouples in field coil and rear end winding, max continuous generation at 140 °C inlet, 4 h stabilised; acceptance coil ≤185 °C. NVH: order analysis 1,000-18,000 rpm, fan orders ≤ baseline −2 dB(A), claw orders unchanged. Durability: overspeed 22,000 rpm × 2 min, weld fatigue test 10⁷ cycles. PPAP: rotor drawing change, die change, end-shield change.
engineering.dfmImplications: One fewer stamping, one fewer weld per rotor (−6 s). Fan indexing pilot ensures the modulated pitch has a fixed relation to claws (repeatable balance). Rear fan die rebuild (~€50k), end-shield die insert (~€20k).
engineering.costBridge: Baseline fans ≈ €1.22 per rotor (front fan €0.45, welds €0.20, rear fan €0.45, balancing share €0.12). Proposed ≈ €0.72 (rear fan €0.55, one weld €0.10, balancing €0.07). Net ≈ €0.50 per vehicle. Not included: CO2/fuel benefit of ~100-200 W lower windage at high speed (small in WLTP), NVH value.

title: Bevelled internal retaining ring replaces BSG drive-end bearing retainer plate and three screws
description: [MHEV] Deletes the retainer plate, three screws and lock washers, three drill-and-tap operations in the casting and three screwdriving/torque checks; adds one bevelled retaining ring and a groove turned in the existing bore set-up. Baseline (alternator heritage): the drive-end (pulley-side) deep-groove ball bearing — typically 6203/6303 class with contact seals — is the locating bearing of the belt machine. It is pressed into the aluminium front end shield and held axially by a stamped steel retainer plate clamped with three screws and lock washers into three drilled and tapped holes; a Delco Remy service sheet specifies three screw/lock-washer assemblies at 5-9 Nm, and US 4113326 describes the retainer-plate principle. That is 7 parts, three drill-and-tap operations in the casting, three screwdriving and torque-audit steps, and a source of swarf near the bearing. Proposal: turn an internal groove in the bearing bore in the same machining set-up as the bore itself and retain the outer ring with a DIN 983-style bevelled (self-tightening) internal retaining ring of the DIN 472 family. The bevelled groove flank and ring take up the axial tolerance stack so the outer ring is held without play, which a flat ring cannot do. ideaData.title: Bevelled internal retaining ring replaces BSG drive-end bearing retainer plate and three screws
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (alternator heritage): the drive-end (pulley-side) deep-groove ball bearing — typically 6203/6303 class with contact seals — is the locating bearing of the belt machine. It is pressed into the aluminium front end shield and held axially by a stamped steel retainer plate clamped with three screws and lock washers into three drilled and tapped holes; a Delco Remy service sheet specifies three screw/lock-washer assemblies at 5-9 Nm, and US 4113326 describes the retainer-plate principle. That is 7 parts, three drill-and-tap operations in the casting, three screwdriving and torque-audit steps, and a source of swarf near the bearing. Proposal: turn an internal groove in the bearing bore in the same machining set-up as the bore itself and retain the outer ring with a DIN 983-style bevelled (self-tightening) internal retaining ring of the DIN 472 family. The bevelled groove flank and ring take up the axial tolerance stack so the outer ring is held without play, which a flat ring cannot do. Axial loads on the drive-end bearing of a belt machine are small — rotor weight under 30-40 g shock, belt-misalignment thrust and magnetic axial pull, together below ~1 kN — while a 47 mm groove in EN AC-46000 can carry over 10 kN. The ring is fitted by an automatic insertion head right after bearing press-in. Benchmark detail on 48 V BSGs could not be found; this is general practice applied to the BSG.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the retainer plate, three screws and lock washers, three drill-and-tap operations in the casting and three screwdriving/torque checks; adds one bevelled retaining ring and a groove turned in the existing bore set-up.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Machining: three drill and tap spindles freed (≈12 s), groove turned in the bore set-up (+3 s). Assembly: screw feeding and torque station replaced by an automatic ring insertion head with seated-ring sensing (≈5 s vs ≈15 s). No swarf from tapping near the bearing seat.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count 7 → 1 (plate, 3 screws, 3 washers → one ring). Ring seating is checked by a laser/vision sensor (ring fully in groove, gap within window) — poka-yoke against a half-seated ring. Service: ring removable with standard pliers; bearing replacement procedure simpler than three seized screws in aluminium.

costSavingPotential.percentage: 65-75 % of the drive-end bearing retention cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate, one machine per vehicle. Cost-bridge lines: Retainer plate (stamped DC01) €0.18→€0.00 (+0.18); Screws and lock washers (3 sets) €0.15→€0.00 (+0.15); Drill and tap three holes in end shield €0.20→€0.00 (+0.20); Screwdriving and torque audit → ring insertion €0.15→€0.05 (+0.10); Bevelled internal retaining ring €0.00→€0.10 (-0.10); Groove turning in bore set-up €0.00→€0.03 (-0.03). Net €0.50 per vehicle; range €0.45-€0.60 reflects supplier quote spread; × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €23K-€30K. Payback = (tooling €15000 + capex €40000 + validation €60000) ÷ (mid annual €26K ÷ 12) ≈ 53 months.

ideaData.riskNotes: A ring that is not fully seated or a groove edge that breaks out in porous die-cast aluminium can release the bearing axially; vibration fretting at the ring/groove may wear the softer aluminium. Validate: axial push-out test of ring retention (≥5 kN), porosity X-ray of the groove zone, ISO 16750-3 engine-mounted vibration, thermal cycling, and belt-load endurance with axial play measurement.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Vehicle alternator drive-end bearing retention (Delco Remy 24SI; US 4113326) — Drive-end bearing held by a retainer plate with three screws and lock washers torqued to 5-9 Nm. How this differs: Replaces the alternator-heritage plate with a bevelled internal retaining ring on the 48 V BSG front end shield — a general-practice proposal; no BSG supplier's retention method was confirmed.

engineering.mechanism: Axial load on the locating bearing: rotor + fans ≈2.5 kg × 30-40 g engine shock ≈ 0.75-1.0 kN peak; belt-misalignment thrust (0.5° at 2.5 kN hub load) ≈ 20-50 N; claw-pole axial magnetic pull from stack offset < 100 N. Groove capacity in aluminium: F ≈ π·d·t·σ_y/(q·S) = π × 47 × 1.5 × 140 / (1.2 × 2) ≈ 12.9 kN with a 1.5 mm groove depth, Rp0.2 ≈ 140 MPa (EN AC-46000) and a safety factor 2 — over 10× the demand. A 15° bevel on the ring and groove flank converts the ring's radial spring force into axial clamp, absorbing ±0.1 mm of stack tolerance without play.
engineering.specDeltas: Front end shield: delete 3 × M4 tapped holes and the plate seat face; add internal groove Ø49.4 H12 × 1.85 mm with 15° bevelled flank at the bearing outer face, edge break 0.2 mm, porosity class in groove zone per VDG P202 (≤ 0.5 mm pores). Delete P/Ns: retainer plate, 3 × M4×8 screws, 3 lock washers. Add: bevelled internal ring for bore 47 mm, C75S, phosphated. Assembly: ring insertion head with seating sensor; axial play of outer ring 0-0.02 mm.
engineering.validationPlan: Component: ring push-out ≥5 kN on 10 shields (incl. 3 from end-of-die-life castings), X-ray of groove zone on first-off and quarterly samples. Machine: ISO 16750-3 engine-mounted random vibration 22 h/axis on 6 machines, ISO 16750-4 thermal shock −40/+150 °C 300 cycles, FEAD belt-load endurance 1,000 h with axial play measured before/after (≤0.05 mm). PPAP: end-shield drawing change, process change (assembly), BOM deletions.
engineering.dfmImplications: Part count −6; three tapping spindles and their tap breakage (a classic aluminium scrap cause) removed; ring insertion is a 5 s automatic step with seating sensor. One groove tool added to the bore operation. Service is easier: no seized steel screws in aluminium threads.

Proposed ≈ €0.18 (insertion €0.05, ring €0.10, groove €0.03). Net ≈ €0.50 per vehicle. Not included: the bearing itself (unchanged), and scrap reduction from tap breakage beyond the stated line.

title: Lundell rotor with integral yoke bosses: separate pole core and one flux joint deleted
description: [MHEV] Deletes the separate pole core (part, facing, logistics) and one press operation; slightly lower ampere-turn demand trims field copper. Larger claw-half forgings cost more and are booked against the saving. Baseline (Lundell practice as described by EEP): the rotor has three magnetic parts — two pole-finger plates and a separate cylindrical yoke (pole core) inside the excitation coil, cold-headed or turned from 11SMn30 — all pressed onto a knurled shaft; the excitation coil sits on its bobbin around the yoke and is sandwiched between the plates. Every joint in the axial flux path (yoke-to-plate faces, two interfaces) adds a parasitic air gap of ~0.02-0.05 mm, and the yoke is a separate part with its own blank, facing operation, logistics flow and press step. Proposal: give each pole-finger plate an integral half-yoke boss in the same hot-working operation, so the rotor has two magnetic parts meeting at a single mid-plane joint inside the coil. The bobbin-wound coil is slipped over one boss before the second plate is pressed on. One part, one press operation and one magnetic interface are removed; the lower interface reluctance lets the same flux be reached with ~3 % fewer ampere-turns, trimmed as coil copper. ideaData.title: Lundell rotor with integral yoke bosses: separate pole core and one flux joint deleted
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (Lundell practice as described by EEP): the rotor has three magnetic parts — two pole-finger plates and a separate cylindrical yoke (pole core) inside the excitation coil, cold-headed or turned from 11SMn30 — all pressed onto a knurled shaft; the excitation coil sits on its bobbin around the yoke and is sandwiched between the plates. Every joint in the axial flux path (yoke-to-plate faces, two interfaces) adds a parasitic air gap of ~0.02-0.05 mm, and the yoke is a separate part with its own blank, facing operation, logistics flow and press step. Proposal: give each pole-finger plate an integral half-yoke boss in the same hot-working operation, so the rotor has two magnetic parts meeting at a single mid-plane joint inside the coil. The bobbin-wound coil is slipped over one boss before the second plate is pressed on. One part, one press operation and one magnetic interface are removed; the lower interface reluctance lets the same flux be reached with ~3 % fewer ampere-turns, trimmed as coil copper. Each plate blank becomes taller and ~0.12 kg heavier and needs ~15 % more press force, booked as an added cost. This is a magnetic-circuit and part-count lever, distinct from changing how the pole fingers are finished.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the separate pole core (part, facing, logistics) and one press operation; slightly lower ampere-turn demand trims field copper. Larger claw-half forgings cost more and are booked against the saving.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Claw forging dies redesigned for the integral boss (higher forging force, ~+15 %, same press class); core forging/turning line freed. Rotor assembly: three press steps → two. Facing of the mid-plane joint done on the claw halves in the same turning set-up as the claw bore.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Rotor magnetic part count 3 → 2; no core orientation step. The coil must be pre-wound on its bobbin (already the case) and slid over the boss. Poka-yoke: the two halves have different boss lengths if the joint is offset, preventing swapped assembly.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — one magnetic part and interface removed from every rotor
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate, one machine per vehicle. Cost-bridge lines: Separate pole core (forging + facing) €0.85→€0.00 (+0.85); Press-fit operations (3 → 2) €0.15→€0.10 (+0.05); Claw-half forgings with integral boss €2.50→€2.85 (-0.35); Field-coil copper (−3 % ampere-turns) €2.40→€2.33 (+0.07). Net €0.62 per vehicle; range €0.55-€0.75 reflects supplier quote spread; × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €28K-€38K. Payback = (tooling €140000 + capex €0 + validation €70000) ÷ (mid annual €33K ÷ 12) ≈ 78 months.

ideaData.riskNotes: Taller boss forging may suffer from fold defects or inadequate fill at the claw root; the mid-plane joint flatness (≤0.02 mm) must be held to avoid a new air gap. Validate: forging micro-structure and ultrasonic checks, magnetisation curve E(I_f) on 10 rotors vs baseline, overspeed burst, claw fatigue at max speed.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Lundell claw-pole rotor (EEP description); 48 V claw-pole BSG (Valeo iBSG) — Field coil wound coaxially and sandwiched from both sides by the pole cores inside interleaved claw poles. How this differs: Integrates the pole core into the claw-half forgings to delete a part and a flux interface; the construction of specific BSG rotors was not confirmed — general-practice proposal.

ideaData.materialGrade: Claw halves C10C (EN 10263-2) + separate C10C/11SMn30 core → two C10C claw halves with integral half-cores
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Three forgings/turnings + three press-fits → two warm forgings + two press-fits, joint faced in claw turning set-up
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Field MMF needed = Φ·ΣR_m; the main air gap (~0.35-0.4 mm × 2 crossings) dominates, but each core-to-claw interface adds an effective gap g_i ≈ 0.02-0.05 mm on a smaller area. Removing one of two interfaces cuts ~0.03 mm on the core cross-section, about 3-4 % of the total magnetic reluctance at operating flux, so the same E(I_f) is reached with ~3 % fewer ampere-turns. Forging: a C10C half with integral boss rises from ~0.45 kg to ~0.57 kg; warm forging at 750-850 °C keeps forging force inside the existing press class and gives a grain flow continuous from boss to claw root.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete pole core P/N and its press-fit spec. Claw-half drawing: add integral boss Ø_core × (L_core/2), joint face flatness 0.02 mm and perpendicularity 0.02 mm to bore, bore Ø shaft knurl unchanged; material C10C to EN 10263-2, warm forged, no fold >0.1 mm at boss root (UT check). Field coil: turns unchanged, wire Ø0.75 → Ø0.74 mm. Assembly: two press steps, force window per half.
engineering.validationPlan: Magnetic: E(I_f) excitation curve on 10 rotors per route at 1,500/6,000 rpm, acceptance ≥ baseline at 3 % lower I_f. Mechanical: burst/overspeed 24,000 rpm on 5 rotors, claw-tip fatigue at max speed (10⁷ cycles), forging UT and micro-sections on 30 parts. Machine: output current map and thermal on 3 machines. PPAP: forging die change, rotor re-PSW, deletion of core supplier.
engineering.dfmImplications: Magnetic parts 3 → 2; one press step and one part logistics flow gone. Forging dies rebuilt (~€140k for two halves); boss joint faced in the same turning set-up as the bore. Coil insertion order changes (coil over first half before second press).
engineering.costBridge: Baseline rotor magnetic parts ≈ €5.90 per rotor (core €0.85, press €0.15, claws €2.50, field copper €2.40). Proposed ≈ €5.28 (claws €2.85, press €0.10, copper €2.33). Net ≈ €0.62 per vehicle. Not included: shaft, slip rings and fans (unchanged), and freed capacity on the core line.

costBridgeLines.basis: 2 halves, +~0.12 kg each, +15 % forging force (added cost)

title: Tooth tips swaged shut over the BSG stator winding replace NMN slot-closure wedges
description: [MHEV] Deletes 48 NMN wedges per stator and the wedge cut/insert station; adds one swaging stroke with a segmented jig. Secondary benefit: lower claw-surface loss from a narrower slot opening. Baseline (general practice for a distributed-wound BSG stator, e.g. 48 slots for a 16-pole, q = 1 three-phase winding): after the winding is inserted, each slot is closed by a Nomex-Mylar-Nomex (NMN, ~0.25-0.35 mm) wedge or closing strip pushed axially into the slot neck, which retains the conductors against magnetic and vibration forces until impregnation and adds a little creepage distance to the air gap. That is 48 wedges cut, formed and inserted per stator on a dedicated station. Proposal: as in alternator practice described in US 6373163 and US 20150001984, plastically deform the tooth tips radially with a segmented swaging jig after insertion so the slot opening narrows from ~2.4-2.8 mm to ~0.8-1.0 mm, mechanically retaining the compacted winding; the slot liner remains and is folded over the conductors before swaging so it closes the slot on the insulation side. Wedges and the wedge-insertion station are deleted. At 48 V the creepage and clearance requirement to the core is tiny (tens of volts working), so the wedge has no insulation role that the liner and enamel do not already fulfil. A narrower slot opening also reduces the slot-ripple flux pulsation that heats the claw surfaces

That is 48 wedges cut, formed and inserted per stator on a dedicated station. Proposal: as in alternator practice described in US 6373163 and US 20150001984, plastically deform the tooth tips radially with a segmented swaging jig after insertion so the slot opening narrows from ~2.4-2.8 mm to ~0.8-1.0 mm, mechanically retaining the compacted winding; the slot liner remains and is folded over the conductors before swaging so it closes the slot on the insulation side. Wedges and the wedge-insertion station are deleted. At 48 V the creepage and clearance requirement to the core is tiny (tens of volts working), so the wedge has no insulation role that the liner and enamel do not already fulfil. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes 48 NMN wedges per stator and the wedge cut/insert station; adds one swaging stroke with a segmented jig. Secondary benefit: lower claw-surface loss from a narrower slot opening.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Wedge-insertion machine (indexing, 48 insertions ~25 s) replaced by a radial swaging press with segmented expanding jig (one stroke, ~6 s). Lamination tooth tips get a small notch/bendable lip designed into the stamping die (insert change).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −48 per stator; no wedge supply, cutting or storage of NMN rolls. Swaging also compacts the winding, aiding impregnation fill. Poka-yoke: press force-displacement window per stroke; slot-opening gauge after swaging (go/no-go pins).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — part and station deletion on every stator
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate, one machine per vehicle. Cost-bridge lines: NMN wedges (48 per stator) €0.55→€0.00 (+0.55); Wedge insertion station (cycle + depreciation) €0.35→€0.00 (+0.35); Radial swaging stroke €0.00→€0.15 (-0.15); Lamination die insert change amortised €0.00→€0.02 (-0.02). Net €0.73 per vehicle; range €0.60-€0.85 reflects supplier quote spread; × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €30K-€43K. Payback = (tooling €60000 + capex €90000 + validation €60000) ÷ (mid annual €36K ÷ 12) ≈ 70 months.

ideaData.riskNotes: Tooth-tip deformation could crack the liner or nick enamel, damage lamination coating (local iron loss) or leave springback that opens the slot. Validate: surge test 100 %, insulation resistance and hipot after swaging, slot-opening gauge, iron-loss ring test, ISO 16750-3 vibration on the impregnated stator, and NVH order check for slot harmonics.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Vehicle alternator stator practice (US 6373163; US 20150001984A1) — Slot openings narrowed after winding insertion by radially pressing and plastically deforming the tooth tips to retain the compacted winding. How this differs: Applies tooth-tip swaging to a 48 V BSG stator to delete NMN wedges; whether BSG suppliers already do so was not confirmed — general-practice proposal.

ideaData.materialGrade: NMN 6640 (Nomex-Mylar-Nomex) 0.30 mm wedges → none; tooth-tip lip in M330-35A lamination
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Axial wedge insertion (48 per stator) → single-stroke radial tooth-tip swaging
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Conductor retention: radial magnetic force on slot conductors at 250 A boost is F ≈ B_slot·I·L ≈ 0.05 T × 250 A × 0.035 m ≈ 0.4 N per conductor — small; vibration (30-40 g engine-mounted) of a ~6 g conductor bundle gives ~2-3 N, carried by a swaged lip of ~0.35 mm thickness easily. Slot-opening effect: the Carter coefficient k_c rises with slot-opening-to-gap ratio; reducing b_o from 2.6 to 1.0 mm with a 0.35 mm gap lowers k_c by ~8-12 %, reducing both the required field ampere-turns and the flux pulsation that drives eddy loss in the solid claw surfaces (pole-face loss ∝ (ΔB)²·f²).
engineering.specDeltas: Lamination: tooth tip gets a bendable lip 0.6 mm × 0.35 mm with a 0.2 mm relief notch (die insert). Stator drawing: delete wedge P/N (NMN 0.30 × 3.2 mm × stack + 2 mm) ×48 and the wedge note; add "slot opening after swaging 0.9 +0.2/−0.1 mm, liner folded closed before swaging". Process: radial swaging press, segmented jig 48 segments, force 25-35 kN window. Surge test threshold unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Process DV: 30 stators — slot opening gauge 100 %, liner/enamel micro-section on 5 stators (no cracks), insulation ≥100 MΩ at 500 V, hipot 1 kV 1 s, surge 1.0 kV. Magnetic: ring iron-loss and E(I_f) on 5 machines vs baseline. Durability: ISO 16750-3 vibration 22 h/axis on impregnated stators, thermal shock 500 cycles, NVH order check. PPAP: lamination die change, stator process change, wedge P/N deletion.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes 48 parts and an indexing station per stator; swaging press with segmented jig (~€90k) and die insert (~€60k). One stroke instead of 48 insertions; force-displacement monitored. Rework: none possible after swaging — insertion quality must be gated before (vision check).
engineering.costBridge: Baseline slot closure ≈ €0.90 per stator (wedges €0.55, insertion €0.35). Proposed ≈ €0.17 (swaging €0.15, die amortisation €0.02). Net ≈ €0.73 per vehicle. Not included: claw-loss/efficiency benefit and slightly lower field ampere-turns from the smaller slot opening.

costBridgeLines.basis: ~6 s press + segmented jig depreciation (added cost)

title: Grade 1 PEI/PAI magnet wire replaces Grade 2 on the 48 V stator
description: [MHEV] Lower wire price per kg from less enamel and higher enamelling line speed; slot-fill gain lets the stack shrink by ~2 %, saving laminations. Added inline inspection and tool maintenance are booked as costs. Baseline (general practice carried over from higher-voltage machines): the BSG stator is wound with IEC 60317-13 class 200 dual-coat wire (polyesterimide base + polyamide-imide overcoat) in Grade 2 build — e.g., multiple Ø1.0-1.3 mm wires in hand for the few-turn 48 V winding. Grade 2 roughly doubles the enamel thickness of Grade 1 (for Ø1.25 mm: increase ≈0.067-0.09 mm vs ≈0.04-0.05 mm). At 48 V (≤60 V operating, 70 V transient per ISO 21780) the turn-to-turn and phase-to-phase voltages are a few volts to tens of volts, two orders of magnitude below the partial-discharge inception of either build, so the thicker enamel is only buying mechanical robustness during insertion. Proposal: Grade 1 build of the same IEC 60317-13 dual-coat chemistry (MWS lists Grades 1, 2 and 3 for this wire), with the insertion tooling polished and a 100 % surge test kept. The thinner build costs less per kg (less enamel, faster enamelling line speed) and gives ~3 % more copper area in the same slot, which is used to shorten the active stack by ~2 % at equal current density.

ideaData.materialGrade: IEC 60317-13 class 200 PEI/PAI Grade 2 → same chemistry Grade 1 build
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Unchanged winding; polished insertion tooling; stack height −2 %
ideaData.regulatoryContext: ISO 21780 caps the 48 V system at 60 V operating / 70 V transient, which sets the insulation voltage stress.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Partial-discharge inception between enamelled wires (Paschen minimum ≈ 330-350 V peak in air) is far above any 48 V machine stress: worst-case phase-to-phase ≈ 70 V transient, turn-to-turn a few volts. Enamel thickness therefore matters only for mechanical damage and thermal ageing. For Ø1.25 mm wire, Grade 2 adds ~0.08 mm to the diameter vs ~0.045 mm for Grade 1: bare-copper fraction of a wire cross-section rises from (1.25/1.33)² = 0.883 to (1.25/1.295)² = 0.932, ≈ +5 % copper per wire envelope, ≈ +3 % net slot copper after liner and packing — taken as −2 % stack height at constant current density.
engineering.specDeltas: Wire spec: IEC 60317-13 Grade 2 → Grade 1, same nominal Ø, same class 200, breakdown voltage per IEC 60317-13 Grade 1 table; continuity per IEC 60851-5 ≤ 5 faults/30 m. Stator drawing: stack height e.g. 32.0 → 31.4 mm (−2 %), slot liner unchanged. Insertion tooling Ra ≤0.2 µm; surge test 1.0 kV, waveform-area difference limit 8 % → 6 %.
engineering.validationPlan: Wire lots: IEC 60851 continuity, elongation, springback, heat shock per lot (3 lots). Insulation system: thermal endurance per IEC 60034-18-21-style motorette test at 3 temperatures (≈ 1,000-5,000 h), or system-level UL 1446 record; ISO 16750-4 damp heat cyclic 21 days and thermal shock on 6 stators; ISO 16750-3 vibration; insulation ≥100 MΩ after 24 h soak. Machine: output and efficiency map on 3. PPAP: material change (IMDS update), stator drawing change.
engineering.dfmImplications: No new equipment; insertion tooling polishing schedule (weekly) and blade inspection; coloured spool flanges avoid mixing grades between lines. Die stack count changed for −2 % height. Rework window stays before impregnation via 100 % surge test.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline wire + stack + inspection ≈ €17.42 per stator. Proposed ≈ €17.10: wire −€0.32, stack −€0.08, tooling +€0.04, inspection +€0.04. Net ≈ €0.32 per vehicle. Not included: any copper saving beyond the stack-height trim, and the cost of the insulation-system requalification (in validation).

tighter surge criteria and wire-lot continuity checks (added cost)

title: BSG rotor shaft in air-cooled 38MnVS6 microalloyed steel replaces quenched-and-tempered 42CrMo4

title: Anti-creep O-ring-groove rear bearing replaces cast-in steel bearing sleeve in the BSG end shield
description: [MHEV] Deletes the steel sleeve, its preheating and robotic placement in the die, and insert-related casting scrap; machining aluminium is quicker than machining steel. engineering.mechanism: Interference loss from differential expansion: Δδ = d·(α_Al − α_steel)·ΔT = 35 mm × (23 − 11.5)×10⁻⁶ × 130 K ≈ 0.052 mm diametral at 150 °C from a 20 °C assembly — larger than any practical interference fit for a 35 mm OD outer ring (typical N7/K7 ≈ 0-0.03 mm), so a plain aluminium bore goes loose when hot and the rotating-load direction (belt pull acts on the front, rear sees a smaller radial load whose direction rotates with unbalance) drives creep. An O-ring with 15-20 % squeeze in a 1.2 mm groove keeps a radial preload and friction moment larger than the creep driving moment; JTEKT notes groove width is limited by stress at the groove base.

title: Slip-ring chamber cover moulded in PPA-GF33 with 2K TPE seal replaces die-cast aluminium cover
description: [MHEV] Moulding replaces die casting plus machining; the 2K seal replaces a separate gasket or FIPG bead; two screws and their torque operations are removed. Tooling is a 2K mould instead of a die-cast die. Baseline (general practice on a water-cooled BSG): the rear brush/slip-ring chamber is closed by a die-cast EN AC-46000 cover (~1.8-2.5 mm walls, ~120-160 g) with a machined sealing face, a formed-in-place or separate elastomer gasket, and four M5 screws; vehicle AC generators have long used a separate slip-ring cover (e.g. US 6710499). The cover carries no structural load and, where the chamber holds only brushes and the shaft-end magnet, needs no EMC shielding because the electronics sit in their own shielded compartment. Proposal: injection-moulded PPA-GF33 (heat-stabilised polyphthalamide, continuous use ~150-170 °C, low moisture uptake versus PA66) cover with a two-shot (2K) TPE-V sealing lip moulded on, two M5 screws plus two moulded snap hooks, an integrated ePTFE vent seat and moulded-in brush-wear inspection window. No machining; seal face is as-moulded (flatness ≤0.15 mm, controlled by rib design). Mass falls by ~60 % and brush-dust tracking is not an issue at 48 V on a material with CTI ≥ 400 V.

title: Class-180 polyester impregnating resin replaces class-200 polyesterimide in a water-jacketed BSG stator
description: [MHEV] Cheaper resin per kg at the same uptake, plus a lower cure temperature and shorter cure cycle that cut oven energy and free oven capacity; no change in parts, tooling or equipment. Baseline (general practice carried over from air-cooled alternators): the BSG stator is impregnated with a class 200 (220) polyesterimide (PEI) resin, the same thermal class as the IEC 60317-13 enamel, because an air-cooled alternator end winding can reach 200 °C hot-spot. In a water-jacketed 48 V machine — Audi uses a water-cooled belt alternator-starter — the stator is conduction-cooled to coolant at ≤105-115 °C, and the measured hot spot at max continuous generation typically sits around 150-170 °C (to be confirmed on the target machine). Proposal: keep the class 200 enamel (which carries the turn insulation) but switch the impregnating resin to a class 180 (H) unsaturated polyester or modified polyester resin (low-styrene or styrene-free) whose role is mechanical bonding, heat transfer and moisture protection. The class 180 resin costs less per kg and cures at a lower temperature (≈140-150 °C vs ≈160-170 °C), shortening the oven cycle. The insulation system (enamel + liner + resin) is requalified as a system, because thermal class is a system property, not a material property.

engineering.mechanism: Insulation life follows Arrhenius ageing: roughly halving for each 8-10 K above the rated temperature (Montsinger rule). A class 180 system rated for 20,000 h at 180 °C has ample life if the hot spot spends most of its life at 120-150 °C and only short peaks at 170 °C. Thermal path in a jacketed stator: end-winding hot spot ≈ T_coolant + P_cu,end × R_th; with 105 °C coolant, ~250 W in the end windings and R_th ≈ 0.2 K/W through resin and liner, the hot spot ≈ 155 °C. The resin carries the conductor bond and heat transfer, so its thermal conductivity (both ~0.2 W/m·K) and fill matter more than its thermal class.
engineering.specDeltas: Material spec: impregnating resin class 200 PEI (IEC 60464-type) → class 180 low-styrene unsaturated polyester, viscosity 300-600 mPa·s at 25 °C, gel time 6-10 min at 120 °C; cure profile 165 °C × 60 min → 145 °C × 50 min. Stator drawing: insulation system class note "200 (H+)" → "180 (H)", resin uptake 0.10-0.14 kg, bond strength ≥ 30 N at 180 °C (IEC 61033 method B). Enamel and liner unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Hot-spot mapping: 3 machines with 8 thermocouples, towing 3,500 kg grade, repeated boost, max continuous generation at 45 °C ambient — hot spot ≤ 165 °C. Thermal endurance: motorettes at 3 temperatures (e.g., 200/215/230 °C) per IEC 60034-18-21-style procedure, extrapolated ≥20,000 h at 180 °C. IEC 61033 bond strength; ISO 16750-4 damp heat and thermal shock; ISO 16750-3 vibration on 6 stators. PPAP: material change, IMDS, process (cure profile) change.
engineering.dfmImplications: No new equipment; oven program change and a bath-management routine. Cure cycle −10-15 % frees oven capacity. Resin drum colour tag and bath controller prevent mixing with the PEI resin still used on other machines in the plant.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline impregnation ≈ €1.32 per stator (resin €1.00, energy €0.18, oven share €0.12, bath control €0.02). Proposed ≈ €1.04 (resin €0.76, energy €0.13, oven €0.10, bath €0.05). Net ≈ €0.28 per vehicle. Not included: enamel (unchanged), labour (unchanged), VOC abatement cost reduction.

title: Legacy B+ radio-suppression capacitor on the BSG deleted; filtering moved onto the inverter DC-link
description: [MHEV] Removes a bought capacitor, its screw and lead, and an assembly operation; replaces it with two ceramic chip capacitors placed with the rest of the board. Baseline (alternator heritage, general practice): many belt machines carry a separate radio-interference suppression capacitor — a metal-can or moulded film capacitor of ~1-2.2 µF screwed to the housing with a lead to the B+ terminal — originally added to suppress diode-rectifier and brush noise for AM radio. On an integrated-electronics 48 V BSG the inverter already has a DC-link of several hundred µF to mF of low-ESL capacitance plus on-board Y-capacitors from the DC rails to the housing, which dominate the high-frequency impedance at the B+ terminal. Proposal: delete the external suppression capacitor, its bracket screw and lead, and add two small ceramic Y-capacitors (or adjust existing ones) on the inverter board close to the B+ busbar entry, so the CISPR 25 conducted-emission limits are met from the board. Brush noise, which the capacitor historically addressed, is filtered at the field bridge (see the excitation ideas). EMC of the integrated electronics is a known design driver, so the change is gated by a full CISPR 25 / ISO 11452 test on the vehicle and component.

engineering.mechanism: Conducted noise voltage at the B+ terminal is the noise current times the terminal impedance. A 2.2 µF film capacitor with ~15 nH lead has |Z| ≈ 0.1 Ω at 1 MHz and is inductive above ~1 MHz; the inverter DC-link (e.g. 4 × 220 µF polymer + 1 µF MLCC close to the switches) is ≪0.1 Ω across 150 kHz-30 MHz and sits a few cm from the B+ busbar, so in parallel it already dominates. The remaining requirement is the common-mode path to the housing, provided by board-mounted Y-capacitors (2 × 47-100 nF) with ≤2 nH loop inductance — more effective above 30 MHz than a leaded can capacitor.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete P/Ns: suppression capacitor 2.2 µF/100 V, M5 screw, B+ lead/clip. Board: add 2 × MLCC 100 nF/100 V X7R soft-termination (AEC-Q200) from B+ and B− to chassis pad within 10 mm of busbar entry. Spec: CISPR 25 class per OEM (e.g., class 3/5 in AM/FM bands) conducted and radiated; ISO 11452-2/-4 immunity unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Component EMC: CISPR 25 conducted (voltage and current method) and radiated (ALSE) on 3 machines in generation and motoring at 3 speeds; ISO 11452-2/-4 immunity. engineering.dfmImplications: Part count −3; one screw joint and a lead connection removed from the housing; two SMT placements added. No tooling. If EMC fails, fallback is a footprint for a larger board capacitor, kept in the layout as an option.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline suppression ≈ €0.73 per machine (capacitor €0.55, screw/lead €0.08, operation €0.10). Proposed ≈ €0.06 (two MLCCs). Net ≈ €0.67 per vehicle. Not included: EMC chamber time (in validation), and any change to the DC-link itself.

ideaData.title: PCB-embedded MOSFET dies replace discrete TOLL devices on IMS in BiSG inverter
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a typical 48 V belt-integrated starter-generator (BiSG) inverter for a 3.0 L inline-6 uses 12 packaged 80-100 V MOSFETs (TOLL or D2PAK-7, two in parallel per switch) soldered onto an aluminium insulated-metal substrate (IMS), a separate 6-layer FR4 control board with gate drivers and MCU, a board-to-board pin header between them, a dispensed thermal interface and a machined cold-plate area sized to the IMS footprint. Proposal: embed 12 bare OptiMOS-class 80 V dies (100 % electrically tested "standard cell" dies) inside a 6-layer power PCB using a chip-embedding process (p² Pack-type: die sintered/soldered to a copper leadframe, laminated into prepreg, contacted by laser-drilled, copper-plated microvias rather than wire bonds or package leads). Gate drivers, shunts and MCU sit on the outer layers of the same board, so the IMS, the board-to-board header and the separate control board are deleted. The physics: microvia contacting replaces package leads and bond wires, cutting commutation-loop inductance from roughly 8-12 nH (two packages plus IMS track) to around 2-3 nH, so turn-off overshoot at 600 A phase peak falls and switching can be faster at the same 80 V device rating; the die sits ~0.3 mm from the copper heat spreader, so junction-to-case resistance falls and the same phase current needs less silicon or less cold-plate area. Benchmark: Continental used Schweizer's Smart p² Pack with Infineon OptiMOS 5 dies in a 48 V starter generator for a European carmaker (production planned 2021) and the partners reported up to 60 % more electrical power than a conventionally built system. For our luxury SUV the same principle is applied to a 15-20 kW BiSG inverter at 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Money comes from deleting the semiconductor package value (leadframe, mould, test-in-package) of 12 devices, the aluminium IMS, the board-to-board connector and the separate control PCB, and from a smaller cold-plate machined area enabled by lower junction-to-coolant resistance; the embedded PCB itself is dearer and carries a die-yield risk premium.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Supplier SMT line loses 12 power-device placements, the IMS reflow pass and the board-to-board mating/press step; the embedding is done at the PCB maker (lamination, laser drilling, plating). Cycle time at module assembly falls by ~25 s. Scrap cost per bad board rises because dies are inside the laminate, so known-good-die sourcing is mandatory.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count falls by 15 (12 MOSFETs, IMS, header, control board → one PCB). One fixture instead of two, no B2B alignment poka-yoke, screw count to cold plate drops from 8 to 6. Not repairable at board level — the whole inverter is the service unit, as it already is in practice.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — removes an entire board and the device packages, but needs new supply chain
costSavingPotential.percentage: 4-5% of the BiSG inverter cost (~€190 baseline)
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Power semiconductors: 12 packaged MOSFETs → 12 bare tested dies €13.80→€9.60; Boards: IMS €9.50 + control FR4 €7.00 + B2B header €2.20 → one embedded-die 6-layer PCB €18.70→€17.40; TIM and cold-plate machining area €6.80→€4.60; Module assembly: device placement, B2B mating, screws €3.10→€1.60; Yield/scrap allowance for non-reworkable embedded board €0.40→€1.00. Net = €8.60 per vehicle; the range €7.50-€9.50 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €375K-€475K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: die-level failure cannot be reworked (yield), delamination at die/prepreg interface under thermal cycling, limited supplier base (single-source exposure). Prove with AQG 324 power cycling, LV 124 / ISO 16750-4 temperature cycling, IPC-TM-650 thermal stress on microvias, and a second-source plan for dies. Keep a TOLL-on-FR4 fallback layout until PPAP.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Continental 48 V starter generator for a European carmaker (SOP planned 2021), Schweizer Smart p² Pack with Infineon OptiMOS 5 — Power MOSFET dies embedded inside the PCB instead of soldered packages, giving reported up to 60 % more electrical power than a conventionally designed system. How this differs: We apply it to a luxury-SUV BiSG inverter with control electronics on the same embedded board (IMS and B2B header deleted); the board integration and our cost figures are our engineering estimate, not Continental's published data.

ideaData.materialGrade: Packaged 80-100 V Si MOSFETs (TOLL/D2PAK-7) on Al IMS (1.5 mm EN AW-5052 base, 2 W/mK dielectric) → bare 80 V Si MOSFET dies embedded in high-Tg FR4/prepreg (Tg ≥ 170 °C) with Cu leadframe and plated microvias
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Package solder reflow on IMS + separate FR4 control board + B2B press → die attach to Cu lead frame, lamination into 6-layer stack, laser microvia drilling and Cu plating, single SMT pass for drivers/MCU
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No homologation impact; functional safety work product (ISO 26262 hardware metrics) must be re-run for the new power stage.

engineering.mechanism: Commutation-loop inductance sets overshoot: ΔV = L·di/dt. With two TOLL packages in parallel on IMS, the loop is ~10 nH; at di/dt of 3 A/ns, overshoot is ~30 V, which forces 100 V devices on a 48 V bus whose LV 148 upper limit is 52-60 V. Embedding cuts loop L to ~2.5 nH (overshoot ~7.5 V), so an 80 V die with lower RDS(on) per mm² is usable. Thermally, the baseline chain is junction→case 0.4 K/W → solder 0.1 → IMS dielectric 0.6 → TIM 0.3 → cold plate 0.2 ≈ 1.6 K/W per device pair; the embedded die sits on a 0.3-0.5 mm Cu leadframe laminated over a thin isolation layer, giving roughly 1.0-1.1 K/W, i.e. ~30 % more current for the same 150 °C junction limit or ~25 % less cold-plate area at the same current.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: 12 × packaged MOSFET part numbers, IMS board (EN AW-5052 base + dielectric), 2 × 20-pin board-to-board header and the separate 6-layer control PCB. Add: 6-layer embedded-die PCB, 1.6-2.0 mm thick, high-Tg (≥170 °C) halogen-free laminate, 2 internal 105 µm power layers, 0.3-0.5 mm Cu leadframe per die, laser microvias Ø100-150 µm plated ≥20 µm Cu, ENIG or OSP finish on outer layers. Die spec: 80 V, ≤1.0 mΩ, front-side Cu metallisation for via contact, 100 % tested at wafer. Cold plate machined area reduced from ~95 × 70 mm to ~75 × 65 mm; flatness 0.05 mm.
engineering.validationPlan: Component: AQG 324 power cycling (ΔTj 100 K, ≥ 60k cycles, n = 6 per lot from 3 lots), temperature cycling −40/+125 °C 1,000 cycles per LV 124 / ISO 16750-4 (n = 6), damp heat 85 °C/85 % RH 1,000 h, microvia reliability per IPC-TM-650 2.6.27 (n = 30 coupons), cross-section after each test. System: ISO 16750-2 / LV 148 electrical tests, CISPR 25 class 5 emissions, ISO 26262 FMEDA update. Acceptance: ΔRDS(on) ≤ 5 %, no delamination in C-SAM. Full PPAP re-submission (new PCB supplier and process), ~12 months of validation.
engineering.dfmImplications: PCB maker takes on die placement and lamination; the inverter line removes one reflow pass, the IMS handling fixture and the B2B press station (~25 s cycle saved). Panelisation: 4-up embedded boards. Poka-yoke: die orientation is fixed at the PCB maker, not on our line. No board rework possible — scrap cost per reject rises, so incoming known-good-die and inline AOI of outer-layer assembly are mandatory.
engineering.costBridge: From a baseline power-and-control electronics cost of about €52 per vehicle (12 packaged MOSFETs, IMS, control PCB, header, TIM/cold-plate machining, assembly) we move to about €43.5. The die cost saving and board consolidation fund the dearer embedded PCB and a yield allowance. Not included: housing tooling changes beyond the cold-plate face, die second-sourcing qualification, and any efficiency benefit (fuel/CO2). Net of the bridge lines: €8.60 per vehicle; investment €600K pays back in ~17 months at the mid-point saving.
