ideaData.title: Delete in-circuit test on 48 V inverter and DC-DC boards: boundary-scan inside functional EOL
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: each 48 V BiSG inverter control/power PCBA and each 48/12 V DC-DC PCBA passes a bed-of-nails in-circuit test (ICT) after SMT — around 45 s per board with a dedicated vacuum fixture per board variant, 300-500 test pads, an ICT operator share and fixture maintenance — before a separate end-of-line (EOL) functional test of the closed unit. Proposal: delete the production ICT. Structural coverage moves to (1) 3D AOI and solder-paste inspection already on the SMT line, (2) IEEE 1149.1 boundary-scan run through the MCU JTAG port inside the existing functional tester (interconnect test of MCU, CAN transceiver, SBC and digital nets, plus flash programming), (3) MCU-driven analogue self-test at power-on — gate-driver bootstrap voltages, shunt amplifier offsets, NTC plausibility, DC-link voltage divider — reported over UDS, and (4) flying-probe ICT retained only for NPI, first-article and failure analysis. The governing logic: for a 48 V board where >80 % of placements are digital or MCU-observable, boundary-scan plus self-test covers the open/short faults that dominate escape statistics, while the few analogue parts are exercised functionally anyway. Test pads shrink from ~400 to ~40 JTAG/power pads, freeing board area. Boundary-scan suppliers state it can eliminate or reduce ICT time for programming and screening, and that ICT carries the cost of extensive test points and fixtures.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Saves ICT machine time and operator share, ICT fixture build and revision cost per board variant, and PCB area occupied by test pads; adds boundary-scan licences, development of BSDL-based test programs and a small increase in functional test duration.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes two ICT stations (one per board family) and their fixtures; functional tester gains a JTAG controller and ~8 s per board. Line balance improves because ICT was the bottleneck at 45 s against a 38 s SMT takt. Flying-probe kept offline for NPI and FA.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Design-for-test rule changes: JTAG header pads on every board, MCU boundary-scan chain enabled in production firmware boot, test pads reduced ~90 %. No fixtures to change per variant — variant handling moves into software. Poka-yoke: tester reads board DMC and selects test program.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — steady test-cost reduction across two board families
costSavingPotential.percentage: 25-35% of PCBA test cost for the 48 V power electronics
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: ICT machine + operator time (2 boards × 45 s) €1.80→€0.32; ICT fixture amortisation and revisions €1.00→€0.10; PCB area for test pads €0.30→€0.10; Boundary-scan licence + program maintenance €0.00→€0.15; Escape/rework allowance €0.40→€0.50. Net = €2.33 per vehicle; the range €2.00-€2.60 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €100K-€130K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: lower analogue coverage (wrong-value resistors, reversed polarised caps, gate resistor values) could escape. Mitigate with AOI polarity/OCR checks, functional measurement of switching waveforms, and a 3-month parallel run (ICT and new strategy on all boards) to prove escape rate ≤ 10 ppm. Quality agreement per IATF 16949 control plan update.

engineering.mechanism: Escape probability is set by fault spectrum × coverage. Typical SMT fault spectrum on automotive PCBAs is dominated by opens/shorts on fine-pitch ICs and missing/misaligned parts (~70-80 % of defects); these are covered by 3D AOI (placement, polarity, solder fillet) and by boundary-scan interconnect test of MCU-connected nets (~250 of ~400 nets on the inverter control section). Remaining analogue nets (gate resistors 2.2-10 Ω, shunt amplifier gain resistors 0.1 %, bootstrap capacitors) are verified functionally: the MCU measures bootstrap voltage (12 V ±0.5 V) and amplifier offset (±5 mV) at power-up and the tester measures switching rise time 20-60 ns. Target combined coverage ≥ 95 % of the ICT fault list.
engineering.specDeltas: PCB: test pads reduced from ~400 to ~40 per board; JTAG pads (TCK/TMS/TDI/TDO/TRST) Ø1.0 mm on 2.54 mm grid added. Firmware: production boot mode exposing boundary-scan and self-test UDS routines (RID 0x0200-0x0210). Test spec: functional EOL extended by 8 s per board; ICT program and two vacuum fixtures retired. Control plan: AOI false-call threshold and polarity OCR mandatory on all polarised parts; flying-probe on first 50 boards of each lot change.
engineering.validationPlan: Coverage analysis: fault-list comparison ICT vs new strategy (all nets, target ≥ 95 %). Seeded-defect study: 50 boards per family with deliberately introduced faults (opens, shorts, wrong values, reversed parts), acceptance ≥ 98 % detection of seeded defects. Parallel run 3 months (~25,000 boards) with both ICT and new strategy, acceptance ≤ 10 ppm ICT-only detections. Gauge R&R on new functional measurements (≤ 10 %). PPAP: process change notification and control-plan update; no product re-qualification as design is unchanged except pads.
engineering.dfmImplications: Two ICT fixtures (~€45k each) and fixture revisions per ECO disappear; variant changes become program changes. Fewer pads ease routing on dense control sections. Handling: one fewer board load/unload per board. Failure analysis moves to flying probe, slower but only for rejects.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (one inverter board and one DC-DC board) ICT machine/operator time of about €1.80 falls to about €0.32 of added functional-test time; fixture amortisation €1.00 falls to €0.10; pad area €0.30 to €0.10; boundary-scan licence/program cost adds €0.15 and an escape allowance adds €0.10. Not included: one-off seeded-defect study labour, and any residual value of retired ICT machines. Net of the bridge lines: €2.33 per vehicle; investment €180K pays back in ~19 months at the mid-point saving.

costBridgeLines.item: ICT machine + operator time (2 boards × 45 s)
costBridgeLines.basis: 90 s at €1.20/min loaded → 16 s extra functional test

ideaData.title: Retire 100% powered burn-in of 48 V inverter and DC-DC via PAT and ORT
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: many tier-1 lines run a 100 % powered burn-in (run-in) on new power electronics — typically 2-4 h at 70-85 °C ambient with the unit switching at partial load — to precipitate infant-mortality failures (weak die, marginal solder joints, cracked MLCCs) before shipment. For a 48 V BiSG inverter and a 48/12 V DC-DC at 50,000 vehicles/yr that is ~100,000 units × 4 h in heated racks, with racks, floor space, energy, loading labour and a day of WIP. Proposal: retire 100 % burn-in once evidence shows it does not precipitate failures: (1) require AEC-Q001 part average testing (PAT) and dynamic PAT on MOSFETs, gate drivers and MCU so electrical outliers are removed at the semiconductor supplier, (2) use AEC-Q100/Q101 early-life failure-rate (ELFR) data — burn-in is not mandatory when ELFR is acceptable, (3) add process controls that target the real board-level infant failures (3D SPI, void X-ray sampling, MLCC flex-crack risk via depanelling strain gauging), and (4) keep an ongoing reliability test (ORT): 1-in-50 units through a 24 h temperature-cycled run with monitoring. Physics: burn-in at 85 °C accelerates only thermally activated mechanisms (Ea ≈ 0.7 eV, acceleration ~10-15× vs 40 °C), so 4 h ≈ 40-60 field hours — it screens a narrow band of defects that PAT and process control already catch at lower cost.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes burn-in rack depreciation, floor space, energy, load/unload labour and one day of WIP for two units per vehicle; adds a small PAT premium on key semiconductors and the ORT sample cost.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes ~60 burn-in rack positions per unit type and the associated conveyor/loading cell; frees ~150 m² floor space; shortens lead time by ~1 day. ORT bench retained (small). No change to SMT or assembly cycle.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No product part change. Line simplification: two fewer handling operations per unit (load/unload burn-in), fewer connector mating cycles on the product (burn-in harness contact wear), lower risk of handling damage. Traceability: ORT samples selected by MES randomly.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — pure process cost removal, gated by fallout data
costSavingPotential.percentage: 1-1.5% of combined inverter + DC-DC conversion cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Burn-in rack depreciation + floor space €1.60→€0.10; Burn-in energy €0.22→€0.01; Load/unload labour €0.80→€0.04; One-day WIP carrying cost €0.15→€0.00; PAT premium on 4 semiconductors + ORT samples €0.00→€0.35. Net = €2.27 per vehicle; the range €2.00-€2.60 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €100K-€130K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: rising 0-km / early field failures if a latent mechanism is not screened by PAT or process control. Mitigation: 6-month step-down (100 % → 25 % → 1-in-50) with Weibull analysis of burn-in fallout (must be zero failures in ≥ 20,000 units to justify), warranty early-warning on 3-month-in-service (3MIS) data, AEC-Q001 PAT contract with suppliers, ISO 16750 conformance unchanged.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: AEC-Q001 Rev-D / AEC-Q100 Rev-J (Automotive Electronics Council, 2011/2023) — Statistical part average testing removes outlier semiconductors; burn-in is not mandatory when early-life failure rate data are acceptable. How this differs: We use the AEC framework to justify deleting the module-level burn-in on the 48 V power electronics; the burn-in baseline is described as general tier-1 practice, not attributed to a named supplier.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Assembly → EOL → 4 h powered burn-in at 85 °C → final test → ship ⟶ Assembly → EOL → ship, with 1-in-50 ORT (24 h, −40/+105 °C cycling, powered)
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No regulatory impact; the change is a PPAP process change notified to the OEM.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Arrhenius acceleration AF = exp[(Ea/k)(1/T_use − 1/T_stress)]. With Ea = 0.7 eV, T_use = 313 K, T_stress = 358 K, AF ≈ 13, so a 4 h burn-in equals ~52 h of 40 °C operation — a tiny fraction of a 15-year / 8,000 h life and only effective on thermally activated die defects. Solder-joint and MLCC infant failures are driven by mechanical strain (ΔT cycling, flex), which steady 85 °C does not exercise. If the burn-in fallout over the last 20,000 units is zero, the 90 % upper confidence on the fallout rate is 2.3/20,000 = 115 ppm, falling to ≈ 23 ppm after 100,000 units; PAT at the die level removes ±6σ outliers that represent most of the early-failure population.
engineering.specDeltas: Control-plan deletion of operation 70 (burn-in, 4 h at 85 °C, 30 % load). Supplier quality requirements: AEC-Q001 static and dynamic PAT on MOSFET, gate driver, SBC and MCU part numbers; ELFR report per AEC-Q100 B2 (n ≥ 800 × 3 lots). Add ORT: 1-in-50 units, 24 h powered, −40/+105 °C cycling at 5 K/min, functional check before/after. Depanelling strain limit ≤ 500 µε near MLCCs (strain-gauged router validation).
engineering.validationPlan: Data gate: burn-in fallout analysis on ≥ 20,000 units per product with zero relevant failures; failure analysis on any fallout. Step-down validation: 100 % → 25 % sample for 3 months (~12,500 units) → 1-in-50 ORT. Supplier ELFR evidence per AEC-Q100 test B2 (3 lots × 800). Field watch: 3MIS and 12MIS warranty rate tracked against baseline with trigger ≥ 1.5× to reinstate burn-in. PPAP: process change, no product re-qualification.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes burn-in harness interface (connector wear on product pins after up to 10 matings from repeated tests), rack loading poka-yoke and WIP storage. Floor space ~150 m² released. Fewer operator touches per unit (2 fewer). ORT bench is a small fixed asset already in place.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (inverter + DC-DC): rack depreciation and floor space €1.60 to €0.10 (ORT only), energy €0.22 to €0.01, load/unload labour €0.80 to €0.04 and WIP carrying €0.15 to zero; PAT premium and ORT add €0.35. Not included: any warranty cost change (assumed neutral) and the residual value of sold racks. Net of the bridge lines: €2.27 per vehicle; investment €150K pays back in ~16 months at the mid-point saving.

title: THT-free 48 V power PCBAs: press-fit headers and terminals delete selective soldering
description: [MHEV] Selective-solder machine time, nitrogen, flux and solder wire, post-solder visual inspection and touch-up, and flux-residue cleanliness checks are removed; press-fit operation time and a small press-fit pin premium are added. Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter and DC-DC PCBAs each carry through-hole parts — the sealed LV signal header (16-24 pins), 48 V/12 V power terminal blocks or busbar pins and sometimes radial DC-link capacitors — soldered on a mini-wave selective soldering machine after reflow (~55 s per board machine time, nitrogen, flux, nozzle wear, plus post-solder inspection and touch-up). Signal headers and power terminals change to press-fit compliant-pin versions (eye-of-needle pins per IEC 60352-5) pressed by a servo press with force-displacement monitoring; any remaining radial parts move to SMD (polymer-hybrid caps) or pin-in-paste reflow. ideaData.title: THT-free 48 V power PCBAs: press-fit headers and terminals delete selective soldering
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter and DC-DC PCBAs each carry through-hole parts — the sealed LV signal header (16-24 pins), 48 V/12 V power terminal blocks or busbar pins and sometimes radial DC-link capacitors — soldered on a mini-wave selective soldering machine after reflow (~55 s per board machine time, nitrogen, flux, nozzle wear, plus post-solder inspection and touch-up). Proposal: make both boards THT-free. Signal headers and power terminals change to press-fit compliant-pin versions (eye-of-needle pins per IEC 60352-5) pressed by a servo press with force-displacement monitoring; any remaining radial parts move to SMD (polymer-hybrid caps) or pin-in-paste reflow. The line becomes SPI → place → single reflow → 3D AOI → press-fit → test, with no selective-solder step. Physics: a compliant pin creates a cold-welded gas-tight contact with 30-60 N retention per pin and contact resistance below ~0.2 mΩ, independent of solder wetting into the thick 105 µm copper planes that make THT soldering of 48 V boards difficult (heavy copper sinks heat, causing incomplete barrel fill). TE and Vincotech state press-fit removes selective soldering of connectors on double-sided boards, is used in automotive control units and power inverters, and allows replacement of a press-fit part up to three times on the same PCB.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Selective-solder machine time, nitrogen, flux and solder wire, post-solder visual inspection and touch-up, and flux-residue cleanliness checks are removed; press-fit operation time and a small press-fit pin premium are added.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Two selective soldering stations removed (one per board family); two servo press cells added (12 s cycle each, force-displacement curve per pin row). Takt improves as selective soldering (55 s) was a bottleneck. No thermal stress on boards after reflow; heavy-copper barrel fill issues disappear.
ideaData.dfmDfa: PCB hole tolerance tightens (finished hole Ø1.00 +0.05/−0.05 mm for 0.64 mm pins, Sn or immersion-Ag finish). Support tool under board for press-in. Press-fit pins are reworkable up to three times (repairability improves vs desoldering). Poka-yoke: keyed connector and force-window reject.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — line simplification; payback limited by press capex
costSavingPotential.percentage: 8-12% of PCBA conversion cost for the two boards
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Selective-solder machine time → press-fit time €1.65→€0.28; Solder wire, flux, nitrogen, nozzle wear €0.30→€0.00; Press-fit pin premium on headers/terminals €3.40→€3.65; Post-solder inspection and touch-up €0.45→€0.10; Flux residue cleanliness checks €0.20→€0.00. Net = €1.97 per vehicle; the range €1.70-€2.20 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €85K-€110K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: PCB barrel cracks or plating damage from press-in force, whisker growth on Sn-plated pins, fretting under engine vibration. Validate per IEC 60352-5 (insertion/retention, cross-section, current), LV 124 / ISO 16750-3 vibration (engine-mounted profile), ISO 16750-4 thermal shock, and 1,000 h 85/85 humidity. Mitigation: immersion-Ag finish, press-fit-qualified laminate.

ideaData.materialGrade: SnPb-free selective-solder joint (SAC305 wire) → CuSn4 / CuNiSi compliant pins, Sn or Ag plated, in PTH with immersion-Sn/Ag finish
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Reflow → selective mini-wave solder (55 s, N2) → inspection/touch-up ⟶ reflow → servo press-fit with force-displacement monitoring (12 s); remaining THT by pin-in-paste
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No regulatory impact.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Selective soldering of 105 µm copper plane connections needs ≥ 75 % barrel fill (IPC-A-610 class 3); heavy copper conducts heat away (copper k = 390 W/mK) so pre-heat and dwell rise to 4-6 s per joint, and fill failures drive touch-up of ~2-4 % of joints. A compliant pin instead deforms elastically in a Ø1.00 mm hole: normal force 100-200 N per pin produces a gas-tight cold-weld zone, insertion force ~100-150 N/pin, retention ≥ 30 N, contact resistance ≤ 0.2 mΩ, unaffected by plane thermal mass. Current capability for a 0.64 mm pin is ~10 A per pin at 40 K rise; 48 V terminals use 4-8 pins or wider press-fit blades.
engineering.specDeltas: Connector: sealed 16-24 way header with THT pins → same housing with eye-of-needle CuSn4 pins, Sn 1-3 µm over Ni. Power terminals: THT terminal blocks → press-fit multi-pin blades (e.g. 6 × 1.0 mm pins per terminal). PCB: finished hole Ø1.00 ±0.05 mm, plating ≥ 25 µm Cu, surface finish immersion-Sn or immersion-Ag (replacing OSP near press-fit zones), keep-out 3 mm around pins for press support. Process: selective solder program, flux and N2 deleted; servo press 0-20 kN with force/displacement window per pin row.
engineering.validationPlan: IEC 60352-5 full test sequence: insertion/push-out force (n = 50 pins), micro-section of PTH (n = 10), contact resistance after 1,000 h at 125 °C dry heat and after thermal shock −40/+125 °C 500 cycles (ISO 16750-4), mixed flowing gas (n = 20). Vibration: ISO 16750-3 engine-mounted profile 22 h/axis with continuity monitoring (≤ 1 µs interruption). Whisker check per JESD201. PPAP: product change on connector and PCB finish, ~6 months validation.
engineering.dfmImplications: Two selective-solder stations and their programs/nozzles removed; press cell needs a board-specific support plate (~€15k each) and a tool per connector. No flux residue, so no cleanliness/ionic test on THT area. Press-fit rework (pull and re-press up to 3 times) replaces desoldering, improving FA and repair yield.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (two boards): selective-solder machine time €1.65 is replaced by €0.28 of press time; solder/flux/N2 €0.30 and cleaning €0.20 disappear; inspection/touch-up €0.45 falls to €0.10; press-fit pins add €0.25 to connector cost. Not included: the residual value of the existing selective solderers and any harness-side connector change. Net of the bridge lines: €1.97 per vehicle; investment €390K pays back in ~48 months at the mid-point saving.

ideaData.title: Lockstep MCU plus safety SBC delete the second monitoring MCU in 48 V inverter
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a common 48 V BiSG inverter control architecture for an ASIL-rated torque path uses a main 32-bit MCU (single core or dual core without lockstep) running field-oriented control, plus a small independent monitoring MCU (or "watchdog processor") that checks torque plausibility and can force safe state, plus a discrete reset supervisor and external window watchdog IC, and three linear regulators fed from a pre-regulator for 5 V / 3.3 V / 1.25 V rails and the CAN transceiver supply. Proposal: one lockstep-core automotive MCU (e.g. AURIX TC3xx-class, where up to four CPUs have lockstep partners so ASIL-D software runs without cyclic CPU self-tests) paired with a safety system-basis chip / PMIC (TLF35584-class: multi-rail supply, configurable functional and window watchdog, error-pin monitoring of the MCU fault-signalling output, two safe-state outputs and input-voltage monitoring). The independent monitoring path that the second MCU provided is replaced by the lockstep comparison (detects random CPU faults instantly) plus the SBC's independent watchdog and safe-state outputs that directly disable the gate drivers. Monitoring software (level-2 torque monitor, E-Gas-style 3-level concept) runs in a separate, freedom-from-interference partition on the lockstep core. The independent monitoring MCU, its crystal, flash programming step, supervisor and watchdog ICs, and ~40 passives are deleted.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes a second MCU, its oscillator and passives, a supervisor and watchdog IC, and the separate regulator chain; the main MCU moves to a slightly dearer lockstep variant and the SBC replaces the regulators. Software maintenance of a second firmware image disappears.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: About 45 fewer placements on the control section, one fewer flash-programming step at EOL (second MCU), smaller board area (~12 cm²). No line equipment change.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −45, one firmware image instead of two (simpler variant/configuration management, one OTA payload), fewer test points. The safe-state path is hardware-simple: SBC safe-state pins wired to gate-driver enable.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — BOM and complexity cut, needs safety case rework
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Monitoring MCU + crystal €1.40→€0.00; Voltage supervisor + external window watchdog €0.85→€0.00; Main MCU → lockstep variant €6.20→€7.10; Regulators + CAN supply → safety SBC €2.60→€2.40; Passives, PCB area and placements €0.95→€0.50; Second firmware image maintenance (amortised) €0.30→€0.05. Net = €2.25 per vehicle; the range €1.90-€2.50 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €95K-€125K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: common-cause failures (shared supply, clock) must be argued in the ISO 26262 dependent-failure analysis; achieving SPFM ≥ 99 % / LFM ≥ 90 % for the ASIL target needs the SBC voltage monitors and MCU safety mechanisms configured. Validate with FMEDA, fault-injection on HIL, ISO 26262-5 hardware metrics review by assessor, LV 124 / ISO 16750-2 supply tests.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Infineon AURIX TC3xx with TLF35584 safety supply (reference architecture, 2018-2024) — Lockstep CPU cores allow ASIL-D software without cyclic CPU self-test; TLF35584 provides window watchdog, MCU error monitoring and two safe-state outputs as the independent monitor. How this differs: We apply this supplier reference architecture to replace a two-MCU 48 V inverter controller on the luxury SUV; the baseline two-MCU design is described as general practice, not attributed to a specific supplier.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Two MCUs + discrete supervisor/watchdog + 3 LDOs → one lockstep MCU + one safety SBC/PMIC
ideaData.regulatoryContext: ISO 26262 safety case must be re-assessed; no homologation impact.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: ISO 26262 requires an independent monitor able to detect faults of the function processor. A second MCU provides diversity but adds a full fault-tree branch. A lockstep core pair compares outputs every cycle with ~1-2 cycle latency, detecting random hardware faults in the CPU with diagnostic coverage ≥ 99 %; the SBC window watchdog (open window e.g. 10-50 ms) detects program-flow and clock faults independently, and its supply monitors (±3-5 % over/undervoltage thresholds) cover common-cause supply faults. Safe-state reaction time: SBC asserts safe-state within ~10 ms, gate drivers disabled in < 1 µs, well within a typical 50-100 ms fault-tolerant time interval for unintended torque at the crankshaft.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: monitoring MCU (16/32-bit, 64-128 kB flash) + 8-16 MHz crystal, voltage supervisor, external window watchdog IC, three LDOs (5 V/3.3 V/1.25 V), ~40 passives. Change: main MCU to lockstep variant in same family/package (pin-compatible where possible). Add: safety SBC/PMIC with integrated CAN supply, window watchdog, two safe-state outputs (SS1/SS2) wired to gate-driver ENABLE and to the phase short-circuit / freewheel selection. engineering.validationPlan: FMEDA and dependent-failure analysis (ISO 26262-5/-9) with assessor review; target SPFM ≥ 99 %, LFM ≥ 90 %, PMHF < 10 FIT for the ASIL C/D torque goal. engineering.dfmImplications: One firmware flash step deleted at EOL (saves ~6 s), one fewer crystal (shock-sensitive part) on board, board area −12 cm² enabling a smaller control section. Variant handling simplified (single image). No fixture changes beyond ICT/boundary-scan program update.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a typical 48 V BiSG inverter carries one NTC per half-bridge leg on the power stage, a separate coolant-inlet NTC probe with its own two connector pins and seal, three phase-voltage divider/filter channels with a comparator for open-phase and short-circuit-to-ground detection, and a hardware over-temperature comparator. Proposal: (1) a single board NTC at the thermal centre of the power stage plus a real-time thermal observer (Foster RC network, 3-4 poles per leg, identified from Zth measurement) estimates each MOSFET junction temperature from measured phase currents, duty and the RDS(on)(T) curve, with coolant temperature taken from the engine ECU over CAN (the BiSG cooling circuit is the engine circuit) and cross-checked against the NTC at standstill; (2) open-phase, phase-to-ground and phase-to-phase faults are diagnosed from the current-signature (three-phase current sum, missing-phase pattern under a test vector at start-up, and expected-vs-measured current response to injected d-axis pulses) rather than from phase-voltage dividers; (3) the hardware over-temperature comparator is replaced by the observer plus the safety SBC plausibility check. This is relevant off-road: during low-speed crawling and towing 3,500 kg up a gradient the BiSG may run high current at low speed with poor airflow; the observer tracks each junction individually (a single NTC cannot see a hot single leg at near-zero electrical frequency), so derating is applied to the hot leg rather than conservatively to the whole machine.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes probe insertion and sealing at assembly (~15 s), ~25 SMD placements and two connector pins; EOL adds a 3 s Zth self-calibration (injected DC current pulse, temperature rise logged) to personalise the observer per unit.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −30 (probe, seal, pins, NTCs, dividers, comparator). One less housing port to machine and seal (also one less wading leak path). Connector pin count drops by two. Calibration per unit runs automatically at EOL.

How this differs: SEG does not state it uses thermal observers; we use the CAN-networked, re-flashable controller principle to replace sensing hardware with model-based diagnostics. The specific deletions are our engineering proposal.

engineering.mechanism: Junction temperature Tj = Tcoolant + P·Zth(t). With P = I²·RDS(on)(Tj) + switching loss, at 400 A rms per switch pair and 0.9 mΩ effective, conduction loss is ~144 W per switch, and Zth junction-to-coolant ~0.25 K/W steady gives ~36 K rise. A 3-pole Foster network identified on the bench predicts Tj within ±5 K across load steps. A single NTC 10 mm from a leg sees a thermal lag of 2-5 s and up to 20 K under-read when one leg is loaded at near-zero electrical frequency (crawling, locked-rotor boost); hence the per-leg observer is more accurate than a per-leg NTC during transients. Open-phase: with a 10 µs injected d-axis pulse, expected di/dt = V/L ≈ 48 V/20 µH = 2.4 A/µs; a missing phase shows zero response, detectable within 1 ms.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: coolant-inlet NTC probe (brass sleeve, O-ring, 2 connector pins, M12 port machining), 2 of 3 leg NTCs and filters, 3 phase-voltage divider chains (2 × 0.1 % resistors + RC each), window comparator and level shifter, hardware OT comparator. Keep: 1 NTC at power-stage centroid. Add: thermal observer (Foster 3-pole per leg, calibrated coefficients in NVM), CAN signal coolant temperature from engine ECU (100 ms cycle, E2E-protected per AUTOSAR profile), start-up phase test vector, EOL Zth calibration routine (3 s, 50 A DC pulse).
engineering.validationPlan: Bench: thermocouple/IR-instrumented open unit, 200 load cycles across −40/+105 °C coolant, acceptance observer error ≤ ±5 K at junction (n = 5 units, 3 lots). HIL: 300 injected faults (open phase, phase short to housing, coolant loss), 100 % detection within FTTI. Vehicle: hot-climate tow test 3,500 kg at 12 % grade, 50 °C, 10 cycles; off-road crawl 1-5 km/h 30 min. ISO 26262 FMEDA update. Software re-qualification and PPAP product change (~9 months).
engineering.dfmImplications: One housing port, one O-ring and one probe press/seal operation deleted (~15 s and a leak-test risk). ~25 placements removed. Two pins removed from the LV connector. EOL adds a 3 s automated calibration — net cycle time falls. Serviceability: fewer parts to diagnose in the field.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: leg NTC channels €0.36 to €0.12, phase-voltage sense €0.95 to zero, OT comparator €0.30 to zero, coolant probe with seal and pins €1.60 to zero, placements/area €0.30 to €0.10; firmware development amortised adds €0.20. Not included: engine-ECU software change for CAN coolant signal (assumed existing signal) and any efficiency gain from less conservative derating. Net of the bridge lines: €3.09 per vehicle; investment €275K pays back in ~22 months at the mid-point saving.

ideaData.title: Laser-welded EN AW-4047 lid replaces FIPG bead and twelve screws on 48 V units
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter and the 48/12 V DC-DC typically close a die-cast EN AC-46000 housing with a machined die-cast cover, a robot-dispensed formed-in-place silicone gasket (FIPG, ~4 g bead, room-temperature or heat-accelerated cure) and 10-14 M5 screws torqued on a multi-spindle station, followed by a pressure-decay leak test. FIPG adds a cure WIP buffer, bead-vision inspection and a gasket-failure leak path that matters on an off-road SUV that wades and is pressure-washed underbody. Proposal: housing frame cast in vacuum HPDC AlSi10MnMg (low-Cu, low-porosity flange, weldable) with a machined 1.5 mm weld flange; lid stamped from 1.5 mm EN AW-4047 (Al-12Si, directly laser-weldable to Al-Si castings without hot cracking) or EN AW-3003 with 4047 filler wire; continuous fibre-laser seam weld (4 kW, wobble head, ~6 m/min, ~35 s per unit), then helium-free pressure-decay leak test. Screws, FIPG, bead inspection and cure WIP are deleted. Physics: a fusion seam is a monolithic metallic seal — no elastomer compression set, no relaxation over −40/+125 °C cycling — and patent literature for transmission controllers notes that gasket-and-screw designs often leak from gasket failure, while laser sealing protects against moisture, oils and ATF. The pressure-compensation vent stays (see separate vent idea) because a sealed volume still breathes with temperature. The unit becomes non-openable; both 48 V units are already replaced, not repaired, in service.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes FIPG material, dispensing and cure, 12 screws and torque station per unit, and replaces a machined die-cast cover with a stamped sheet lid; adds laser-weld cell time, a vacuum-HPDC weldable frame premium and slightly higher service-replacement cost because units can no longer be opened.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One laser cell (fixture, fibre laser, fume extraction, seam tracking) replaces the FIPG dispense robot, cure buffer and screw station on both lines. Cycle ~35 s vs ~70 s for dispense+cure-handling+screwing. Cover die-casting tool and machining operation replaced by a progressive stamping tool.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −13 per unit (cover becomes lid, 12 screws gone, gasket bead gone). Fixture clamps lid flat to ≤ 0.1 mm gap. Poka-yoke: lid orientation tab, seam vision. Serviceability: unit is not openable — acceptable as the whole unit is the service part.

engineering.mechanism: FIPG silicone seals by compression (20-30 % squeeze); compression set after 1,000 h at 125 °C is typically 20-40 %, and with ±0.1 mm flange flatness the effective squeeze can fall below the threshold where 10 kPa wading/pressure-wash differential is held. A laser fusion seam of 1.2-1.5 mm width and ≥ 0.8 mm penetration gives a metallic joint with shear strength > 100 MPa, no compression set. Hot-cracking susceptibility of Al-Mg-Si is high at 0.5-1.5 % Si; using AlSi10MnMg frame and 4047 (12 % Si) lid moves the weld pool to ~10-12 % Si, outside the crack-sensitive band. Heat input ~40 J/mm limits flange temperature 8 mm inboard to < 150 °C for < 2 s.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: HPDC EN AC-46000 cover (tool and machining), FIPG silicone (e.g. ~4 g bead, 3 × 2 mm), 12 × M5 × 12 8.8 screws and threaded bosses (12 tapped holes), bead vision step. Change housing to vacuum HPDC AlSi10MnMg (Cu ≤ 0.03 %, porosity ≤ 1 % in flange zone per X-ray class), flange machined to 1.5 ±0.05 mm, flatness 0.1 mm. Add stamped EN AW-4047 1.5 mm lid with 0.5 mm locating step. Weld: fibre laser 4 kW, spot ~0.3 mm, wobble 1.0 mm circular, 6 m/min, Ar shield 15 l/min.
engineering.validationPlan: Weld qualification: macro-sections (n = 20 per parameter set), CT of full seam (n = 10), tensile peel coupons. Ingress: ISO 20653 IP6K7 and IPX9K (n = 6 per unit type), pressure-decay leak ≤ 1 cm³/min at 30 kPa on 100 % of production. Durability: ISO 16750-4 thermal shock −40/+125 °C 300 cycles, ISO 16750-3 vibration, LV 124 damp heat cyclic 21 days (n = 6), followed by leak re-test. Electronics thermal exposure during welding: thermocouples on nearest parts ≤ 125 °C. PPAP: product and process change for both units, ~12 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: Screw station (multi-spindle nutrunner) and FIPG robot removed; one laser cell shared by both product lines. Lid stamping replaces cover casting + machining. Poka-yoke: vision checks seam continuity, laser power monitoring per mm. Not reworkable — failed welds scrap the unit, so first-time yield target ≥ 99.5 %.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle across both units: FIPG and its process €2.50 and screws with torque €2.00 disappear, the cast and machined covers (€9.60) become stamped lids (€3.20); laser cell time adds €1.70, the weldable vacuum-HPDC frame premium adds €1.40, and higher service-replacement cost adds €0.40. Not included: laser cell residual value and any warranty gain from fewer leaks. Net of the bridge lines: €7.40 per vehicle; investment €1230K pays back in ~40 months at the mid-point saving.

title: Copper-clip bonded dies replace heavy aluminium wire bonds in BiSG power module
description: [MHEV] Wire-bonder cycle time and bond inspection fall, DBC substrate area and silicone gel volume shrink, and lower interconnect resistance allows smaller dies; copper clips cost more than aluminium wire. Baseline: where a 48 V BiSG inverter uses a bare-die power module (common on higher-power 48 V machines of 15-25 kW), six or twelve 80-100 V MOSFET dies are soldered to a DBC (Al2O3 direct-bonded copper) substrate and their source and gate contacts are made with ultrasonic heavy aluminium wire (typically 8-10 wires of 300-500 µm per die), then the module is filled with silicone gel above the wire loops. Proposal: replace the source wire bonds with soldered copper clips (0.2-0.3 mm Cu, pre-tinned) placed by pick-and-place and reflowed in the same pass as the die attach; the gate keeps one thin wire or a small clip. ideaData.title: Copper-clip bonded dies replace heavy aluminium wire bonds in BiSG power module
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: where a 48 V BiSG inverter uses a bare-die power module (common on higher-power 48 V machines of 15-25 kW), six or twelve 80-100 V MOSFET dies are soldered to a DBC (Al2O3 direct-bonded copper) substrate and their source and gate contacts are made with ultrasonic heavy aluminium wire (typically 8-10 wires of 300-500 µm per die), then the module is filled with silicone gel above the wire loops. Proposal: replace the source wire bonds with soldered copper clips (0.2-0.3 mm Cu, pre-tinned) placed by pick-and-place and reflowed in the same pass as the die attach; the gate keeps one thin wire or a small clip. Effects: interconnect resistance per die drops (published clip data: about 0.3 mΩ for Cu clip vs 0.6 mΩ for Al ribbon and roughly 90 % lower than Cu wire bonds), loop inductance falls, so a ~10 % smaller die meets the same conduction loss; the low clip profile (~1.2 mm vs ~3 mm wire-loop height) reduces gel volume; DBC area falls because wire landing pads and bond-tool clearance are no longer needed. Toshiba states it has used copper clips instead of wire bonds in automotive DPAK/D2PAK power packages since 2011/2015. This idea applies the clip principle at module level; it is distinct from switching to packaged discrete devices.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Wire-bonder cycle time and bond inspection fall, DBC substrate area and silicone gel volume shrink, and lower interconnect resistance allows smaller dies; copper clips cost more than aluminium wire.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Supplier swaps a heavy-wire bonder pass (~20 s per module) for clip placement in the existing pick-and-place and reflow; adds clip carrier tooling. Bond pull testing on 100 % of a sample is replaced by X-ray void and clip-position checks.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Process steps −1 (no separate bonding), fewer consumables. Clip carriers with self-alignment features act as poka-yoke for orientation. Module height reduced ~2 mm, easing packaging behind the BiSG.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: solder fatigue under the clip from CTE mismatch (Cu 17 ppm/K vs Si 2.6 ppm/K), voids under the clip, die cracking from clip placement force. Prove with AQG 324 power cycling, thermal shock, C-SAM and X-ray void limits, and AEC-Q101-style HTRB/H3TRB on module samples.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Toshiba automotive power MOSFET packages (DPAK since 2011, D2PAK since 2015) and UTAC Cu-clip packaging study — Copper-clip internal connections replace wire bonds, reducing on-resistance and raising current capability; clip ≈ 0.3 mΩ vs 0.6 mΩ Al ribbon. How this differs: We move the clip interconnect from discrete packages to the BiSG bare-die module, using the resistance gain to shrink dies; module-level adoption and costs are our engineering estimate.

engineering.mechanism: Conduction loss P = I²(RDS(on),die + R_interconnect). At 300 A rms per switch position with two dies in parallel (150 A each), a wire-bond source path of ~0.5 mΩ per die gives 11 W per die; a clip at ~0.25 mΩ gives 5.6 W — a 5.4 W reduction, equivalent to ~0.25 mΩ of die resistance, which allows ~10 % die-area shrink for the same total loss at 150 °C. Inductance: 8 parallel wires 10 mm long contribute ~3-4 nH; a clip ~1 nH, reducing turn-off overshoot. Reliability: wire-bond heel cracking and lift-off are the main power-cycling failure modes (ΔTj 100 K); clip solder fatigue follows Coffin-Manson with lower strain if the clip is thin (≤ 0.3 mm) and dimpled.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: Al heavy wire bonding of source (8-10 × 400 µm per die), wire-bond pad areas on DBC. Add: Cu-ETP (CW004A) clips 0.25 mm, Sn pre-tinned, dimpled for solder fillet control, one per die; gate via 125 µm Al wire or mini-clip. Die: 80 V MOSFET, area −10 %, front metal changed to solderable NiAu/NiPdAu. DBC: 0.32 mm Al2O3 with 0.3 mm Cu, area −12 %. Silicone gel fill height 4 mm → 2.5 mm. Solder: SAC305 preform/paste, void limit ≤ 10 % per joint.
engineering.validationPlan: AQG 324 power cycling PC-sec (ΔTj 100 K, ton 2 s, n = 6 modules × 3 lots, target ≥ 60k cycles to 5 % ΔVce/ΔRDS(on) drift), PC-min (ton 60 s). Thermal shock −40/+150 °C 1,000 cycles. H3TRB 1,000 h, HTRB 1,000 h at 80 % VDS. X-ray void ≤ 10 %, C-SAM delamination ≤ 5 %. Inverter-level: LV 124 / ISO 16750-4 temperature cycling and CISPR 25 class 5 re-check (faster edges). PPAP: supplier module design and process change, ~10 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: One process step and one capital-intensive wire bonder per line freed; clips placed by existing pick-and-place with dedicated nozzles and tape-and-reel or waffle carriers. Clip self-alignment during reflow; X-ray replaces destructive pull testing. No rework possible after gel fill, same as today.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: wire-bond machine time €0.65 falls to €0.20 of clip placement, Al wire €0.08 becomes €0.72 of copper clips, DBC €6.50 → €5.70, gel €1.10 → €0.70, dies €9.00 → €8.10 and bond inspection €0.35 → €0.15. Not included: efficiency benefit and supplier wire-bonder residual value. Net of the bridge lines: €2.11 per vehicle; investment €420K pays back in ~48 months at the mid-point saving.

ideaData.title: Ground-plane stack-up and via fence delete MCU shield can and clip-on ferrites
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: 48 V inverters frequently reach CISPR 25 radiated-emission limits late in development and are "fixed" with add-on parts: a two-piece tin-plated steel shield can over the MCU/clock area, two snap-on MnZn ferrite cores on the 12 V signal pigtail or harness, and three individual ferrite rings around the BiSG phase busbars. Proposal: design EMC in rather than bolt it on. (1) Stack-up: control section uses an uninterrupted ground plane on layer 2 directly under all clocked signals, MCU crystal and SBC switching node, with a stitching-via fence (vias every 3-4 mm, i.e. < λ/20 at 1 GHz) around the clock zone and along the board edge, so the board forms its own partial cavity; (2) a single common-mode MnZn/nanocrystalline core sized for the three phase busbars together replaces three individual rings, because the radiated problem is common-mode current, not differential; (3) gate-driver programmable slew rate (two-step turn-on) trims dV/dt in the 30-100 MHz band at a small switching-loss cost; (4) the 12 V signal connector filter (feedthrough-style capacitors at the connector entry, referenced to the housing) removes the need for harness ferrites. The previous 48 V pack covered DC-DC input/output filter staging via interleaving and spread spectrum; this idea targets the inverter's radiated add-ons, which that idea does not touch.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes a stamped shield can and its placement, two clip-on ferrites and their harness assembly labour, and two of three phase ferrite rings; adds via-stitching drill hits and some EMC test iterations at development.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes shield-can placement and solder (large part needing extra paste and coplanarity check), manual snap-ferrite fitting at harness or module assembly (~20 s), and two ring insertions. Slight increase in PCB drill count (~250 vias).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −6. No manual ferrite fitting (a frequently forgotten part — removes a poka-yoke check). Rework access to the MCU improves without the can. One common-mode core is fixed by a moulded holder.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — EMC parts designed out at layout stage

Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: MCU shield can (frame + lid) and placement €0.65→€0.00; 2 snap-on ferrites on 12 V/signal leads + fitting €1.70→€0.00; Phase ferrite rings: 3 individual → 1 common-mode core €2.10→€0.90; Via stitching / ground fence in PCB fab €0.00→€0.15. Mitigate by pre-compliance scans at each prototype, near-field scanning of the board, and keeping footprints for the can and a ferrite as a contingency (populated only if needed). Tests: CISPR 25 (conducted, radiated ALSE), ISO 11452-2/-4 immunity, OEM EMC spec.

ideaData.materialGrade: Tin-plated steel shield can + 2 snap-on MnZn ferrites + 3 MnZn rings → PCB ground-plane/via fence + 1 common-mode MnZn or nanocrystalline core
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: SMT shield-can placement, manual ferrite snap-on, ring insertion ⟶ PCB stitching vias in fabrication, single core in moulded holder

engineering.mechanism: Radiated emission from a cable scales with common-mode current: E ≈ 1.26×10⁻⁶ · f · I_cm · L / r (V/m); at 100 MHz, a 1 m lead and 3 m distance, 5 µA of common-mode current already gives ~38 dBµV/m, near class 5 limits. Common-mode current is driven by dV/dt across parasitic capacitance (I = C·dV/dt; 20 pF × 48 V/10 ns ≈ 96 mA peak at the switching node). A continuous reference plane 0.1 mm below signals reduces loop area ~10×; via fences at < λ/20 spacing (3 mm at 5 GHz, ample at 1 GHz) contain fringing fields. One common-mode core around all three phases acts only on common-mode current (differential flux cancels), so one larger core replaces three that each saturate on differential current.
engineering.specDeltas: PCB: layer 2 solid GND under control section (no splits), stitching vias Ø0.3 mm every 3 mm around clock zone and board edge (~250 vias), crystal guard ring. Delete: shield can frame + lid (tin-plated steel 0.2 mm), 2 snap-on MnZn ferrites (Ø7 mm cable type), 2 of 3 phase rings. Add: one common-mode core (MnZn µi ≈ 5,000 or nanocrystalline) around three phase busbars in a PA66-GF30 holder; gate-driver two-step turn-on configured (e.g. 3 Ω → 10 Ω after Miller plateau); connector-entry filter capacitors 1 nF C0G per signal line to housing.
engineering.validationPlan: CISPR 25 ed. 5: conducted voltage and current, radiated ALSE 150 kHz-2.5 GHz, class 5 target, on 3 DV and 3 PV units with production harness. Immunity: ISO 11452-2 (ALSE, 100 V/m), ISO 11452-4 BCI (100 mA), ISO 10605 ESD ±8 kV contact. Thermal: verify efficiency loss from slower slew ≤ 0.2 % at peak (dyno). Contingency footprints retained to PV. PPAP: product change, EMC re-test is the main cost (~€220k incl. chamber time across iterations).
engineering.dfmImplications: Shield-can placement and its larger paste deposit gone; manual ferrite fitting step removed from harness/module assembly; ring insertion reduced from three to one. Via fence adds ~250 drill hits (negligible cycle at fab). Contingency footprints stay unpopulated, so no line change if not needed.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: shield can and placement €0.65 and two snap-on ferrites with fitting labour €1.70 are deleted; phase ferrite rings fall from €2.10 to €0.90; via stitching adds €0.15. Not included: development EMC chamber costs (in validation investment) and a contingency case where the can must be re-populated. Net of the bridge lines: €3.40 per vehicle; investment €230K pays back in ~16 months at the mid-point saving.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter and 48/12 V DC-DC each have a sealed low-voltage signal connector of about 16 ways carrying 12 V logic supply and ground, powertrain CAN-FD, a private CAN pair to the battery management/hybrid controller, a KL15 ignition sense line, a dedicated hardwired wake line, a hardwired safety enable and several spare/sensor circuits. Each line needs a harness wire (~2.5-3 m of 0.35 mm² FLRY-B), two terminals and seals, and on-board input protection (TVS/RC). Proposal: use ISO 11898-2:2016 partial-networking transceivers with selective wake-up frame detection (ISO 11898-6) so the units sleep on the bus and wake on a dedicated CAN frame; delete KL15 and the separate wake line, and move the private CAN traffic onto the powertrain CAN-FD at 2 Mbit/s (bus load checked) — four circuits deleted per unit. The hardwired safety enable stays (independent shutdown path). Both connectors drop to a 12-way family, which also lets inverter and DC-DC share one connector part number. The previous pack consolidated three connectors into one 16-way hybrid; this idea reduces the circuit count itself, which the consolidation did not touch.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Fewer pins on both device headers and harness mating connectors, four wires per unit deleted from the engine-bay harness with their terminals and seals, and four input-protection networks per unit deleted; partial-networking transceivers cost more than standard ones.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Harness: 8 fewer circuits to cut, crimp, seal and insert; device side: smaller header. Connector moulding tools change (new 12-way family). Test: EOL adds a selective-wake test step (~2 s).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count: −8 terminals, −8 seals, −8 wires, −16 board protection parts per vehicle; one common header part number for both units. Smaller connector improves mating ergonomics and reduces mis-mating risk.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium-High — harness and connector savings on two units
costSavingPotential.percentage: 20-30% of the LV connection cost of the two units
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Device headers 16-way → 12-way (2 units) €4.80→€3.00; Harness mating connectors, terminals, seals (2 units) €3.60→€2.10; 8 harness circuits deleted (~2.8 m FLRY-B 0.35 mm² each, terminals) €2.30→€0.00; On-board input protection per deleted pin €0.96→€0.00; CAN transceivers → partial-networking type (2 units) €1.10→€1.70. Net = €5.96 per vehicle; the range €5.20-€6.60 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €260K-€330K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: unwanted wake or failure to wake (network management), bus load on powertrain CAN-FD, loss of the independent KL15 signal for diagnostics. Validate network management per ISO 11898-2:2016 conformance, AUTOSAR NM, quiescent-current tests (≤ 100 µA per node in sleep), and bus-load simulation ≤ 60 %.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: NXP TJA1145A partial-networking CAN transceiver (ISO 11898-2:2016 / ISO 11898-6) — Selective wake-up frame detection lets a node sleep on the bus and wake on a dedicated CAN frame, with autonomous bus biasing and an optional local WAKE pin. How this differs: We use selective wake to delete KL15 and wake wires on the 48 V units of the luxury SUV; the pin-count and cost figures are our estimates, no OEM implementation is claimed.

engineering.mechanism: Each discrete wake/ignition circuit costs a wire run, two terminations and board protection, while carrying a single bit. A partial-networking transceiver decodes a configured wake frame (ID + data mask) in hardware at < 1 mA quiescent, so the bit moves onto the existing bus. Bus load: the private CAN carried ~250 frames/s × 8 bytes; on CAN-FD at 2 Mbit/s data phase this adds ~8-10 % load, keeping powertrain CAN-FD below 60 %. Quiescent current of the vehicle is unchanged (transceiver ~60 µA in sleep vs wake-line input ~50 µA).
engineering.specDeltas: Delete per unit: KL15 pin, WAKE pin, private CAN-H/CAN-L pins; their TVS, RC filters and divider (~8 parts); harness circuits 4 × ~2.8 m FLRY-B 0.35 mm² with 0.64 mm terminals and single-wire seals. Change: header 16-way → 12-way sealed (same terminal system), common to inverter and DC-DC. Transceiver: standard HS-CAN FD → partial-networking CAN FD (ISO 11898-2:2016). Software: AUTOSAR CanNm with PN filter, wake-frame ID configured, private-CAN signals remapped to powertrain CAN-FD with E2E protection.
engineering.validationPlan: Network: ISO 11898-2:2016 PN conformance (supplier), OEM network-management test catalogue (≥ 150 test cases: wake, sleep, false-wake immunity under bus disturbance per ISO 7637-3), bus-load test ≤ 60 %. Electrical: ISO 16750-2 / LV 124 E-xx supply tests on the remaining pins, quiescent current ≤ 100 µA per unit. Connector: LV 214 / USCAR-2 sealing and vibration on the new 12-way. PPAP: connector, harness and ECU software changes (~9 months).
engineering.dfmImplications: Harness lead-prep and insertion of 8 fewer circuits per vehicle; one common connector part number for two units reduces variants. Device-side header smaller with same press-fit or solder process. EOL test adds selective-wake step. Service: fewer pins to diagnose.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (two units): device headers fall from €4.80 to €3.00, harness mating connectors with seals from €3.60 to €2.10, the eight deleted circuits save €2.30 and the input protection €0.96; partial-networking transceivers add €0.60. Not included: harness engineering change cost and gateway/network-management software change in other ECUs. Net of the bridge lines: €5.96 per vehicle; investment €340K pays back in ~14 months at the mid-point saving.

ideaData.title: Delete conformal coating on 48 V inverter and DC-DC boards via inner-layer routing
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: many tier-1s apply selective acrylic or silicone conformal coating (25-75 µm, robot spray with UV-tracer inspection and connector/test-point masking) on both the inverter and DC-DC PCBAs as insurance against condensation inside the sealed, vented housing. Proposal: run both boards uncoated, justified by design rather than habit: (1) at 48 V (LV 148 maximum ~60 V transient), creepage needs on an uncoated external layer are small (IPC-2221 B4 class spacing ~0.13 mm for 31-50 V and ~0.4 mm for 51-100 V, pollution degree 2 inside an IP6K7 housing); design rule set to ≥ 0.6 mm between 48 V nets and 0.5 mm between 48 V and ground on outer layers; (2) high-potential-difference nets (48 V bus to signal) routed on inner layers, which are immune to surface contamination; (3) no-clean low-ionic solder paste with ionic-cleanliness limits (≤ 1.56 µg/cm² NaCl-eq, plus localized SIR); (4) solder mask over all copper except pads; (5) housing kept sealed with an ePTFE vent so liquid water never reaches the board and dew formation is limited to thin films. Note: industry guidance states clearance is always measured as an air gap with coating ignored, and coating only reduces creepage when specifically qualified, so the coating was not buying spacing in the first place.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes coating material, selective-coat robot time, UV inspection, masking/demasking and coating rework; adds cleanliness testing and a small board-area increase from wider outer-layer spacing.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Two selective coating cells (spray robot, UV cure or drying oven, UV inspection) removed from the line; WIP time for drying (10-30 min) disappears. Masking labour (~20 s per board) eliminated. Rework/repair access to boards improves.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No masking boots or tapes on connectors and test points; test pads remain probe-able after assembly (supports boundary-scan/functional test). Board-level repair and FA much easier without coating removal.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — removes a whole process step on two boards
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Conformal coating material (2 boards) €0.40→€0.00; Selective-coat robot + UV inspection time €1.33→€0.00; Masking/demasking labour and parts €0.50→€0.00; Coating rework/scrap €0.20→€0.00; Ionic cleanliness / SIR control €0.00→€0.25; PCB area for wider outer-layer spacing €0.00→€0.10. Net = €2.08 per vehicle; the range €1.80-€2.40 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €90K-€120K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: electrochemical migration and leakage under condensation (dendrites between 48 V and ground), especially with flux residues. Validate with ISO 16750-4 damp heat cyclic, condensation test (e.g. VDA/OEM dew test), SIR per IPC-TM-650 2.6.3.7, and LV 124 humidity; keep coating as a fallback if SIR fails.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: IPC-2221 spacing practice as summarised by conformalcoating.co.uk and TI SLUP419 — Clearance is an air gap independent of coating; coating reduces creepage only when qualified; inner-layer routing avoids contamination and humidity exposure. How this differs: We use these spacing rules to delete coating on 48 V boards in a sealed housing; no OEM is claimed to run uncoated 48 V boards — this is our engineering proposal.

benchmarkAnchor.platform: IPC-2221 spacing practice as summarised by conformalcoating.co.uk and TI SLUP419
benchmarkAnchor.borrowedFeature: Clearance is an air gap independent of coating; coating reduces creepage only when qualified; inner-layer routing avoids contamination and humidity exposure
benchmarkAnchor.difference: We use these spacing rules to delete coating on 48 V boards in a sealed housing; no OEM is claimed to run uncoated 48 V boards — this is our engineering proposal.

ideaData.materialGrade: Acrylic/silicone conformal coating 25-75 µm → none; no-clean low-ionic paste (ROL0) with solder mask over all bare copper
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Reflow → mask → selective spray coat → UV/dry → UV inspection → demask ⟶ reflow → ionic cleanliness sampling (no coating)
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No regulatory impact.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Electrochemical migration rate scales with field strength and ionic contamination: time-to-failure ∝ d²/(V·c). At 48 V across 0.6 mm (80 V/mm), and with ionic residue ≤ 1.56 µg/cm² NaCl-eq, SIR stays > 10⁸ Ω under 85 °C/85 % RH. Coating at 50 µm adds a moisture-permeable barrier (acrylic water vapour transmission is significant) that delays rather than prevents condensation at the copper; inner-layer routing places 48 V-to-signal differences under 0.1-0.2 mm of glass-epoxy, which no surface film can bridge. Clearance at 60 V in air needs only ~0.1 mm per IPC-2221 B4, so outer-layer 0.6 mm gives > 4× margin.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: conformal coating spec (e.g. acrylic 25-75 µm with UV tracer), masking drawing, coating keep-out notes. PCB: outer-layer spacing ≥ 0.6 mm 48 V–48 V and ≥ 0.5 mm 48 V–GND; 48 V-to-logic adjacencies routed on inner layers; solder mask defined over all copper; no exposed vias in 48 V zones (tented). Process: no-clean ROL0 paste, ionic cleanliness ≤ 1.56 µg/cm² NaCl-eq (IPC-TM-650 2.3.25), SIR sampling weekly. Housing: IP6K7 with ePTFE vent.
engineering.validationPlan: SIR per IPC-TM-650 2.6.3.7 on production-representative comb patterns (40 °C/93 % RH, 168 h, ≥ 10⁸ Ω). Condensation/dew test per OEM spec or VDA (e.g. 10 cycles, powered), ISO 16750-4 damp heat cyclic (n = 6 per unit type), LV 124 humidity test, followed by insulation and functional test. Salt-mist not applicable (sealed). Fallback: if SIR or dew fails, revert to selective coating on 48 V zones only. PPAP: process deletion, product change for PCB layout.

title: Windowpane stencil void control lets 48 V power boards skip vacuum reflow
description: [MHEV] Deletes solder preforms and the vacuum stage (throughput and depreciation premium of a vacuum oven), slightly reduces nitrogen use; adds X-ray sampling to monitor voiding more frequently. Baseline: to keep solder voids under the exposed drain pads of TOLL/TOLT/D2PAK-7 MOSFETs below ~10 %, some 48 V inverter and DC-DC lines use solder preforms on each power pad plus a vacuum reflow oven (vacuum stage of 30-60 s at peak) — both expensive in consumables and throughput. Proposal: achieve a ≤ 15-20 % void specification (sufficient at 48 V where thermal margin is designed with a measured Rth) in a standard nitrogen convection reflow by: windowpane / cross-hatch stencil apertures on the thermal pads at ~60-70 % paste coverage with 0.25 mm webs, letting flux volatiles escape through the channels; a step stencil (150 µm → 180 µm) on the power pads; a paste with low-voiding flux chemistry; an optimised soak profile (150-180 °C, 90 s); and PCB pad design with solder-mask-defined outgassing channels and plugged (not open) thermal vias. Industry papers on QFN/bottom-terminated components show segmented apertures at 50-80 % coverage and 0.2-0.3 mm webs reduce voiding, with ~25 % of pad area often taken as the upper limit; we set 20 % with margin and confirm the thermal effect by measuring Zth per device type rather than assuming it.

ideaData.materialGrade: SAC305 paste + SAC305 preforms on power pads → SAC305 low-voiding paste only, windowpane apertures (60-70 % coverage)
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Paste print + preform placement + vacuum reflow (30-60 s vacuum stage) ⟶ step-stencil windowpane print + N2 convection reflow with extended soak

engineering.mechanism: Void effect on Rth: voids under a 10 × 11 mm drain pad act as parallel insulation; for distributed small voids the solder-layer resistance rises roughly as 1/(1 − void fraction), so 20 % voids raise the ~0.05 K/W solder-layer term to ~0.063 K/W — +0.013 K/W, i.e. +2 K at 150 W device dissipation, inside a typical 10-15 K design margin. Large single voids under the die hotspot are the danger, hence the ≤ 5 % single-void limit. Windowpane apertures give flux-volatile escape channels; a step stencil raises paste height to compensate for the 30-40 % lower coverage so stand-off stays ~70-90 µm.
engineering.specDeltas: Stencil: 150 µm base, step to 180 µm on power pads; thermal-pad aperture split into 4-9 panes, 60-70 % coverage, 0.25 mm webs, 0.05 mm corner radii. Delete: SAC305 preforms (e.g. 12-16 per board) and vacuum profile. Reflow: N2 (≤ 1,000 ppm O2), soak 150-180 °C 90 s, peak 245 °C, TAL 60-75 s. PCB: plugged thermal vias (IPC-4761 Type VI) under pads, solder-mask channels. Acceptance: total void ≤ 20 %, single void ≤ 5 %, 2D/3D X-ray.
engineering.validationPlan: DOE on aperture coverage (55/65/75 %) and paste (2 suppliers), n = 30 boards each, X-ray void distribution. Transient thermal impedance per JESD51-14 on 10 devices per variant comparing vacuum vs proposal (acceptance ΔZth ≤ 5 %). Board-level power cycling ΔTj 80 K (n = 6), ISO 16750-4 temperature cycling −40/+125 °C 1,000 cycles (n = 6) with cross-section. PPAP: process change, ~6 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: Preform feeders and placements removed (12-16 per board); standard oven replaces vacuum oven — one fewer oven type to maintain, recipe simplified. X-ray sampling plan intensified during ramp then reduced. Stencil cost ~€2k each, re-made per revision.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle across two power boards: vacuum reflow throughput and depreciation €1.90 fall to €0.70 in standard convection, preforms €0.60 disappear, nitrogen €0.25 falls to €0.20, while X-ray void sampling rises from €0.30 to €0.40. Not included: residual value of the vacuum oven. Net of the bridge lines: €1.75 per vehicle; investment €165K pays back in ~23 months at the mid-point saving.

engineering.mechanism: Test time is dominated by sequential instrument switching (relay matrix settling 10-50 ms per step × ~400 steps ≈ 10-20 s), thermal and load dwell (30-60 s), and flash/verify (10-20 s). MCU-reported measurements are taken in parallel inside the unit in < 1 s; the tester checks only reference points to validate the MCU chain. Two-up nesting overlaps handling with testing so effective time per unit ≈ max(test, handling)/2 + overhead. A regenerative source/load at 95 % recovery means a 3 kW DC-DC step costs ~150 W net, not 3 kW of heat, removing the need for long cool-down.
engineering.specDeltas: Test spec: inverter EOL 110 s → 60 s; DC-DC 90 s → 35 s; full-load dwell 30 s → 5 s; thermal step replaced by SPC sample test (1 in 200 units, 60 s full load). Firmware: UDS routines (e.g. RID 0x0300-0x0310) returning calibrated ADC data and self-test flags. Equipment: bidirectional regenerative DC source/load 60 V / 300 A, two-up fixtures with coolant quick couplings and DMC readers. Control plan: reference-point check of DC-link voltage, phase current, 12 V output.
engineering.validationPlan: MSA: Gauge R&R ≤ 10 % on all retained measurements (10 parts × 3 operators × 3 trials). Correlation: 4-week parallel run (~8,000 units) old vs new sequence, acceptance zero discrepant passes on known-bad seeded units (n = 30 seeded faults per product). Capability Cpk ≥ 1.67 on key parameters. Product unchanged, so no ISO 16750 re-test; PPAP process change notification with updated control plan and PFMEA.
engineering.dfmImplications: Fixtures: two nests per tester with poka-yoke nest identification; coolant quick-couplings for inverter. Handling robot or operator loads one nest while the other tests. One fewer tester per product at 50,000/yr. Test program becomes variant-agnostic via UDS.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: tester time for both units falls from €3.67 to €1.74, regenerative loading reduces energy from €0.05 to €0.02, handling from €0.55 to €0.35, while two-up fixture amortisation rises from €0.15 to €0.30. Not included: freed tester capacity value and the residual value of existing load banks. Net of the bridge lines: €2.01 per vehicle; investment €360K pays back in ~44 months at the mid-point saving.

title: Leaded LQFP-144 inverter MCU lets control board drop HDI microvias to through-hole six-layer
description: [MHEV] Moves the control PCB from HDI (sequential lamination, laser drilling, copper filling) to a single-lamination through-hole 6-layer; removes BGA underfill/corner-bond and BGA X-ray inspection; LQFP variant costs about the same as the BGA variant. Baseline: the 48 V inverter control section often uses its MCU in a fine-pitch BGA (e.g. 0.8 mm pitch, ~290 balls) because the part was chosen from a family whose high-pin-count variants are BGA-only; escaping inner ball rows forces an HDI build (1+4+1 with laser microvias, 75-100 µm lines/spaces), and BGA requires corner-bond or underfill for engine-mounted vibration and thermal cycling, plus X-ray inspection of hidden joints. Proposal: select the MCU variant in a leaded exposed-pad LQFP-144 (0.5 mm pitch) — feasible because a 48 V BiSG inverter uses ~90-110 MCU I/O (3 PWM pairs, 6-9 ADC channels, 2 CAN-FD, SPI to gate driver and SBC, resolver/angle interface, JTAG) — and build the control board as a conventional 6-layer through-hole-via FR4 (125 µm lines/spaces, 0.25 mm mechanical drill), with all signals escaping on outer layers. Lead compliance of gull-wing LQFP absorbs CTE mismatch (FR4 ~16 ppm/K vs package ~10 ppm/K) so no underfill is needed; joints are fully visible to AOI. The first 48 V pack and a zone-controller idea reduced layer count by partitioning silicon; this idea changes the MCU package to remove the HDI proces

ideaData.materialGrade: MCU BGA-292 on HDI 1+4+1 FR4 (laser microvias, Tg 170) → MCU LQFP-144 exposed pad on 6-layer through-hole FR4 (Tg 170, IPC-4101/126)
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Sequential lamination + laser drilling + Cu via fill; BGA placement + underfill + X-ray ⟶ single lamination, mechanical drilling; LQFP placement, AOI only
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No regulatory impact.

engineering.mechanism: Escape routing: a 0.8 mm BGA with 17 × 17 array needs one routing channel per ball row; with 100 µm L/S only one trace fits between 0.4 mm pads, so inner rows require microvias and a 1+N+1 build. A perimeter LQFP-144 needs no inner escape — all leads route on the top layer with 125 µm L/S. Solder-joint fatigue scales with ΔCTE·ΔT·DNP/h: BGA balls (h ≈ 0.4 mm, DNP ≈ 9 mm) have ~5-10× the strain of compliant gull-wing leads, which flex and absorb the mismatch, so underfill becomes unnecessary for the same 1,000-cycle −40/+125 °C target.
engineering.specDeltas: MCU: BGA-292 (0.8 mm) → LQFP-144 exposed pad (0.5 mm pitch, 20 × 20 mm), same silicon family/firmware. PCB: HDI 1+4+1 (laser microvia Ø100 µm, Cu-filled, 75-100 µm L/S) → 6-layer through-hole, 0.25 mm drill, 125 µm L/S, 1.6 mm thick, Tg 170 IPC-4101/126, ENIG or OSP. Delete: BGA underfill or corner-bond epoxy spec and dispense step; BGA X-ray sampling instruction. Board area 85 → 92 cm².
engineering.validationPlan: Package and joint: AEC-Q100 Grade 1 (supplier), IPC-9701 thermal cycling on daisy-chain boards −40/+125 °C, 1,000 cycles, n = 32 joints sites, acceptance no opens. Vibration: ISO 16750-3 engine-mounted random profile 22 h/axis on 6 boards. Thermal: MCU junction ≤ 125 °C at 105 °C ambient with exposed pad soldered (thermal vias). Signal integrity: CAN-FD 5 Mbit/s eye diagram. EMC: CISPR 25 regression. PPAP: product change (PCB and MCU part number), ~9 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes underfill dispense and cure (~60 s oven WIP), BGA X-ray sampling, and HDI special processes at the PCB fab. QFP placement uses standard nozzles; AOI inspects every lead. Rework possible on the line. Board area +7 cm² absorbed in existing housing.

Not included: firmware pin-mapping changes (minor) and any PCB tooling NRE beyond stencils. Net of the bridge lines: €2.65 per vehicle; investment €210K pays back in ~19 months at the mid-point saving.

title: Plugged IPC-4761 Type VI thermal vias replace filled-and-capped via-in-pad under MOSFETs
description: [MHEV] Removes epoxy/copper-paste fill, planarisation and cap plating at the PCB supplier on both power boards; adds minor paste compensation and more X-ray sampling. Baseline: FR4 power boards for 48 V inverters and DC-DCs that cool bottom-side MOSFETs through the board often specify via-in-pad plated over (VIPPO, IPC-4761 Type VII): thermal vias under each drain pad are epoxy- or copper-paste-filled, planarised and cap-plated so solder cannot wick into them. This adds fill, cure, planarisation and a second plating cycle at the PCB maker — typically a 15-25 % adder on the power board. Proposal: specify IPC-4761 Type VI (filled and covered) or Type III/IV (plugged from the bottom side with solder-mask or epoxy plug) arrays of 0.3 mm vias at 1.0 mm pitch within the pad, with the solder side open but the bottom side plugged, and compensate for solder wicking with a windowpane paste aperture whose webs sit over the via rows. Because the via barrels are filled with solder or plug material either way, the thermal conductance through the board is nearly the same: the copper barrel (25 µm) dominates conductance, not the fill. For a 48 V board with ~12 MOSFET pads (inverter) or ~8 (DC-DC), the VIPPO adder is removed while keeping a measured Rth within ±5 % of baseline. IPC/SMTA voiding studies show pad and aperture design control voiding of bottom-terminated power packages.

ideaData.title: Plugged IPC-4761 Type VI thermal vias replace filled-and-capped via-in-pad under MOSFETs
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: FR4 power boards for 48 V inverters and DC-DCs that cool bottom-side MOSFETs through the board often specify via-in-pad plated over (VIPPO, IPC-4761 Type VII): thermal vias under each drain pad are epoxy- or copper-paste-filled, planarised and cap-plated so solder cannot wick into them. This adds fill, cure, planarisation and a second plating cycle at the PCB maker — typically a 15-25 % adder on the power board. Proposal: specify IPC-4761 Type VI (filled and covered) or Type III/IV (plugged from the bottom side with solder-mask or epoxy plug) arrays of 0.3 mm vias at 1.0 mm pitch within the pad, with the solder side open but the bottom side plugged, and compensate for solder wicking with a windowpane paste aperture whose webs sit over the via rows. Because the via barrels are filled with solder or plug material either way, the thermal conductance through the board is nearly the same: the copper barrel (25 µm) dominates conductance, not the fill. For a 48 V board with ~12 MOSFET pads (inverter) or ~8 (DC-DC), the VIPPO adder is removed while keeping a measured Rth within ±5 % of baseline. IPC/SMTA voiding studies show pad and aperture design control voiding of bottom-terminated power packages.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes epoxy/copper-paste fill, planarisation and cap plating at the PCB supplier on both power boards; adds minor paste compensation and more X-ray sampling.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: PCB fab: one fewer plating cycle and the planarisation step removed, shortening lead time by 2-3 days. SMT: new stencil with via-aligned webs; X-ray sampling raised for ramp. No line capex.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No change to part count. Stencil design rule: aperture webs over via rows. Bottom-side plug prevents solder flowing through to the TIM side (protects the insulating TIM interface flatness).

engineering.mechanism: Thermal conductance of a via array: each 0.3 mm via with 25 µm Cu barrel in 1.6 mm board has R ≈ L/(k·A) = 1.6e-3/(390 × 2.2e-8) ≈ 186 K/W; 30 vias in parallel ≈ 6.2 K/W through the board for one pad. A solder- or epoxy-filled core adds k = 60 (solder) or 1-3 W/mK (epoxy) over 0.25 mm diameter — at most ~10-15 % extra conductance with solder fill, negligible with epoxy. So VIPPO's cap buys solder-joint integrity, not heat flow; the same integrity is achieved with bottom plugging plus aperture webs that keep paste off the via mouths, limiting wicking to ≤ 20 % paste volume loss.
engineering.specDeltas: PCB drawing: IPC-4761 Type VII → Type VI (or III-b) for thermal vias under MOSFET pads; drill 0.3 mm, pitch 1.0 mm, barrel ≥ 25 µm Cu; bottom-side plug flush ±25 µm; top side open. Stencil: windowpane aperture with 0.25 mm webs located over via rows, coverage 60-70 %, step 150 → 180 µm. Acceptance: void ≤ 20 % total, ≤ 5 % single void (X-ray); no solder protrusion on bottom side > 25 µm (protects TIM interface).
engineering.validationPlan: Thermal: JESD51-14 transient thermal impedance on 10 devices per board type, acceptance ΔRth ≤ 5 % vs VIPPO baseline. Reliability: IPC-TM-650 2.6.8 solder float thermal stress (n = 10 coupons), ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling −40/+125 °C 1,000 cycles (n = 6 boards) with cross-section of joints and plugs; power cycling ΔTj 80 K (n = 6). X-ray void study n = 30 boards per stencil variant. PPAP: PCB specification change at supplier, ~6 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: PCB supplier lead time −2-3 days; no planarisation-related thickness variation at pads. SMT needs the new stencil only. Bottom-side plug keeps the TIM face flat — avoids solder bumps that would puncture insulating TIM film.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle across inverter and DC-DC power boards: the VIPPO adder of €2.40 falls to €0.60 for plugging, PCB lead-time/yield adder €0.30 falls to €0.10; stencil compensation adds €0.05 and extra X-ray sampling €0.10. Not included: the stencil cost (in tooling investment). Net of the bridge lines: €1.85 per vehicle; investment €165K pays back in ~21 months at the mid-point saving.

title: Insulating phase-change TIM film replaces dispensed two-part gap filler under 48 V power stages
description: [MHEV] Less TIM mass and no meter-mix dispensing, mixer nozzles or purge waste; the added cost is precision machining of the cold-plate pedestal flatness and height. Baseline: the 48 V inverter and DC-DC power boards sit on the housing cold face through a dispensed two-part silicone gap filler (3-3.5 W/mK, ~1.0 mm bond line, ~45 g per unit, dispensed by a meter-mix robot with static mixers, then compressed by the board). Gap filler is used because cast-face tolerance stacks of ±0.3-0.5 mm are absorbed by its softness. Proposal: tighten the stack — machine the cold-plate pedestal to 0.05 mm flatness and ±0.05 mm height relative to the PCB datum bosses — and replace the gap filler with a die-cut phase-change material (PCM) on a polyimide carrier (e.g. 25 µm PI + 2 × 50 µm PCM, melting ~50-60 °C, 1.5-3 W/mK) for electrical isolation of the drain-potential thermal vias. Above its melt point the PCM flows to a 20-30 µm bond line per side, so total interface resistance falls despite lower bulk conductivity. Industry catalogues state PCMs are used for tight tolerances at up to ~0.15 mm thickness with bond lines of 20-30 µm, while gap fillers run 0.25-5 mm; and gap-filler resistance depends strongly on how thin the bond line can be made. Pads are placed by pick-and-place from reels, no mixing, no cure, no silicone outgassing near connectors.

engineering.mechanism: Interface resistance R = BLT/k + contact terms. Gap filler: 1.0 mm / 3.5 W/mK = 2.9 cm²K/W bulk → over a 40 cm² footprint ≈ 0.07 K/W. PCM film: PI 25 µm / 0.4 W/mK ≈ 0.63 cm²K/W plus two 25 µm PCM layers at 3 W/mK ≈ 0.17 cm²K/W, total ~0.8 cm²K/W plus contact ≈ 1.0 cm²K/W → ~0.025 K/W over 40 cm². At 150 W board loss that is ~7 K lower than gap filler, which pays for itself thermally. The condition is tolerance: PCM absorbs only ~±0.03 mm, so pedestal flatness 0.05 mm and height ±0.05 mm to the board datum are required.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: 2K silicone gap filler (e.g. ~45 g/unit, 3.5 W/mK), meter-mix dispense program, static mixer nozzles. Add: die-cut PCM-on-PI pad, 40-60 cm² per unit, 125 µm total, dielectric strength ≥ 4 kV, with Ø4 mm locating holes. Housing drawing: cold-plate pedestal flatness 0.05 mm, height ±0.05 mm relative to PCB support bosses, Ra ≤ 1.6 µm. PCB: bottom side free of solder protrusion > 25 µm (plugged vias). Screw torque pattern specified to reach PCM compression > 0.2 MPa.
engineering.validationPlan: Thermal: Rth junction-to-coolant measurement on 10 units per type, acceptance ≤ baseline. Durability: ISO 16750-4 −40/+125 °C 1,000 cycles and power cycling 50,000 cycles at ΔT 60 K with Rth drift ≤ 10 % (n = 6). Isolation: hipot 500 V DC, insulation ≥ 100 MΩ before/after damp heat 85/85 1,000 h. Vibration ISO 16750-3. 100 % pedestal flatness CMM/laser check in ramp then SPC. PPAP: product and process change, ~8 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: Dispense cells, pumps and material pot-life control removed; reel-fed pad placement on existing pick-and-place or a simple pad applicator. CNC finishing pass adds ~10 s per housing. No cure WIP. Board removal for FA no longer requires scraping silicone.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle across both units: TIM material falls from €3.60 to €2.10, dispensing from €1.05 to €0.25 of pad placement, mixer and purge waste €0.30 and silicone contamination control €0.10 disappear, and pedestal flatness machining adds €0.45. Not included: possible downsizing of cooling from lower Rth. Net of the bridge lines: €2.25 per vehicle; investment €200K pays back in ~22 months at the mid-point saving.

title: Dual-die TMR shaft-end angle sensor replaces resolver and RDC in integrated BiSG
description: [MHEV] Resolver stator and rotor, excitation/RDC electronics, sensor lead and mechanical alignment are replaced by a small magnet, two sensor dies, a shield cup and a software calibration step. Proposal: where the inverter sits on the machine rear (integrated BiSG), place a diametrically magnetised bonded magnet on the shaft end and a dual-die TMR angle sensor on the inverter PCB, 1.5-2.5 mm air gap.
