A thin soft-magnetic shield cup protects the sensor from stray fields of the machine end-winding and phase busbars. The resolver, its rotor, the excitation chain, the shielded lead and the mechanical angular alignment step are deleted; the electrical offset between magnet and rotor poles is calibrated in software at EOL (spin test). engineering.mechanism: Torque error from angle error: T ∝ cos(Δθe), so ±3° electrical costs < 0.2 % torque, but ±10° costs 1.5 % plus higher current for the same torque. With 7 pole pairs, ±1° mechanical = ±7° electrical, so calibration is required: a stored 64-point harmonic correction (EOL spin at 1,000 rpm) brings residual to ±0.3° mechanical (±2° electrical). Stray field: 600 A in a busbar 20 mm away gives B = µ0I/(2πr) ≈ 6 mT; relative to a 40 mT working field that would be ~8.5° error, so a soft-magnetic cup with shielding factor ≥ 10 is mandatory. Magnet: bonded NdFeB loses ~0.1 %/K reversibly; 20-100 mT window maintained from −40 to +150 °C with 40-60 mT nominal.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: VR resolver stator and rotor, resolver connector, 6-wire shielded lead, excitation amplifier and RDC (or demodulation ADC channels), alignment fixture. Add: Ø7 × 3 mm diametric bonded NdFeB (or Sm2Co17 for > 150 °C) magnet in shaft-end pocket with PA holder, air gap 2.0 ±0.3 mm; dual-die TMR angle sensor IC on inverter PCB centred on shaft axis ±0.2 mm; 0.5 mm soft-magnetic shield cup around sensor zone; EOL calibration routine storing offset + harmonic table in NVM.
engineering.validationPlan: Angle accuracy bench: −40/+25/+150 °C, 0-18,000 rpm, with 600 A phase current, acceptance ±2° electrical after calibration (n = 6 machines). Stray-field immunity ISO 11452-8 and internal busbar fields. Magnet: 1,000 h at 150 °C, flux loss ≤ 3 %. Mechanical: ISO 16750-3 engine-mounted vibration, ISO 16750-4 thermal shock. Safety: FMEDA, dual-die cross-check diagnostic coverage ≥ 99 %. Machine-level: dyno torque accuracy and efficiency map vs resolver baseline. PPAP: product change on machine and inverter, ~12 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: Resolver stator press and angular alignment fixture removed; magnet press with adhesive dispense added; EOL spin-calibration adds ~8 s but replaces the mechanical alignment (~25 s). One fewer cable and connector to route and seal. Not applicable to designs with a remote inverter.

title: Thread-forming screws in as-cast cored holes delete tapping and swarf in 48V housings
description: [MHEV] Deletes drilling and tapping of ~20 holes per vehicle, shortens the post-machining wash and cleanliness check, and lowers the particle-related failure allowance; thread-forming screws cost a little more and core pins add die maintenance. Baseline: inside the 48 V inverter and DC-DC die-cast housings, the PCB(s), power busbars and connector flange are fastened with ~10 metric M4/M5 machine screws per unit into holes that are drilled and tapped after casting. Tapping aluminium creates conductive swarf and burrs; electronics housings must then be industrially washed and checked for technical cleanliness (VDA 19.1 / ISO 16232 particle counts), because a single 400-600 µm aluminium chip between 48 V and ground pads or across a gate-drive net is a latent short. Proposal: cast the screw holes as cored pilots (core pins in the die, 1-1.5° draft, diameter set for the thread-forming screw, e.g. Ø3.6 mm for a 4 mm trilobular screw in AlSi alloy), delete drilling and tapping entirely, and fasten with thread-forming screws (trilobular cross-section, per DIN 7500 type principles for metal, or a high-performance aluminium-specific form) that cold-form the internal thread without producing chips. Formed threads have work-hardened flanks and higher strip-to-drive torque ratio than cut threads in cast aluminium, so clamp-load consistency improves. Only casting release-agent residue remain

The idea is described as general fastening practice; no vehicle-specific source was confirmed in this session, and the evidence cited only documents the conventional screw-and-gasket electronics housing baseline.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes drilling and tapping of ~20 holes per vehicle, shortens the post-machining wash and cleanliness check, and lowers the particle-related failure allowance; thread-forming screws cost a little more and core pins add die maintenance.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Housing CNC cycle drops by ~20-25 s per unit (drill + tap of 10 holes and tool changes); tap breakage and thread-gauge checks disappear. Die gets 10 extra core pins (wear item). Screwdriving station needs higher drive torque and a torque-angle strategy for thread forming.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No change in part count; screw part numbers change to thread-forming types. Torque-angle monitoring detects missing or mis-formed threads (poka-yoke). Re-use: formed threads accept re-insertion of the same screw for service at least 3-5 times.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — machining and cleanliness cost removed, latent-short risk reduced
costSavingPotential.percentage: 8-12% of housing machining and fastening cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Tapping 20 holes €0.80→€0.00; Drilling pilots → as-cast cored holes (core-pin maintenance) €0.60→€0.10; Wash + cleanliness check €0.60→€0.25; Screws: machine → thread-forming €0.50→€0.70; Particle-related failure allowance €0.20→€0.05. Net = €1.60 per vehicle; the range €1.40-€1.90 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €70K-€95K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: cored hole porosity reducing strip torque, cracking of thin bosses during forming, clamp-load loss under thermal cycling. Validate with drive/strip torque studies (n = 30 per hole type), ISO 16750-3 vibration with clamp-load monitoring, ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling, and VDA 19.1 cleanliness analysis of the housing.

How this differs: Thread-forming screws in cored holes are described as general engineering practice; only the conventional screw-fastened baseline is sourced, and the cost figures are our estimates.

ideaData.materialGrade: M4/M5 property class 8.8 machine screws in drilled + tapped EN AC-46000 → thread-forming trilobular steel screws (case-hardened) in as-cast cored holes in EN AC-46000 / AlSi10MnMg
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: HPDC → drill → tap → wash → particle check → screw ⟶ HPDC with cored pilots → shortened wash → thread-forming screwdriving with torque-angle monitoring
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No regulatory impact.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Cut threads remove material and leave chips; a thread-forming screw displaces it plastically, so no chip is generated and flank hardness rises 20-30 % by work hardening. Strip torque in AlSi castings for a 4 mm thread-forming screw with 8 mm engagement is typically ~2-3× the drive torque, giving a wide window for torque-angle control. Particle risk: at 48 V a short needs only a bridging conductive particle; a 500 µm Al chip bridges 0.5 mm spacing. Removing the chip source cuts the probability of a latent short by more than an order of magnitude, beyond what washing alone achieves (wash efficiency ~90-95 % per cycle).
engineering.specDeltas: Housing drawing: 10 drilled/tapped M4/M5 holes per unit → cored pilots Ø3.6/4.5 mm, 1-1.5° draft, depth 10 mm, boss OD ≥ 2.5 × screw diameter, porosity class in boss zone per X-ray. Delete: drill and tap operations, thread go/no-go gauging. Screws: 8.8 machine screws with pre-applied patch → case-hardened trilobular thread-forming screws, same head/drive. Assembly: torque-angle strategy (seat detection + final torque window). Cleanliness spec: VDA 19.1 extraction, max particle ≤ 400 µm metallic.
engineering.validationPlan: Fastening study: drive torque, strip torque and clamp load on 30 holes per type from 3 casting lots, acceptance strip/drive ≥ 2.0. Durability: ISO 16750-3 vibration (engine/body-mounted profile) with clamp-load measurement before/after, ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling −40/+125 °C 500 cycles, re-insertion test 5 cycles. Cleanliness: VDA 19.1 / ISO 16232 extraction on 10 housings before/after change. PPAP: product (housing, screw) and process change, ~6 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: CNC loses ~20-25 s per housing and two tool types (drill, tap) with their breakage risk; die gets core pins with scheduled replacement. Screwdriver spindles need higher torque range. Torque-angle signature acts as automatic poka-yoke for cross-threading and missing pilots.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle across both units (~20 holes): tapping €0.80 and drilling €0.60 are replaced by cored holes costing €0.10 in core-pin maintenance; wash and cleanliness checks fall from €0.60 to €0.25; screws rise from €0.50 to €0.70; particle-related failure allowance falls from €0.20 to €0.05. Not included: CNC capacity freed for other work. Net of the bridge lines: €1.60 per vehicle; investment €150K pays back in ~22 months at the mid-point saving.

title: Soft-termination series-pair X7R MLCC Y-capacitors replace screw-mounted film Y-capacitor block
description: [MHEV] A leaded film block, its M4 screw, the tapped housing hole and its THT soldering are replaced by eight small, cheap MLCCs and one stamped spring ground contact, all placed and reflowed in the normal SMT pass with no manual operation. ideaData.title: Soft-termination series-pair X7R MLCC Y-capacitors replace screw-mounted film Y-capacitor block
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V inverter and DC-DC commonly use a leaded metallised-polypropylene film capacitor block (two capacitors, 48 V+ and 48 V− to housing, ~1-2.2 µF, 100 V) mounted with a screw and ground tab to the housing, its leads soldered through the board, to shunt common-mode noise to chassis. Film was chosen historically for its self-healing behaviour and no DC-bias derating. Proposal: replace each block with SMD Y-capacitance built from AEC-Q200 soft-termination (flexible-termination) X7R MLCCs in 1210 size, 100 V, arranged as series pairs (two in series per branch, two branches in parallel per rail) so that a single flex crack — the dominant MLCC failure mode — cannot short the 48 V rail to chassis, placed directly at the housing ground contact (a stamped spring contact soldered to the PCB, compressed against the housing on assembly). Physics: at 48 V a 100 V X7R loses ~40-50 % capacitance to DC bias, so the bank is sized on effective capacitance (e.g. 8 × 2.2 µF nominal → ~1.1 µF effective per rail); MLCC ESL is ~0.5-1 nH vs ~10-15 nH for a leaded film block with tab, so the Y-path is far more effective above 10 MHz where radiated emissions problems arise. At 48 V there is no touch-current limit driving Y-capacitance (unlike 400/800 V systems), so the value is free to choose for EMC.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: A leaded film block, its M4 screw, the tapped housing hole and its THT soldering are replaced by eight small, cheap MLCCs and one stamped spring ground contact, all placed and reflowed in the normal SMT pass with no manual operation.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes a THT component (selective solder or hand solder) and a screw operation per unit; adds 8 SMD placements and a spring contact placement. Supports the THT-free line idea.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count per unit: 1 block + 1 screw → 9 SMD parts placed automatically; no manual handling. Ground contact by spring removes a screw torque operation. Board layout keeps MLCCs away from depanelling edges and screw bosses (flex strain).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — cheaper parts and a THT/screw step removed on two units
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Y-cap function: film block → 8 MLCC + spring contact (2 units) €3.60→€1.12; Screw + ground tab assembly (2 units) €0.60→€0.00; THT soldering of block leads (2 units) €0.20→€0.00; Housing: tapped M4 hole → machined flat contact pad (2 units) €0.10→€0.06. Net = €3.32 per vehicle; the range €2.80-€3.60 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €140K-€180K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: MLCC flex cracking (board bending at screw-down, depanelling), DC-bias capacitance loss, piezoelectric noise. Mitigate with soft termination, series pairs (fail-safe), strain-gauge validation ≤ 500 µε, AEC-Q200 board flex test, CISPR 25 regression, and ISO 16750-3 vibration.

How this differs: Only the low-inductance PCB principle is sourced; the MLCC Y-cap arrangement is our engineering proposal and not attributed to any OEM.

ideaData.materialGrade: Leaded MKP film Y-capacitor block 2 × 2.2 µF 100 V → 8 × AEC-Q200 soft-termination X7R 1210 2.2 µF 100 V MLCC per unit (series pairs) + CuSn6 spring ground contact
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: THT block insertion + selective/hand solder + screw to housing ⟶ SMT placement and reflow; spring contact compression at housing assembly
ideaData.regulatoryContext: UN ECE R10 EMC compliance must be maintained.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Y-capacitor effectiveness above its self-resonance f = 1/(2π√(LC)) collapses: a leaded film block with 12 nH and 2.2 µF resonates at ~1 MHz and is inductive (Z ≈ 2πfL = 7.5 Ω at 100 MHz); four parallel MLCC branches each with 0.8 nH give ~0.2 nH effective → Z ≈ 0.13 Ω at 100 MHz, ~35 dB better shunting. DC bias: X7R 100 V 1210 retains ~50-60 % at 48 V; series pairing halves capacitance again, so 8 × 2.2 µF nominal → 2 parallel branches × (2.2 × 0.55/2) ≈ 1.2 µF per rail, comparable to the film block's effective value. A flex crack shorts one MLCC; its series partner still blocks DC — no rail-to-chassis short.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: film Y-block (e.g. 2 × 2.2 µF MKP 100 V, leaded, with M4 screw and ground tab), housing tapped hole M4 (one per unit). Add per unit: 8 × X7R 1210 2.2 µF 100 V, AEC-Q200, soft (flexible) termination, arranged as 2 rails × 2 parallel × 2 series; CuSn6 stamped spring ground contact (SMD), compressed 0.5-1.0 mm against a machined housing pad, contact resistance ≤ 5 mΩ. Layout: MLCCs ≥ 5 mm from board edges and screw bosses, oriented parallel to the bending axis.
engineering.validationPlan: AEC-Q200 board flex (2 mm, n = 30 per footprint), strain gauge at assembly screw-down and depanelling ≤ 500 µε. Electrical: CISPR 25 class 5 conducted and radiated regression with 3 units; ISO 7637-2 / LV 124 transients; insulation rail-to-housing ≥ 10 MΩ at 100 V after damp heat 85/85 1,000 h (n = 6). Mechanical: ISO 16750-3 vibration and thermal shock with contact-resistance monitoring of spring. PPAP: product change, ~6 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: THT part and screw removed — no hand or selective soldering for this part; 9 SMD placements added at negligible time. Spring contact makes ground connection automatic at housing closure. Housing machining loses a tapped hole and gains a flat pad.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (two units): film blocks €3.60 become €1.12 of MLCCs and spring contacts, the screw operation €0.60 and THT soldering €0.20 disappear. Not included: possible further EMC benefit allowing smaller common-mode chokes. Net of the bridge lines: €3.32 per vehicle; investment €150K pays back in ~11 months at the mid-point saving.

ideaData.title: Adhesive ePTFE vent on cast-through port replaces screw-in pressure-compensation element
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the sealed 48 V inverter and DC-DC housings each carry a screw-in or snap-in pressure-compensation element (PCE): a PA66 body with an ePTFE membrane, an O-ring, a protective cap, fitted into a drilled and tapped port, and torqued at assembly. Venting is essential — in unvented housings a pressure differential as small as ~7 kPa can make seals fail after several temperature cycles; for an off-road SUV the critical case is a hot unit plunged into cold water during wading, where internal cooling creates vacuum that pulls water past seals. Proposal: an adhesive ePTFE vent (oleophobic membrane on a pressure-sensitive acrylic adhesive ring, ~Ø10-12 mm) applied over a Ø3 mm through-hole cast directly in the housing wall (core pin in the die, spot-faced by the existing machining op), with an as-cast rib shield around it that deflects pressure-wash jets (replacing the separate cap). Adhesive vents are made for manual or automated installation on metal and plastic housings and equalise pressure while blocking liquids and dirt. Airflow is sized to the housing free volume (~0.6-1 L) so that a 60 K temperature drop during wading equalises in < 30 s, keeping the differential well under the 7 kPa threshold.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cheaper vent part (no moulded body, O-ring or cap), no drilled-and-tapped port, faster application than torqueing, and the separate splash cap replaced by a cast rib.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Housing: drilling and tapping (~6 s) replaced by a cast core hole plus spot-face in existing op. Assembly: torque station step replaced by automated vent application with press roller (~3 s) and vision check. Die insert modification for the core pin and rib.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count per unit −3 (PCE body, O-ring, cap). Vent applied on a flat spot-faced pad; vision verifies presence and centring (poka-yoke). Serviceable only by unit replacement, as today.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — low-risk part swap on both 48 V units, wading-relevant
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Vent part: PCE with O-ring → adhesive ePTFE vent (2 units) €1.90→€0.76; Port: drill + tap → cast core hole + spot-face €0.50→€0.20; Assembly: torque → adhesive application €0.20→€0.12; Splash cap → as-cast rib shield €0.60→€0.00. Net = €2.12 per vehicle; the range €1.80-€2.40 brackets piece-price uncertainty. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €90K-€120K per year (no realisation factor applied).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: adhesive peel under pressure-wash, membrane blockage by mud in off-road use, water entry at wading. Validate with ISO 20653 IPX9K and IP6K7 on mud-contaminated units, ISO 16750-4 thermal shock by water splash, ISO 16750-5 chemical resistance, adhesion/peel after ageing, and airflow retention measurements.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: GORE Automotive Vents, adhesive series (2025 datasheet) — Adhesive ePTFE vents for manual or automated installation on metal and plastic electronics housings, equalising pressure while blocking liquids and dirt. How this differs: We apply the adhesive vent to the luxury-SUV 48 V units with a cast-in shield rib sized for wading and pressure-wash; no OEM implementation is claimed and costs are estimates.

ideaData.materialGrade: PA66 PCE body + ePTFE + FKM/silicone O-ring + PA cap → adhesive-backed oleophobic ePTFE vent on acrylic PSA
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Drill + tap port, torque PCE, fit cap ⟶ cast core hole + spot-face, automated adhesive vent application with roller and vision
ideaData.regulatoryContext: No regulatory impact.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Pressure change from cooling: Δp ≈ p0 · ΔT/T = 101 kPa × 60/358 ≈ 17 kPa for a sealed housing cooling from 85 °C to 25 °C in a wading splash — far above the ~7 kPa that drives seal leakage. A vent with airflow Q ≈ 50-100 ml/min at 7 kPa equalises a 0.8 L housing's required ~135 ml mass change within ~2 min under constant Δp, and faster in practice since Δp falls with flow; with the cast rib preventing direct jet impact, water-entry pressure of the oleophobic membrane (≥ 60-100 kPa) is not exceeded at 1 m immersion (10 kPa).
engineering.specDeltas: Delete per unit: PCE (PA66 body, ePTFE, O-ring), protective PA cap, M12 × 1.5 tapped port. Add: Ø3.0 ±0.1 mm cast core hole, spot-face Ø14 mm Ra ≤ 3.2 µm flatness 0.05 mm, as-cast U-rib shield 4 mm high around the vent; adhesive ePTFE vent Ø12 mm, oleophobic grade, water-entry pressure ≥ 60 kPa, airflow ≥ 50 ml/min at 7 kPa. Surface prep: plasma or isopropanol wipe before application; roller pressure ≥ 20 N.
engineering.validationPlan: Ingress: ISO 20653 IPX9K (80 °C, 8-10 MPa jet) and IP6K7 (1 m, 30 min) on 6 units per type, including after mud slurry contamination (off-road dust/mud test, OEM spec). Thermal shock by splash water ISO 16750-4 (n = 6). Adhesion: peel/pull after 1,000 h at 125 °C and 85/85 damp heat. Airflow retention ≥ 70 % after durability. Chemical: ISO 16750-5. PPAP: product change, ~6 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: Housing machining loses drill/tap cycle (6 s), die insert gains a core pin and rib. Assembly replaces a torque operation with automated vent application and vision check (~3 s). Fewer parts to kit. The cast rib replaces a separate cap that could be forgotten.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (two units): vents fall from €1.90 to €0.76, port drilling/tapping €0.50 becomes €0.20 for spot-facing, assembly €0.20 becomes €0.12, and the €0.60 splash caps are replaced by the cast rib. Not included: die modification (in tooling investment). Net of the bridge lines: €2.12 per vehicle; investment €150K pays back in ~17 months at the mid-point saving.

Port: drill + tap → cast core hole + spot-face

title: Power-sized 48 V battery: 0.45 kWh high-power LFP replaces 0.9 kWh pack
description: [MHEV] Cell cost scales with Ah: halving capacity removes roughly half the cathode/anode material even though high-power cells cost more per kWh (~€290/kWh vs ~€220/kWh). Housing, thermal interface and mounting all shrink with the cell stack. Baseline: many luxury-SUV 48 V batteries are specified around 0.8-1.0 kWh (14s or 12s, 18-25 Ah energy-leaning cells) because the first sizing pass was done on usable energy for coasting and boost. The governing requirement of a P0/P1 BSG at 15-25 kW is power, not energy: a 4 s boost of 20 kW consumes only 22 Wh and a 10 s braking event at 15 kW returns ~42 Wh. Proposal: re-size the pack on a power-and-throughput basis to ~0.45 kWh using 14s1P high-power LFP cells of ~9-10 Ah (pouch or hard-case prismatic) with DCIR ≤1.6 mΩ at 50 % SOC/25 °C, which comfortably supplies the BSG rating of 15-18 kW (375-450 A at ~40 V for 10 s) — about 40-45C on a 10 Ah cell, inside LFP power-cell capability. Usable window 20-80 % SOC gives ~0.27 kWh, which covers three back-to-back boosts with no recuperation. Benchmarks: the Mazda CX-60 3.3 e-Skyactiv D M Hybrid Boost runs a 0.33 kWh, 44.4 V battery; A123 published an 8 Ah, 0.4 kWh 14S1P pouch pack for 48 V mild hybrids; the Evoque MHEV is described at about 200 Wh. Audi MHEV plus shows the opposite design point (1.76 kWh for ~20/25 kW) because it adds electric creeping, which our SUV does not.

engineering.mechanism: Energy per event is small: boost 18 kW × 4 s = 20 Wh; regen 15 kW × 10 s = 42 Wh; even three consecutive full boosts use 60 Wh. Power is the constraint: at 40 V a 15 kW BSG draws 375 A. Cell heat per cell P = I²R = 375² A² × 1.6 mΩ = 225 W, i.e. ≈3.15 kW for the 14s string during a 10 s pulse (31.5 kJ), raising a 0.45 kWh pack (~5.5 kg cells, cp ≈1,000 J/kgK) by ~5.7 K per full 10 s pulse — acceptable because real boosts last 2-4 s (≈1.1-2.3 K) and cool between events, but it is why a power-sized pack needs the BMS derating map. Life is governed by Ah throughput: assuming 60,000 Ah over life on a 10 Ah cell = 6,000 equivalent full cycles at shallow DoD, inside LFP power-cell capability (A123 quotes >5,600 W/kg).
engineering.specDeltas: Cell spec: capacity 10 Ah ±3 %, DCIR(10 s, 50 % SOC, 25 °C) ≤1.6 mΩ, 10 s discharge ≥45C, 10 s charge ≥30C at 25 °C and ≥5C at -10 °C. Pack: 14s1P, 44.8 V nominal, 0.45 kWh, usable 20-80 % SOC. Peak current limit 450 A/10 s, continuous 120 A. Housing length reduced ~70 mm; busbar pitch new. Deleted: one cell-format variant, the 0.9 kWh capacity drawing. Requirement document SOC-window and boost-energy budget re-baselined with powertrain calibration.
engineering.validationPlan: Cell: IEC 62660-1/-2 performance and reliability, 6 cells × 3 temps; UN 38.3 for transport. Pack: ISO 21780 / LV 148 electrical (E48-01..E48-22), ISO 16750-3 vibration (random, 3 × 8 h per axis, 3 packs), ISO 16750-4 thermal shock 300 cycles, ISO 6469-1 protections. Durability: 3 packs on a 15-year throughput profile (WLTP + motorway + 3,500 kg towing grade) to <20 % power fade; acceptance DCIR rise ≤30 %. Vehicle: hot-climate (+45 °C) and cold (-30 °C) boost/regen availability. PPAP: new cell part number, full PPAP level 3 and pack re-qualification (~9 months).
engineering.dfmImplications: One new carrier insert and housing tool modification; weld programme updated for new pitch. Same 14 cells and 13 welds so cycle time and fixture count stay; EOL capacity step shorter. Pack weight under 8 kg allows one-person service handling and a lighter bracket.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: cells €198 (0.9 kWh × €220/kWh) → €131 (0.45 kWh × €290/kWh); housing and lid €38 → €33; thermal interface €6 → €4; bracket €9 → €8; a warranty reserve of +€3 for higher C-rate stress is added. title: Heaterless 48 V battery: inverter AC ripple self-heats LFP cells below 0 °C
description: [MHEV] Deletes the heater foil, its switch, fuse branch, connector pins and insulation pad; adds only software in the inverter and BMS. Avoids the LTO route, which would roughly double the cell cost for a cold-acceptance benefit used a few weeks per year. Baseline: graphite-anode 48 V packs that must accept regen in the cold are often given a 150-300 W polyimide or PTC heater foil under the cells, a heater MOSFET or relay, a fused branch and an extra harness pair, because graphite risks lithium plating when charged below 0 °C. The alternatives are LTO cells (Toshiba SCiB, which cold-crank at -30 °C and avoid lithium deposition, but cost roughly 2× per kWh at 2.3 V/cell, needing 20s) or simply accepting reduced cold regen. Proposal: keep LFP/graphite, delete the heater, and warm the cells from inside: at key-on below 0 °C the BSG inverter, with the engine running, drives a bidirectional 1-2 kHz current of ±120 A through the battery (charge and discharge alternately, net zero Ah), so heat is generated in the cell DCIR, which at -20 °C is ~4-5× its 25 °C value. Plating risk is avoided because each charge half-cycle is <0.5 ms. Cold-start cranking is assumed to remain on the 12 V pinion starter (common on I6 MHEV applications); where the BSG is the only starter this idea does not apply. Regen is derated until the cell core passes +5 °C, typically after 4-6 minutes.

engineering.mechanism: Internal heating power P = I_rms² × R_string. At -20 °C a 10 Ah LFP power cell has DCIR ≈7 mΩ (vs ~1.6 mΩ at 25 °C), so 14 cells ≈ 98 mΩ; at 85 A rms, P ≈ 700 W, about 3× a foil heater, and it is deposited in the cell core rather than conducted through the can. Cell mass ~5.5 kg × 1,000 J/kgK → 0.13 K/s, i.e. -20 °C to +5 °C in ~3.5 min. Plating limit: graphite anode overpotential stays above 0 V vs Li/Li+ when each charge pulse is shorter than the double-layer/diffusion time constant (~ms), hence the 1-2 kHz excitation.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: heater foil (PI, 200 W), heater MOSFET + driver, 15 A fuse branch, 2-pin heater connector and harness, silicone insulation pad. Add: inverter software function "BatHeat" (current amplitude ≤120 A peak, 1-2 kHz, enable at T_cell < 0 °C and engine running), BMS temperature-rise monitoring and regen derate map (0 kW at ≤-20 °C rising to full at +5 °C). Battery requirement spec: cold acceptance requirement moved from -20 °C/5 kW to +5 °C/full power after ≤6 min.
engineering.validationPlan: Cell: 3-electrode reference cells, 6 samples, 300 ripple-heating events at -30 °C, then teardown for lithium plating (acceptance: none visible, capacity loss ≤2 %). Pack: ISO 21780 E48 tests during ripple; CISPR 25 conducted emissions; inverter DC-link capacitor ripple life to AEC-Q200 with 1.5× margin. Vehicle: climatic chamber -30 °C cold soak 12 h × 10 starts; winter test trip 2 weeks. PPAP: battery change-point (deleted parts), inverter software release; no cell re-qualification.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes one lamination step and one connector mating (~25 s cycle), EOL heater resistance test removed. Fewer parts in stores (4 part numbers). No new fixtures. Service diagnostics simplified: heater DTC family retired.
engineering.costBridge: Heater foil €6.5 → 0; heater switch and driver €2.2 → 0; harness pair, pins and fuse €1.2 → 0; insulation pad €1.0 → 0; inverter/BMS software and calibration amortised +€0.3. Net ≈€10.6 per vehicle. Not included: fuel penalty from reduced cold regen (estimated negligible in WLTP at 23 °C) and the validation spend (in investment).

title: Sodium-ion power cells remove cold-power capacity oversizing from the 48 V battery

ideaData.title: Sodium-ion power cells remove cold-power capacity oversizing from the 48 V battery
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: graphite-anode lithium chemistries (LFP, NMC) lose most of their low-temperature performance: at -20/-30 °C internal resistance climbs 4-5×, so the string is commonly given a 15-20 % Ah margin, a heater, or both, purely to meet winter requirements. Lithium titanate (Toshiba SCiB) fixes the cold but roughly doubles €/kWh and needs ~20 cells at 2.3 V. Proposal: qualify sodium-ion — hard-carbon anode, layered-oxide or polyanion cathode, aluminium current collectors on both electrodes — as a third chemistry. CATL launched Naxtra sodium-ion in April 2025, claiming discharge capability at -30 °C three times that of LFP, 90 % usable retention at -40 °C, and an integrated 24 V start-stop truck battery. Fourteen sodium-ion cells between 2.6 and 3.85 V span 36.4-53.9 V, inside the ISO 21780 36-54 V window, so BSG, DC-DC and loads see nothing new. The winter Ah margin is deleted, the sloping open-circuit-voltage curve makes state-of-charge estimation easier than with flat LFP, and the bill of materials carries no lithium, nickel or cobalt. Treat as a 2028+ option: automotive high-rate sodium-ion supply and price at scale are the open questions; LFP stays as fall-back source.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Same housing, carrier and BMS hardware (14 channels) — only calibration differs, so the chemistry-agnostic housing concept can take it as a third family. Service parts unchanged except cell-family code.

For LFP at -20 °C, R per cell rises from ~1.6 to ~7 mΩ, so 10 Ah LFP cannot give 15 kW without either more Ah (R ∝ 1/Ah) or heat. title: BMS board mounted on the busbar carrier deletes internal cell-sense harness
description: [MHEV] Deletes the discrete sense harness, one connector pair and the separate BMS housing/screws, paying back the flex circuit; removes manual harness routing labour. Baseline: in many 48 V batteries the BMS is a separate PCB in its own compartment, connected to the cell stack by a discrete sense harness: 15 voltage-sense wires with ring or welded terminals, 4-6 NTC leads, two board-to-wire connectors and harness clips. Proposal: put the AFE/BMS PCB directly on the busbar carrier. A flexible printed circuit (cell-sense flex) runs along the carrier; its nickel tabs are laser-welded to each busbar in the same weld programme that welds the busbars to the cells, and the flex terminates in a press-fit or soldered stiffener on the BMS board, which clips onto the carrier. There is no internal wire harness, no wire-to-board connector pair and no separate BMS compartment. At 48 V (single AFE, no isolation barrier between string and BMS, as the string negative is vehicle ground), this layout is simpler than in HV packs. The BMS keeps one sealed external connector (CAN, wake, 12 V supply, crash line).

ideaData.materialGrade: PVC/XLPE sense wires with CuSn terminals → PI-based flex with Cu 35 µm traces and Ni 200 tabs
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Manual harness routing + connector mating → flex placed on carrier, tabs laser-welded in busbar weld programme
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: The sense path carries only µA-mA (measurement) and ≤300 mA (balancing), so 35 µm × 1 mm traces (R ≈ 0.5 Ω/m) give <0.2 mV error at measurement current. A single 14-16 channel AFE needs all 15 sense points within ~250 mm of the chip, which a carrier-mounted board achieves. Vibration: flex mass is ~15 g vs ~110 g for the wire harness, reducing inertial load on terminals; the tab weld is placed on a strain-relief loop sized for ±0.3 mm busbar movement from thermal expansion (Al α = 23 ppm/K over 100 K across 280 mm ≈0.6 mm, shared over 13 loops).
engineering.specDeltas: New drawing: cell-sense flex, PI 25 µm / Cu 35 µm / PI coverlay, Ni 200 tabs 0.2 mm, 15 sense + 4 NTC circuits. BMS PCB re-laid to sit on carrier, 4 snap features + 2 heat-stakes. Deleted: sense harness assembly, 2 × 16-pin board-to-wire connector pair, BMS compartment cover and 4 screws. Weld programme: +15 tab welds, 0.6 kW, wobble 0.3 mm. Carrier tool: add flex locating pins.
engineering.validationPlan: ISO 16750-3 random vibration 8 h/axis on 3 packs plus mechanical shock 50 g; ISO 16750-4 thermal shock -40/+85 °C, 300 cycles; humidity 85 °C/85 % RH 1,000 h (IEC 60068-2-78). Tab pull ≥40 N before and after ageing (n=30), sense-voltage accuracy ±2 mV through test. EMC CISPR 25. PPAP: new BMS and flex part numbers, pack re-qualification (~6 months).
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes manual harness routing (~90 s) and two connector matings; adds automated flex placement and 15 welds. One fewer sub-assembly kitted to the line. BMS faults now replaced at carrier level; spare-part strategy updated.
engineering.costBridge: Sense harness €4.5 → 0; cell-sense flex +€3.2; BMS connectors €2.4 → €0.6 (one board-edge stiffener); separate BMS housing/cover and screws €2.0 → €0.4; assembly labour €1.5 → €0.8. Net ≈€5.4 per vehicle. Not included: BMS re-layout engineering (in validation investment).

title: Sub-60 V design rules: 48 V battery drops insulation monitor, isolators and HiPot
description: [MHEV] Removes components that address a hazard (electric shock) that does not exist below 60 V, and the associated EOL test time. Smaller creepage allows a tighter, cheaper carrier and fewer barrier sheets. Baseline: 48 V batteries designed by teams used to HV packs often inherit HV features they do not need: an insulation-resistance monitoring circuit, galvanic isolation (digital isolator and isolated DC-DC) between the cell string and the vehicle CAN, HV-style creepage ribs and Kapton/PC barrier sheets, and a 2.5 kV HiPot test at EOL. Under ISO 21780 the 48 V system lives below the 60 V dynamic limit, and below 60 V DC no protection against direct contact is required; insulation monitoring, orange cabling and HV labelling fall away. Proposal: design the battery explicitly to sub-60 V rules: string negative is referenced to vehicle ground through the battery negative terminal, so the BMS needs no isolation barrier; delete the insulation monitor; size creepage/clearance to IEC 60664-1 for 60 V working voltage and pollution degree 2 (~1.0 mm creepage instead of HV-derived 8 mm); replace HiPot by a 500 V DC insulation check between cell stack and housing only where the housing is conductive. Keep functional safety (over/under-voltage, over-current switch, crash disconnect) unchanged.

Short-circuit energy is still high (kA): arc and fire protection remain. Validate to ISO 6469-1 (where applicable), ISO 21780, and the OEM 48 V safety standard; LV 148 E48 tests.

ideaData.materialGrade: PC/PI barrier sheets (HV-derived) → removed or 0.25 mm PP sheet where needed
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: EOL 2.5 kV HiPot → 500 V DC insulation check (conductive housing) or deleted (plastic housing)
ideaData.regulatoryContext: ISO 21780:2020 voltage classes keep the 48 V system below the 60 V DC protection threshold (UNECE R100 high-voltage requirements apply above 60 V DC).
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Shock hazard needs touch voltage above ~60 V DC; the 14s LFP string peaks at 14 × 3.65 = 51.1 V (52-54 V for NMC 12s/13s at full charge), and ISO 21780 caps the dynamic overvoltage at 60 V. Creepage per IEC 60664-1, Table F.5, working voltage 63 V, pollution degree 2, material group IIIa: ~1.0-1.25 mm (versus 8 mm typical in 800 V packs). Isolation monitoring detects a fault path to chassis — meaningless when the string negative is the chassis. CAN transceivers referenced to the same ground need no isolator if ground offset stays inside ±2 V common mode (ISO 11898-2) with the battery grounded within 0.5 m of the body stud.
engineering.specDeltas: BMS: delete digital isolator (2-ch), isolated DC-DC (1 W), IMD measurement network (high-ohm dividers, switches). Carrier/housing: delete HV creepage ribs, set creepage ≥1.25 mm / clearance ≥0.5 mm per IEC 60664-1 at 63 V, PD2. Delete 2 of 3 PC barrier sheets. EOL: HiPot 2.5 kV/60 s → 500 V DC insulation resistance ≥10 MΩ (metal housing only). Requirement document: safety goal list re-based on ISO 21780 voltage classes.
engineering.validationPlan: ISO 21780 E48 tests (E48-01 to E48-22) incl. 60 V dynamic overvoltage and ground offset; ISO 16750-2 electrical. CAN physical layer to ISO 11898-2 with ±2 V ground shift. Humidity/condensation IEC 60068-2-30 6 cycles with creepage check (no tracking). Functional safety: ISO 26262 safety analysis updated (no new ASIL). Samples: 3 packs + 6 BMS boards. PPAP: BMS and carrier change-point, control-plan update.
engineering.dfmImplications: BMS assembly −12 placements; carrier tool simplified (ribs removed); two fewer barrier sheets to place; EOL station time −35 s per pack, which frees a HiPot tester and its safety guarding. No HV-qualified staff needed at the line.
engineering.costBridge: Insulation-monitor circuit €3.0 → 0; galvanic isolation (isolator + isolated supply) €1.8 → €0.3 (non-isolated transceiver only); barrier sheets and creepage ribs €2.5 → €1.2; EOL HiPot test time €1.2 → €0.4. Net ≈€6.6 per vehicle. Not included: certification paperwork savings.

title: Chemistry-agnostic 48 V housing accepts 14s LFP or 12s NMC cells for dual sourcing
description: [MHEV] Competitive tension between two qualified cell families is assumed worth ~5 % on cell price; spot/expedite premiums during allocation are avoided. The added cost is a second carrier insert and busbar set plus calibration. Baseline: a 48 V battery is usually designed around one cell from one supplier; the housing, carrier, busbar pitch and BMS channel count are frozen to that cell. Single sourcing leaves no price leverage and exposes the line to allocation risk. Proposal: design one housing and one BMS that accept two cell families: 14s LFP prismatic (44.8 V nominal, 40.6-51.1 V window) or 12s NMC/LMO power cells (44.4 V nominal, as on the Mazda CX-60 3.3 diesel MHEV, 36-50.4 V window). Both stay inside the ISO 21780 48 V unlimited-operation range at the bus side after the BMS switch. The housing has a common cell bay with two carrier inserts (14-position and 12-position), one BMS PCB with a 16-channel AFE (14 or 12 channels populated in software), two busbar sets and two calibration datasets. Cell envelopes are pre-agreed with two suppliers (a common prismatic size such as a 148 mm-wide low-height can, or equivalent). Two-supplier quotation is run every two years.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: NMC 12s and LFP 14s have different SOC-OCV curves, thermal propagation and cold behaviour; the vehicle energy management must accept both (two calibrations). Validate each variant fully: IEC 62660, UN 38.3, ISO 16750, ISO 21780. Thermal propagation is worse with NMC; keep the venting path rated for NMC.

ideaData.materialGrade: Single-source cell → two qualified families: LFP (LiFePO4/graphite) and NMC (LiNiMnCoO2/graphite) power cells

ideaData.regulatoryContext: Both variants must carry their own UN 38.3 transport certification and EU Battery Regulation labelling of chemistry.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Bus voltage compatibility: 14s LFP 2.9-3.65 V/cell → 40.6-51.1 V; 12s NMC 3.0-4.2 V/cell → 36-50.4 V. Both sit inside ISO 21780 (36 V lower limited, 48 V unlimited, 52 V upper limited), so the BSG, DC-DC and loads see the same envelope. Energy: 14 × 3.2 V × 10 Ah = 0.45 kWh vs 12 × 3.7 V × 10 Ah = 0.44 kWh — equal within 2 %. Price: with two qualified sources, purchasing assumes a 4-6 % reduction on the ~€130 cell set.
engineering.specDeltas: Housing: cell bay length set for 14 × 27 mm LFP or 12 × 31 mm NMC pitch (same stack length ±2 mm). Two carrier inserts (14-pos, 12-pos) with keying ribs. Two busbar sets. BMS: 16-channel AFE, channel population by EEPROM coding; two SOC/SOH model datasets. Cell specs: two drawings with identical terminal height ±0.3 mm and can width ±0.2 mm. Vent path sized for NMC venting rate.
engineering.validationPlan: Full qualification per variant: IEC 62660-1/-2/-3, UN 38.3, ISO 16750-3/-4, ISO 21780 E48 tests, thermal propagation test (nail or heater trigger) on NMC variant with no fire outside housing for 5 min. Vehicle: energy-management calibration for both chemistries, -30 °C/+45 °C climatic tests. PPAP: two cell PPAPs and two pack PPAPs; later re-sourcing becomes a change-point, not a new project.
engineering.dfmImplications: Two carrier inserts and two weld recipes on one line; insert change ~10 min with keying. One housing tool. Stores carry two cell part numbers and two busbar sets. Service: one housing/BMS spare, two cell-family pack assemblies.
engineering.costBridge: Cells €130 → €123.5 (assumed 5 % from dual sourcing); expedite/spot premium average €1.5 → €0.4; added dual calibration amortised +€0.6; added keyed spacer insert +€0.8. Net ≈€6.2 per vehicle. Not included: risk value of avoided line stoppage.

title: Ground-referenced manganin sense element with inverter plausibility retires 48 V Hall sensor
description: [MHEV] A shunt element costs a fraction of a Hall sensor with core and housing; the connector and wiring disappear because the shunt sits on the BMS board edge; better accuracy narrows SOC margins (minor energy benefit not counted). Baseline: some 48 V batteries count charge with a purchased open-loop magnetic-field transducer (ferrite core, ±500 A, its own PBT housing and a 4-wire pigtail to the BMS), sometimes kept from HV practice where galvanic separation from a floating string is mandatory. In a 48 V MHEV the string negative IS chassis ground, so that separation buys nothing, while the transducer offset drift of ±1-2 A over temperature makes coulomb counting wander by 10-20 Ah over a long drive on a 10 Ah pack, forcing frequent OCV-based SOC resets that LFP's flat curve makes unreliable. ideaData.title: Ground-referenced manganin sense element with inverter plausibility retires 48 V Hall sensor
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: some 48 V batteries count charge with a purchased open-loop magnetic-field transducer (ferrite core, ±500 A, its own PBT housing and a 4-wire pigtail to the BMS), sometimes kept from HV practice where galvanic separation from a floating string is mandatory. In a 48 V MHEV the string negative IS chassis ground, so that separation buys nothing, while the transducer offset drift of ±1-2 A over temperature makes coulomb counting wander by 10-20 Ah over a long drive on a 10 Ah pack, forcing frequent OCV-based SOC resets that LFP's flat curve makes unreliable. Proposal: a 100 µΩ CuMn12Ni2 (manganin) resistive element, electron-beam joined between two Cu-ETP CW004A blocks, forms the last link of the string negative; Kelvin pins go straight into the BMS board, read by the AFE current channel at ground potential with no isolation. Integrated offset is in the µV range (≈0.1 A equivalent). Functional-safety redundancy comes from the BSG inverter: its DC-link current, reconstructed from phase currents and duty cycle, is compared with the BMS reading over CAN (±10 % / 50 A), instead of a second physical transducer. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: A shunt element costs a fraction of a Hall sensor with core and housing; the connector and wiring disappear because the shunt sits on the BMS board edge; better accuracy narrows SOC margins (minor energy benefit not counted).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Hall sensor placement, screw and connector mating (~25 s) deleted; shunt busbar welded as a busbar in the existing weld cell. EOL adds a 2-point current calibration (~5 s) on the existing cycler.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −3 (sensor, screw, harness pigtail). The shunt busbar is keyed so it cannot be fitted on the positive side. No orientation error possible (Hall sensors have a direction arrow).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — one component replaced by a cheaper, more accurate one

Per-vehicle bridge (baseline − proposed): Hall current sensor +€6.50; Shunt busbar (incremental over plain busbar) €-1.60; Shunt amplifier / ADC channel €-0.40; Sensor pigtail / connector +€0.80; EOL calibration time €-0.15; net €5.15, stated as a ±10 % range €4.64-€5.67. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €232K-€284K (no realisation factor). Investment (tooling €40,000, capex €60,000, validation €180,000) excluded from the piece-cost saving.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: shunt self-heating at 450 A peak (20 W for 10 s) and thermal EMF at Cu-manganin junctions. Mitigate by sizing for temperature rise <40 K and placing sense pins symmetrically. Validate: AEC-Q200-like stress on the shunt, ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling, accuracy ±0.5 % over -40/+85 °C. Functional safety: ISO 26262 analysis with inverter-current plausibility as second path.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: LEM BMS current sensing portfolio (2023-2024) — LEM states shunts are cost-effective and preferred for automotive BMS current measurement; its HSU combines shunt and open-loop Hall channels in one part.. How this differs: For a grounded 48 V string we use a single shunt and take redundancy from inverter current; LEM's combined part targets HV packs that need two physical channels.

ideaData.materialGrade: Hall IC + ferrite core in PBT housing → CuMn12Ni2 (manganin) 100 µΩ element, EB-welded to Cu-ETP CW004A terminals
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Purchased Hall sensor screwed over busbar → shunt busbar welded in string weld cell, Kelvin pins soldered to BMS
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Shunt: V = I × R = 450 A × 100 µΩ = 45 mV full scale; dissipation P = I²R = 20 W peak (10 s) and ~1.4 W at 120 A continuous. Manganin TCR ≈ ±10 ppm/K, so a 60 K swing changes R by 0.06 % — versus Hall offset drift of ±1-2 A, which over a 10-hour drive of shallow cycling accumulates 10-20 Ah error on a 10 Ah pack. Thermal EMF of Cu/manganin ≈1 µV/K, i.e. <0.2 A equivalent with symmetric sense points.
engineering.specDeltas: New busbar drawing: Cu-ETP CW004A 3 × 20 mm blocks, CuMn12Ni2 element 100 µΩ ±1 %, TCR ≤20 ppm/K, EB-welded, Sn-plated Kelvin pins Ø0.64 mm. BMS: shunt amplifier/ADC channel (or AFE current input), calibration coefficients in EEPROM. Delete: Hall sensor part number, M5 screw, 4-way pigtail. Diagnostic: plausibility vs inverter DC-current estimate, threshold ±10 % / 50 A.
engineering.validationPlan: Accuracy: ±0.5 % of reading +0.2 A from -40 to +85 °C on 10 boards (ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling 500 cycles before/after). Pulse load: 450 A/10 s, 10,000 pulses, ΔR ≤0.2 %. Vibration ISO 16750-3 for the welded joint. Shunt resistor stress per AEC-Q200 test groups (thermal shock, humidity). Pack: ISO 21780 E48 tests; SOC accuracy on a 72 h vehicle drive cycle ≤3 % error. PPAP: BMS and busbar change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes one purchased part and one screw/connector operation (~25 s). Shunt busbar handled like other busbars in the weld cell; keying prevents swapped position. EOL adds 5 s two-point calibration on the existing cycler. Service: no separately replaceable sensor (fault → BMS/carrier).
engineering.costBridge: Hall sensor €6.5 → 0; shunt busbar +€1.6 (vs a plain busbar); ADC/amplifier channel +€0.4; pigtail/connector €0.8 → 0; EOL calibration +€0.15. Net ≈€5.2 per vehicle. Not included: any SOC-window benefit from better coulomb counting.

title: Thirteen 48 V busbars stamped as one lead-frame, insert-moulded, tie-bars punched out
description: [MHEV] Deletes 15 manual/robot placements and ~30 heat-stakes per pack, reduces weld rework from poor fit-up, and simplifies logistics (one moulded subassembly instead of 15 loose parts plus a carrier). Baseline: the 13 series interconnects plus the two end terminals of a 14s 48 V battery are typically stamped as loose parts, bagged, then picked one by one into the plastic carrier and heat-staked or clipped (15 placements and ~30 stakes), after which the carrier is placed on the cell stack for laser welding. Positional scatter of loose busbars (±0.3 mm) adds to the weld gap, which drives weld spatter and rework. Proposal: stamp all 15 conductors as one lead-frame in a progressive die, connected by 2 mm tie-bars, insert-mould the lead-frame into the carrier in one shot (the carrier material is unchanged), then punch the tie-bars out in a post-mould trim station (or in-tool), electrically separating the conductors. Every busbar is located by the mould to ±0.1 mm, carrier-to-busbar retention comes from the overmould rather than stakes, and the 15 picks and 30 stakes disappear. The cell-sense flex tabs then land on precisely located pads. The welding process (remote laser, wobble) is unchanged; the improved fit-up narrows the gap tolerance window that the weld process must tolerate.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Carrier supplier moves from plain moulding to insert moulding (vertical press with shuttle table, ~€300k) plus a trim punch; mould cycle +8 s. Pack line: busbar placement and heat-stake station removed (~70 s). Tie-bar scrap ~4 % of busbar strip.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count at the pack line falls from 16 (15 busbars + carrier) to 1. Wrong-busbar-in-wrong-slot defect becomes impossible. Tie-bar trim verified by an in-line continuity/isolation check between adjacent conductors.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — certain labour and quality saving per pack
costSavingPotential.percentage: 25-35 % of the busbar-carrier subassembly conversion cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Engineering estimate. Per-vehicle bridge (baseline − proposed): Busbar placement labour +€0.90; Heat-staking +€0.40; Weld rework from fit-up +€0.30; Tie-bar scrap €-0.15; Insert moulding cycle + trim €-0.30; net €1.15, stated as a ±10 % range €1.03-€1.26. × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €52K-€63K (no realisation factor). Investment (tooling €140,000, capex €300,000, validation €90,000) excluded from the piece-cost saving.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: incomplete tie-bar separation (short between cells) and overmould cracking at the busbar edges under thermal cycling (Al α 23 ppm/K vs PP-GF ~30-40 ppm/K in-flow). Mitigations: 100 % isolation test after trim (≥10 MΩ at 100 V), radiused busbar edges, glass-fibre orientation. Validate ISO 16750-4 thermal shock, ISO 16750-3 vibration, weld pull after ageing.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Tab-to-busbar welding practice for EV packs (2025 review) — Laser, ultrasonic and resistance welding of tab-to-busbar joints are reviewed for EV packs, with fit-up/gap control as a key condition for laser joint quality.. How this differs: We control fit-up by insert-moulding a lead-frame; lead-frame overmoulding is general electronics practice and is not attributed to a named 48 V battery.

ideaData.materialGrade: Busbar alloy unchanged; carrier unchanged (insert-moulded instead of plain moulded)
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: 15 loose stamped busbars picked + heat-staked into moulded carrier → lead-frame progressive-die stamping, insert moulding, tie-bar punch-out
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Laser lap/fillet welds on 1-1.5 mm Al tolerate a gap of roughly 10 % of sheet thickness (0.1-0.15 mm) before undercut/porosity rises. Loose busbars in a carrier with ±0.3 mm positional scatter plus cell-height tolerance ±0.2 mm can exceed this, driving rework; a mould-located lead-frame (±0.1 mm) removes most of the busbar contribution so the gap budget is dominated by cell height. Tie-bars of 2 mm × 1.5 mm section are sheared in one punch stroke; creepage after trim ≥2 mm, ample for ≤3.65 V between neighbours and 51 V end-to-end.
engineering.specDeltas: New lead-frame drawing: 15 conductors joined by 2 × 1.5 mm tie-bars at 22 positions, pilot holes for the progressive die, edges radiused R0.3. Carrier drawing: insert-moulded, no stake bosses; 22 trim windows for punch access. Trim station: 22-punch tool, isolation test ≥10 MΩ at 100 V between adjacent conductors. Delete: 15 busbar part numbers (become one lead-frame), heat-stake programme.
engineering.validationPlan: 100 % isolation test after trim; Cpk ≥1.67 on busbar position (CMM, n=125). ISO 16750-4 thermal shock 300 cycles and ISO 16750-3 vibration on 3 packs with overmould crack inspection (dye penetrant). Weld fit-up study: gap distribution before/after, rework rate. Retention push-out per busbar ≥150 N after ageing. PPAP: carrier supplier new process (level 3); pack change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Pack line loses a station (placement + heat-stake ~70 s). Carrier supplier adds an insert-moulding press and trim tool. Logistics: one subassembly part number instead of 16. Poka-yoke: wrong-slot busbars impossible; trim completeness tested 100 %.
engineering.costBridge: Busbar placement labour €1.1 → €0.2; heat-staking €0.4 → 0; weld rework from fit-up €0.5 → €0.2; added tie-bar scrap +€0.15; added insert-moulding cycle and trim +€0.3. Net ≈€1.15 per vehicle. Not included: logistics/packaging savings on loose busbars.

title: Coulomb counter folded into one 48 V AFE, deleting gauge IC and isoSPI link
description: [MHEV] Consolidating three chips (two AFEs, current gauge) and a communications link into one 16-channel AFE removes ICs, a transformer pair and supporting passives and PCB area. Baseline: older 48 V BMS designs often split monitoring across a cell-voltage AFE (sometimes two smaller AFEs daisy-chained by an isoSPI/transformer link because each covered only 6-12 cells), a separate current-measurement / coulomb-counting IC or MCU ADC channel, and a supervisor. Proposal: a single 16-channel automotive AFE covering all 14 cells, with an integrated current-sense input and coulomb counter, communicating over SPI directly to the BMS microcontroller on the same board. With one AFE there is no daisy chain, so the isoSPI transceivers and pulse transformers go. NXP material for 48 V packs notes a single AFE is the norm; current 16-channel parts (e.g. ADI ADBMS6948) cover a 14s string with two spare channels. Redundant over-voltage detection — needed for the safety goal — uses the AFE's secondary comparator path rather than a second chip.

Mitigate with the AFE's independent secondary measurement path and MCU plausibility; ISO 26262 FMEDA must show the SPFM/LFM targets met. Validate AFE to AEC-Q100 Grade 1; BMS to ISO 16750-4, LV 124 and CISPR 25; voltage accuracy ±2 mV.

ideaData.materialGrade: 2 × 8-12 ch AFE + isoSPI + gauge IC → 1 × 16-ch AFE with current input (AEC-Q100 Grade 1)
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Two-pass SMT incl. tall transformers → single-pass SMT
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: A 14s string spans 0-51 V, within the common-mode range of a 16-channel AFE (≈80 V absolute max on parts in this class), so no stacking of chips is needed. The isoSPI link exists only to cross the voltage difference between stacked AFEs; with one AFE the MCU can share its ground. Coulomb counting integrates the shunt voltage at ≥1 kHz; an integrated ΔΣ current channel with ±10 µV offset gives 0.1 A offset on a 100 µΩ shunt — better than a discrete gauge with a 0.5 A budget.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: second AFE, two isoSPI transceivers, two pulse transformers, discrete coulomb-counter IC, ~25 passives. Keep: one 16-ch AFE (AEC-Q100 Grade 1) with current input, SPI to MCU. PCB: 4-layer, area −18 %. Software: AFE driver merged, cell-channel map, secondary OV comparator configured, plausibility AFE-sum vs pack-voltage ±0.5 V.
engineering.validationPlan: AFE: AEC-Q100 Grade 1 (supplier data). Board: ISO 16750-4 thermal 500 cycles; LV 124 E-tests on supply; CISPR 25 class 5 radiated/conducted; voltage accuracy ±2 mV, current ±0.5 % on 10 boards. Safety: ISO 26262-5 FMEDA (SPFM ≥90 %, LFM ≥60 % for ASIL B goal assumed). Pack: ISO 21780 E48. PPAP: BMS re-qualification (~6 months).
engineering.dfmImplications: One SMT pass instead of two (tall transformers removed), ~40 fewer placements, simpler ICT with fewer probes. Smaller BMS board fits the carrier-mounted layout. No new line equipment; one AFE part number across 14s LFP and 12s NMC variants.
engineering.costBridge: Second AFE €4.2 → 0; isoSPI transceivers and transformers €2.6 → 0; discrete gauge IC €2.0 → 0; primary AFE upgraded to 16-ch with current input €3.1 → €4.0. Net ≈€7.9 per vehicle. Not included: software re-work (in validation investment).

title: Inline OCT weld-depth monitoring replaces destructive pull tests on 48 V busbar welds
description: [MHEV] Fewer scrapped audit packs, less pull-test labour, retired X-ray audit and lower field warranty for high-resistance joints, minus the OCT equipment amortisation. Baseline: laser welds between busbars and cell terminals in 48 V batteries are commonly controlled by process parameters plus periodic destructive sampling (one pack per shift or per 500 is sacrificed for peel/pull tests and cross-sections), and sometimes X-ray/CT audits; weld depth itself is not measured on every weld. Proposal: add optical coherence tomography (OCT) to the existing remote laser welding head. OCT projects a low-power NIR measurement beam through the welding optics and measures true keyhole depth in-process; research on remote laser welding of battery tab connectors (including Cu-Al) shows it monitors weld penetration depth directly. Every one of the 26 welds (13 busbars × 2) is recorded with a depth trace; out-of-window welds (penetration <0.8 mm or through-weld risk >1.4 mm into a 1.5 mm terminal) are flagged and the pack goes to rework before EOL. Destructive sampling drops from 1/500 to 1/5,000 as an audit, and the X-ray audit is retired.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: OCT module retrofit on the scanner head (~€180k for two heads), no cycle-time impact (measurement is coaxial and simultaneous). Rework loop moves upstream of EOL. Destructive lab workload falls ~90 %.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No product change. 100 % weld traceability per pack serial for the battery passport and field analysis. Poka-yoke: the line PLC blocks transfer of any pack with a red weld.

Investment (tooling €0, capex €180,000, validation €60,000) excluded from the piece-cost saving.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: OCT signal noise on reflective Al/Cu surfaces and false calls. Mitigate with correlation study to cross-sections (n ≥200 welds), threshold tuning, and keep a reduced destructive audit. Standards: control plan per IATF 16949; product validation unchanged (ISO 16750-3 vibration on joints). MSA required for the OCT gauge (gauge R&R ≤20 %).

How this differs: We use it to replace destructive sampling on a small 48 V pack line; adoption by any named OEM is not claimed.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Parameter control + 1/500 destructive sampling + X-ray audit → 100 % in-process OCT depth measurement + 1/5,000 audit
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Joint resistance depends on fused area: a 6 mm seam at 0.8 mm penetration in Al gives ~4.8 mm² weld cross-section per seam; two seams carry 450 A at ~47 A/mm², with resistance ≈10 µΩ. If penetration falls to 0.4 mm (focus drift, contamination), the joint resistance roughly doubles and I²R heating at 450 A rises from 2 W to 4 W per joint, which in a 26-joint string is detectable only by in-process depth or EOL DCIR. OCT resolves depth to ~±50 µm at kHz sampling, so a shallow weld is caught on the weld it happens.
engineering.specDeltas: Process: add OCT measurement to both scanner heads; weld window penetration 0.8-1.2 mm (terminal 1.5 mm), seam length 6 ±0.5 mm. Control plan: 100 % OCT, reaction plan (red → rework station, 2 red/shift → stop). Destructive audit 1/500 → 1/5,000; X-ray audit deleted. Data: depth trace stored per weld per pack serial for 15 years.
engineering.validationPlan: Correlation study: 200 welds sectioned vs OCT reading, R² ≥0.9, no false accepts at the lower limit. MSA: gauge R&R ≤20 % of tolerance. Process capability Cpk ≥1.67 on penetration over 30 days. Product: no change, but a confirmation ISO 16750-3 vibration on 3 packs built under OCT control. PPAP: process change-point (PFMEA/control plan update), no product re-qualification.
engineering.dfmImplications: No new station or fixture; OCT sensor head on the existing scanner. Rework station receives flagged packs before EOL, so EOL scrap falls. Lab destructive testing workload −90 %. Calibration of OCT reference weekly.
engineering.costBridge: Scrapped audit packs €0.5 → €0.05; pull-test/cross-section labour €0.6 → €0.1; X-ray audit €0.4 → €0.1; warranty for high-resistance joints €0.8 → €0.4; OCT depreciation +€0.35. Net ≈€1.3 per vehicle. Not included: reputational value of avoided field fires.

title: Four NTCs on the cell-sense flex plus thermal model replace fourteen leaded NTCs
description: [MHEV] Ten fewer sensors with leads, clips and potting; fewer AFE inputs and no external multiplexer; automatic placement on the flex at the flex supplier instead of manual sensor fitting on the pack line. Baseline: some 48 V battery designs fit one leaded NTC per cell (14 sensors), each potted or clipped to the can and wired back to the BMS, carried over from HV practice where cell-level thermal runaway detection drives the count. Proposal: four SMD NTCs soldered or conductively bonded on the cell-sense flex at the busbar weld points of cells 1, 5, 10 and 14 (ends and hottest middle positions found by CFD), plus one NTC on the BMS board for ambient and one on the shunt. A lumped thermal model in the BMS estimates every cell temperature from current, DCIR and the measured points. In a 0.45 kWh pack with a common conductive floor, cell-to-cell temperature spread under drive cycles is small (CFD and test target ≤3 K), and the busbar is a good thermal tap into the cell (Al conductor attached directly to the terminal). AFE GPIO count drops, and the AFE without external multiplexer suffices.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −10 sensors and their clips; no mis-seated sensors or loose leads to trap under the lid. Diagnostic coverage is maintained by model-vs-measurement plausibility and per-cell DCIR monitoring.

Mitigate with DCIR monitoring per cell (voltage response to current pulses, which the AFE measures every cycle) and OCT-controlled welds. Validate on 3 packs with heated-cell fault injection: detection within 30 s. ISO 16750-4 thermal; ISO 26262 safety analysis for over-temperature goal.

ideaData.materialGrade: 14 × leaded epoxy-bead NTC 10 kΩ → 4 × SMD 0603 NTC 10 kΩ ±1 % (AEC-Q200) on flex
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Manual sensor clip/pot on cans → SMD placement during flex fabrication
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Heat per cell at 120 A continuous: 120² × 1.6 mΩ = 23 W across 14 cells (1.6 W/cell). With a common floor conductance of ~1.5 W/K per cell, steady-state rise is ~1 K, and differences between cells come mainly from position (end cells lose more to the housing). A 4-point measurement plus a lumped RC model (Rth ~0.7 K/W, Cth ~280 J/K per cell) reconstructs intermediate cells within ±2 K. An internal fault adding 5 W shows up as a DCIR/voltage anomaly faster than as a conducted temperature rise at a can-mounted NTC.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: 14 leaded NTCs, 14 clips/potting dots, NTC wire leads, AFE external mux. Add: 4 × 0603 NTC 10 kΩ B25/85 3435 K ±1 % on the flex at busbar tabs of cells 1, 5, 10, 14; 1 board NTC; 1 shunt NTC. Software: lumped thermal model, per-cell DCIR estimator, plausibility check (model vs measured ±4 K). Requirements: over-temperature detection time ≤30 s.
engineering.validationPlan: CFD and thermocouple-instrumented pack (28 TCs) on WLTP, motorway, towing-grade and -30/+45 °C soaks: model error ≤±2 K (n=3 packs). Fault injection: heater on one middle cell at 5 W, detection ≤30 s. ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling; AEC-Q200 NTCs. ISO 26262 FMEDA update. PPAP: BMS and flex change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes 14 manual placements and potting dots (~84 s), adhesive cure WIP and a dispense valve. NTCs come pre-placed on the flex, so the pack line has no sensor-fitting step. Fewer pack-line rejects for sensor mis-seating or missing potting.

title: 48 V pack EOL: DCIR pulses and OCV replace the full capacity cycle
description: [MHEV] Cycler channel time falls ~85 %, so fewer channels and less floor space; energy for the cycle (partly recovered) drops; WIP between assembly and shipment shrinks. Baseline: some 48 V battery EOL lines discharge and recharge every pack at ~1C to confirm capacity (≈55-65 min on a cycler channel including rests), then charge to shipping SOC. Proposal: since cells arrive formation-graded (capacity, ACIR/DCIR, self-discharge measured by the cell maker) and the pack is a 14s1P string, pack capacity equals the lowest cell capacity, already known from the birth data. Replace the capacity cycle with: (1) per-cell OCV check (balance ±10 mV), (2) a 10 s discharge pulse at 5C and 10 s charge pulse at 3C measuring string and per-cell DCIR — which also detects any high-resistance weld or busbar — (3) BMS functional and switch tests, and (4) a short top-up to shipping SOC. Total ~6 min on the cycler. Capacity is audited 1 pack in 200 with the full cycle. Battery Design notes DCIR is typically quoted for a 10 s pulse; cell makers grade capacity and DCIR at formation.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: EOL 1C discharge + charge capacity cycle (≈60 min) → OCV check + 10 s DCIR pulses + BMS functional test + top-up (≈6 min) with 1/200 capacity audit
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: In a 1P series string the pack Ah equals min(cell Ah): assembly cannot add or remove capacity, only resistance (welds) and imbalance (SOC). A 10 s pulse at 50 A (5C) produces ΔV ≈ I × DCIR = 50 A × 1.6 mΩ = 80 mV per cell, resolvable to ±1 mV, so a weld adding 0.2 mΩ (12 %) is visible. A full 1C cycle at 10 A takes 60 min discharge + 60 min charge (or ~55 min with partial-window testing) — it measures what the cell maker already measured on 100 % of cells.
engineering.specDeltas: EOL specification: delete capacity cycle; add OCV per cell (balance ≤10 mV), discharge pulse 50 A/10 s and charge pulse 30 A/10 s, per-cell DCIR limits (mean ±15 %, string ≤25 mΩ incl. busbars), BMS switch on/off and current-sensor 2-point calibration, top-up to 30 % SOC. Audit: full 1C capacity test 1/200 packs. MES: pack capacity record = min(cell birth capacity).
engineering.validationPlan: Parallel run 1,000 packs: both test methods, zero escapes of packs failing capacity spec; DCIR repeatability gauge R&R ≤10 %. Seeded defects: packs with one deliberately poor weld (n=10) detected 10/10. Process capability on DCIR Cpk ≥1.33. PPAP: process change-point; customer notification; no product re-qualification.
engineering.dfmImplications: Cycler channels 12 → 3, floor space ~40 m² released, WIP buffer from ~12 packs to ~3. Test-adapter contact wear reduced (fewer hours under current). EOL becomes a stronger weld check because per-cell DCIR is recorded for every pack.

title: 48 V battery-to-BSG cable in 50 mm² aluminium with ultrasonically welded Cu-Sn ends
description: [MHEV] Al conductor at ~€3/kg vs Cu at ~€9.5/kg, with 43 % of the mass of the copper cable; the transition ends cost more than plain crimped lugs but less than the copper saved. Baseline: the 48 V positive cable from a rear-underfloor or cabin battery to the engine-bay BSG/DC-DC junction (~4.5 m) is typically 35 mm² Class 5 copper with T3 (125 °C) insulation, with tinned copper tube lugs crimped at both ends. Proposal: 50 mm² EN AW-1370 aluminium conductor (same DC resistance as ~31 mm² Cu, adequate for the 15-18 kW BSG duty), T3 thin-wall insulation, and an Al-Cu transition at each end made by ultrasonically welding the Al strands onto a tin-plated Cu-ETP (CW004A) contact part, then sealing the joint with an adhesive-lined heat-shrink to keep electrolyte out of the bimetal interface. Ultrasonic welding of compacted Al strands to Cu is solid-state, so brittle Al-Cu intermetallics stay thin (<2 µm) compared with fusion welding. The lug part remains Cu, so the battery and BSG terminal studs and torque specs do not change. Bimetal Al-Cu busbar and terminal joints are an established published solution in battery assemblies.

engineering.mechanism: Resistance R = ρL/A: Cu 35 mm² × 4.5 m → 0.0172 × 4.5 / 35 = 2.21 mΩ; Al (ρ ≈0.0282) 50 mm² → 2.54 mΩ (+15 %). At a 15 kW boost (375 A) loss rises from 311 W to 357 W for ≤10 s, i.e. +46 W transiently and ~+3 W at 35 A RMS average — negligible. Thermal: same rated rise with +43 % section. Mass: Cu 4.5 × 35 × 8.96 = 1.41 kg; Al 4.5 × 50 × 2.7 = 0.61 kg (−0.8 kg). Ultrasonic welding removes Al2O3 by scrubbing at 20 kHz, bonding solid-state.
engineering.specDeltas: Cable: FLRY-type T3 50 mm² EN AW-1370 Class 5, wall 1.0 mm, OD ~11.5 mm (from 10.0). Ends: Cu-ETP CW004A Sn 3-5 µm contact plate with M8 eye, ultrasonic weld pull ≥2,500 N, joint resistance ≤40 µΩ. Seal: adhesive-lined polyolefin shrink 3:1, 40 mm. Clips: OD 12 mm. Delete: 35 mm² Cu cable, 2 crimped Cu tube lugs. Drawing note: Al cable must never be crimped directly to studs.
engineering.validationPlan: ISO 6722-1 (Al conductor cables) incl. pressure, abrasion, fluids; USCAR-38/LV 214 weld tests (pull n=30, resistance), thermal cycling 1,000 × -40/+125 °C, current cycling 1,000 × 450 A/10 s, salt spray IEC 60068-2-52 severity 3, humidity IEC 60068-2-30, vibration ISO 16750-3. Acceptance ΔR ≤20 % from initial, no corrosion beyond seal. Vehicle: hot-climate road test with thermocouples. PPAP: harness supplier new process PPAP level 3.

title: Inter-cell barrier: PC sheets and PI corner tape replaced by supplier double PET wrap
description: [MHEV] Second wrap done in-line at the cell maker is cheaper than 13 die-cut PC sheets plus manual corner taping in the pack plant; one fewer adhesive interface. Baseline: prismatic cells in 48 V batteries are delivered with a single 0.11 mm blue PET wrap on the aluminium can (the can is often at positive or floating potential), and the pack assembler adds a 0.5 mm polycarbonate (PC) sheet between each pair of cells plus polyimide (PI) tape over the can corners, for dielectric margin and abrasion protection — 13 sheets and ~28 tape pieces per pack. Proposal: specify a second 0.11 mm PET wrap applied by the cell maker on its existing wrapping machine (two layers, staggered seams), giving 0.22 mm total PET and >8 kV dielectric strength — far above the ~51 V maximum between adjacent cans — and delete the PC sheets and PI tape. Abrasion protection at corners comes from the double wrap plus a 1 mm radius on the carrier rib that touches the can. For LFP cells at 48 V the thermal-propagation barrier role of the PC sheet is minor; propagation is managed by chemistry and the vent path. The adhesive structural bond (where used) is applied directly to the PET.

engineering.mechanism: Voltage stress between adjacent cans is at most one string voltage step: worst case ≈51 V (if cans float at terminal potentials across the string), typically ≤3.65 V between neighbours. PET dielectric strength ~100 kV/mm, so 0.22 mm withstands ~20 kV theoretically and >8 kV with defects; the PC sheet adds no needed margin. Mechanical: vibration-induced fretting at corners is the real failure mode; the double wrap doubles the wear-through life, and a 1 mm radius on the carrier halves the contact pressure peak compared with a sharp edge.
engineering.specDeltas: Cell drawing: add second blue PET wrap 0.11 mm, seams staggered ≥90°, 500 V/1 s dielectric test 100 %, wrap adhesion ≥4 N/25 mm. Pack: delete PC sheet (13 ×) and PI tape (~28 pieces), stack length −6.5 mm (end-plate/strap length adjusted), carrier contact rib radius 1.0 mm. Vision check "sheet present" deleted.
engineering.validationPlan: ISO 16750-3 random vibration 3 packs × 8 h/axis, then 500 V DC insulation between all adjacent cans ≥100 MΩ. Thermal shock ISO 16750-4 300 cycles. Humidity IEC 60068-2-78 85/85 500 h. Abrasion: reciprocating test on wrap at corner, ≥10⁵ cycles. Cell supplier PPAP for the wrap change (process change notification); pack change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes two manual operations (~40 s) and two part numbers of die-cut sheets/tape; vision station step deleted. Stack gets shorter, which needs one strap/end-plate dimension change. Cell maker adds a second pass on an existing automated wrapper.

title: Stamped closed-barrel Cu-ETP lugs replace machined tube lugs on 48 V branch cables
description: [MHEV] Strip stamping at high stroke rate with reel plating is much cheaper than cutting, flattening and drilling tube; material utilisation is similar but processing steps fall from ~5 to 2. Baseline: 48 V branch and ground cables of 16-25 mm² (battery negative to body, DC-DC 48 V input, e-ARB/e-compressor feeds where present) are commonly terminated with DIN 46235-style tube cable lugs made from drawn or machined Cu-ETP tube, tin-plated, crimped hexagonally. Proposal: progressive-die stamped and rolled closed-barrel lugs from Cu-ETP (CW004A) or Cu-OF strip 1.5-2.0 mm, tin-plated in strip (reel-to-reel) before stamping, with a brazed or laser-welded seam on the barrel to keep it closed under crimp, and an eye with anti-rotation tab. The crimp profile changes from hex to a 4-indent or B-crimp compatible with the stamped barrel. At 48 V, the termination must carry 100-250 A continuous peaks and hold clamp force; it need not meet HV creepage or shielding requirements. Four lugs per vehicle are in scope (two per affected cable).

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Tube cut/flatten/punch/plate → progressive-die stamp and roll, seam laser-weld, reel-fed crimp
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Crimp performance depends on compaction ratio (target 85-90 % of strand area) and barrel wall section; a stamped 1.8 mm strip barrel rolled to Ø8.0 mm gives the same wall as a 1.8 mm tube. Current density in the palm at 250 A over a 1.8 × 14 mm section = 9.9 A/mm² for ≤10 s, acceptable. Voltage drop: crimp resistance ~30-50 µΩ when compaction is in window, i.e. 12 mW/A²-scale loss, identical to a tube lug once the seam is closed (laser-welded seam prevents barrel opening under 50-60 kN crimp force).
engineering.specDeltas: New lug drawings (16 mm² M6, 25 mm² M8): CW004A strip 1.8 mm, barrel ID 6.0/7.2 mm, seam laser weld, Sn 3-5 µm reel-plated (edges unplated allowed outside contact face), anti-rotation tab 3 mm. Crimp spec: B-crimp/4-indent, crimp height tolerance ±0.05 mm, CFM 100 %. Deleted: 2 tube-lug part numbers. Harness drawing: termination call-out updated.
engineering.validationPlan: USCAR-21 / LV 214 crimp qualification on both sizes: pull-out (n=30) ≥ 1,800 N (16 mm²) / 2,300 N (25 mm²), voltage drop initial and after 1,000 h at 125 °C (ΔR ≤50 %), thermal shock 1,000 cycles, salt spray 96 h IEC 60068-2-52, vibration ISO 16750-3 on harness. PPAP: harness supplier and lug supplier PPAP level 3; vehicle validation not required (fit/form unchanged).
engineering.dfmImplications: Reel-fed applicators allow semi-automatic crimping; anti-rotation tab removes a mis-orientation defect at fitting. Same studs and torques. One crimp tool insert per press changed. Lug inventory as reels instead of bags.
engineering.costBridge: Battery-negative lug (25 mm²) €1.4 → €0.6; DC-DC input lug (25 mm²) €1.4 → €0.6; two 16 mm² branch lugs €2.0 → €0.8; crimp-monitoring audit +€0.1. Net ≈€2.7 per vehicle. Not included: crimp tooling inserts (in investment).

title: 58 V MINI blade fuses replace bolt-down fuses on 48 V branches ≤30 A
description: [MHEV] A MINI blade fuse costs a fraction of a bolt-down fuse; the holder replaces studs, nuts and busbar fingers; fitting is a push instead of two torqued nuts. Baseline: 48 V branch protection is often done with bolt-down fuses (MIDI/CF8-style, 58 V rated) on a busbar block next to the battery or DC-DC, even for low-current loads such as the 48 V electric cooling fan, catalyst heater relay supply, seat or screen heaters, and the BMS/inverter control supplies (5-30 A), because one fuse family was chosen for all 48 V circuits. Proposal: keep bolt-down 58 V fuses only for branches above 40 A (BSG, e-ARB); move branches ≤30 A to 58 V-rated MINI blade fuses in a 48 V plug-in fuse holder moulded into the existing distribution block. Littelfuse catalogues 58 V MINI blade fuses (ISO 8820) as well as 58 V MAXI blades with 1000 A interrupting rating at 58 V DC, so the blade format is qualified for 48 V arc interruption. Critical poka-yoke: 32 V and 58 V MINI fuses share a footprint, so the 48 V holder uses keyed cavities and the 58 V fuse colour/marking is controlled, and the service label states 58 V only.

ISO 21780 voltage envelope covered by the 58 V rating.
