ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Bolt-down fuses torqued on studs → blade fuses inserted in moulded keyed holder
ideaData.regulatoryContext: ISO 8820 (road vehicle fuses) governs both formats; the 58 V rating covers ISO 21780 static overvoltage (54 V).
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: DC arc interruption is the constraint: at 48-54 V an arc does not self-extinguish as easily as at 14 V, so the fuse element and body must be rated for 58 V DC (1000 A breaking capacity at 58 V per the MAXI datasheet). For ≤30 A branches, I²t and continuous rating are inside MINI capability; prospective short-circuit current at a branch ~1-2 m from the battery with 4-6 mm² wire is limited to ~1-2 kA by wire resistance (2 m × 2 × 3.5 mΩ/m + battery 25 mΩ ≈ 39 mΩ → ~1.3 kA at 51 V), within the class of tested ratings — to be confirmed per circuit.
engineering.specDeltas: Fusing schedule: branches ≤30 A moved to 58 V MINI (ISO 8820) in keyed cavities; ≥40 A keep 58 V bolt-down. Distribution block: tool insert adds 3 keyed blade cavities with tuning-fork terminals CuSn0.15 Sn-plated; delete 3 pairs of M5 studs/nuts and busbar fingers. Label: "48 V — 58 V fuses only". Workshop manual and parts catalogue updated.
engineering.validationPlan: ISO 8820-1 and -3/-9 at 58 V DC in the actual holder: breaking capacity, time-current at 1.35/2/3.5 × In, temperature rise at In (≤ holder limit 125 °C), 1,000 h at 0.8 × In, ISO 16750-3 vibration, ISO 16750-4 thermal shock. Short-circuit test per branch at prospective current measured on vehicle. Poka-yoke test: 32 V fuse cannot be inserted (n=50 attempts). PPAP: fuse box change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Two torque operations per fuse removed (~36 s total), automated insertion possible. Keyed cavities avoid wrong-fuse insertion. Service: tool-free fuse change, but technician must use 58 V parts (keying enforces). Fewer studs reduce corrosion points.
engineering.costBridge: Three bolt-down fuses €6.6 → 3 MINI 58 V €1.35; fuse block busbar/studs €3.5 → €1.6 (moulded holder); torque labour €0.9 → €0.15; keying and labelling +€0.3. Net ≈€7.6 per vehicle. Not included: changes on branches above 40 A, which keep bolt-down fuses.

title: Cell-sense flex on PET with crimped NTC pads replaces polyimide flex circuit
description: [MHEV] PET substrate and roll-to-roll processing cost less than PI film and panel processing; low-temperature NTC attach avoids a reflow pass, and reel supply cuts handling. Baseline: where the 48 V battery uses a flexible printed circuit (FPC) for cell-voltage sensing, it is typically polyimide (PI) 25 µm with rolled-annealed Cu 35 µm and PI coverlay, chosen because PI survives SMT reflow (260 °C) for the on-flex NTCs and connector. Proposal: a PET-based flexible circuit (PET 50-75 µm base, etched Cu 35 µm or 70 µm Al, PET/adhesive coverlay) processed reel-to-reel, with the four NTCs attached by low-temperature methods — conductive adhesive or crimp/pierce terminals — instead of reflow, and with nickel tabs resistance-welded or laser-welded to the traces before they are laser-welded to the busbars. PET is cheaper than PI by a wide margin, and at the battery's maximum operating temperature (~65 °C cells, ≤85 °C local) it stays well below its ~105 °C long-term rating. The measurement current is µA-level, so trace resistance is irrelevant; only the balancing current (≤300 mA from the AFE) sets trace width.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Panel FPC + SMT reflow of NTCs → reel-to-reel PET flex + conductive-adhesive or crimp NTC attach
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Trace sizing: balancing 270 mA on 1 mm × 35 µm Cu (0.035 mm²) gives 7.7 A/mm² and a temperature rise of a few K — fine. Sense error from 0.5 Ω/m traces at µA is <1 µV. Thermal duty: cells ≤65 °C, flex near busbars ≤85 °C during 450 A pulses; PET RTI ~105 °C, PI ~200 °C+, so PI capacity is unused. The only reason for PI was reflow; low-temperature NTC attach (conductive epoxy cured at 120 °C/10 min) removes it.
engineering.specDeltas: Flex drawing: base PET 50 µm hydrolysis-stabilised, Cu 35 µm ED, PET coverlay 50 µm with acrylic adhesive; trace width 1.0 mm (balancing), 0.3 mm (NTC). NTC attach: Ag-filled epoxy, die-shear ≥20 N, or crimp terminals. Ni 200 tabs 0.2 mm resistance-welded to pads. Stiffener FR4 0.8 mm at connector only. Operating range -40/+105 °C.
engineering.validationPlan: IEC 60068-2-78 damp heat 85/85 1,000 h; ISO 16750-4 thermal shock 500 cycles -40/+105 °C; ISO 16750-3 vibration on pack (3 packs); tab peel and NTC die-shear before/after (n=30); insulation resistance between traces ≥100 MΩ at 100 V after humidity. Sense accuracy ±2 mV. PPAP: flex supplier change, BMS change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Reel-to-reel supply allows automatic placement on the carrier. No reflow profile constraints at the flex supplier. Pack line unchanged; the same flex locating pins and tab-weld programme are used, so no fixture or cycle-time change.
engineering.costBridge: Flex substrate and processing €3.2 → €1.6; NTC attach by conductive adhesive +€0.4; connector stiffener €0.3 → €0.2; yield allowance +€0.1. Net ≈€1.2 per vehicle. Not included: the flex-on-carrier architecture itself (separate idea).

title: Single-shot TPV lip-seal grommet for 48 V cable replaces EPDM grommet and tape
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Thermoplastic injection moulding is faster and cheaper than EPDM vulcanisation; lip seals replace the taping operation; the integrated fir-tree deletes a separate clip. Baseline: where the 48 V main cable passes from cabin or underfloor through the floor or front bulkhead, a moulded EPDM grommet (often with a PA insert for snap retention) is used, the cable is taped to the grommet neck for sealing, and a separate fir-tree clip holds it. For an off-road SUV with 850-900 mm wading depth this pass-through must be watertight under splash and static head. Proposal: a single-shot TPV (EPDM/PP thermoplastic vulcanisate, Shore 60A) grommet injection moulded with three internal lip seals sized to the cable OD (interference 0.6-0.8 mm), an integrated snap flange for the sheet-metal hole and an integrated fir-tree for cable retention. The tape wrap and separate clip disappear. TPV is injection moulded in ~35 s versus compression/transfer-moulded EPDM with vulcanisation (~180 s), and its sprue is recyclable.

ideaData.materialGrade: EPDM 60 Shore A with PA6 insert + PVC tape → TPV (EPDM/PP) Shore 60A, 125 °C grade
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Transfer-moulded EPDM + manual tape seal + separate clip → single-shot TPV injection with integral lip seals and fir-tree
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Sealing is set by contact pressure p ≥ water head: at 1.0 m head p = ρgh = 9.8 kPa. A lip with 0.7 mm interference on Shore 60A TPV (modulus ~3 MPa) produces ~0.3-0.5 MPa contact pressure, a 30-50× margin, persisting while compression set stays below ~40 %. Tape seals depend on operator wrap tension and adhesive creep, typically the leakage path at wading. TPV processes as a thermoplastic: injection cycle governed by cooling of a 3 mm wall (t ∝ s²; ~25-35 s) versus EPDM cure time ~3 min.
engineering.specDeltas: New grommet drawing: TPV Shore 60A ±5, 125 °C grade, compression set ≤35 % (125 °C/70 h), 3 inner lips for OD 11.5 mm ±0.3, interference 0.6-0.8 mm, snap flange for 1.0-2.0 mm sheet, integral fir-tree for Ø6.5 hole. Delete: EPDM grommet + PA insert, PVC tape spec, separate fir-tree clip. Hole in sheet unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: ISO 20653 IPX7 and IPX9K, vehicle wading test 900 mm, 30 min static + 7 km/h bow wave; water-head bench test 1.0 m/30 min after thermal ageing 1,000 h at 125 °C (n=10). Push-in ≤60 N, pull-out ≥150 N. ISO 16750-4 thermal shock 300 cycles, vibration ISO 16750-3 with cable oscillation. PPAP: grommet supplier level 3, harness change-point.
engineering.dfmImplications: Two fewer parts and one operation (taping) at the harness supplier; vehicle fitting is a single snap with audible/tactile confirmation. Grommet is reusable in service (cable replacement without new tape). Moulding scrap recyclable.
engineering.costBridge: Grommet €1.6 (EPDM + insert) → €0.9 (TPV); tape wrap €0.25 → 0; separate fir-tree clip €0.2 → 0; labour €0.35 → €0.15. Net ≈€1.35 per vehicle. Not included: any change in wading-related warranty claims.

title: 48 V cell gap filler: 3 W/mK silicone becomes 1.5 W/mK polyurethane
description: [MHEV] PU gap filler is cheaper per kg than silicone, less dense, and a thinner bondline cuts the quantity; no siloxane-cleaning step before the lid joining. Baseline: 48 V batteries with conductive cooling to the housing floor often carry over a 3 W/mK two-component silicone gap filler (alumina-filled, density ~3.0 g/cm³) from HV packs, dispensed at ~1.5 mm bondline under the cells (~180 g per pack). Proposal: an ATH/alumina-filled two-component polyurethane gap filler at 1.5 W/mK and ~2.2 g/cm³, dispensed at a controlled 1.0 mm bondline (~140 g; achieved by flatter carrier datum and floor ribs). Heat flux in a 48 V MHEV pack is low (≈23 W total at 120 A continuous), so the bondline thermal resistance rise is small, and the change removes the siloxane-contamination concern for later bonding or welding of the lid. Polyurethane TIMs are positioned by their makers as a cost reduction versus industry-standard materials; Henkel launched a 2 W/mK PU thermally conductive adhesive in 2026.

engineering.mechanism: Bondline resistance R = t/(k·A). Cell footprint area 14 × (27 × 148 mm) ≈ 0.056 m². Silicone: 1.5 mm/(3.0 × 0.056) = 0.0089 K/W; PU: 1.0 mm/(1.5 × 0.056) = 0.0119 K/W (+0.003 K/W). At 23 W continuous the extra rise is 0.07 K; at a 225 W boost pulse the transient increment is ~0.7 K but limited by thermal capacitance. Mass: silicone 0.056 m² × 1.5 mm × 3.0 = 252 g (≈180 g with bead pattern); PU 0.056 × 1.0 × 2.2 ≈ 123 g (≈140 g with squeeze-out).
engineering.specDeltas: Material spec: 2K PU gap filler, k ≥1.5 W/mK (ASTM D5470), density ≤2.3 g/cm³, Shore 00 ≤70 after cure, dielectric ≥10 kV/mm, V-0 (UL 94). Bondline 1.0 ±0.3 mm via carrier datum ribs. Dispense: bead pattern 6 × Ø6 mm, ~140 g. Delete: siloxane cleaning step before lid joining. Dispenser: new static mixer and dry-air blanket on PU isocyanate tank.
engineering.validationPlan: Thermal: 3 packs instrumented, towing-grade cycle at +45 °C ambient, cell ΔT ≤2 K vs silicone baseline. Ageing: IEC 60068-2-78 85/85 1,000 h and 1,000 h at 105 °C, then k and adhesion (lap shear) retention ≥70 %. ISO 16750-4 thermal shock 300 cycles, ISO 16750-3 vibration. Fire: UL 94 V-0. PPAP: material change-point, dispense process PPAP.
engineering.dfmImplications: Dispense time −25 % (less volume), cleaning station step deleted, static mixer change. Isocyanate moisture handling added (dry-air, shelf-life control). Same cure WIP; PU green strength helps hold cells during cure.
engineering.costBridge: Filler €5.0 (180 g × €28/kg) → €1.7 (140 g × €12/kg); mixer consumables €0.25 → €0.2; siloxane cleaning €0.3 → 0; moisture-control handling +€0.05. Net ≈€3.6 per vehicle. Not included: the minor mass saving value.

title: Paint-cutting flange nut on 48 V return studs deletes masking caps and lock washers
description: [MHEV] Deletes caps (fit and remove labour plus part), the lock washer, and EOL ground rework from residual paint; the special nut costs slightly more than a plain nut. Baseline: the 48 V return (battery negative and DC-DC/BSG return) is often connected to welded M8 body studs that must be kept free of e-coat and paint: masking caps are pushed on in the body shop before e-coat and removed in final assembly, and the cable lug is secured with a hex nut plus an external tooth lock washer to bite through residual coating. Three such points per vehicle are typical for the 48 V return. Proposal: leave the studs unmasked and use a thread-cutting, serrated-flange ground nut (case-hardened steel, Zn-Ni coated) whose leading threads cut through the e-coat on the stud and whose serrated bearing face cuts the lug/stud interface, giving a gas-tight metal contact. This type of paint-cutting ground nut is established in body electrics; at 48 V return currents (up to ~450 A peak through the main return, ~100 A continuous) the contact resistance target is ≤50 µΩ. Masking caps, their fitting and removal, and the lock washer disappear.

Validate: voltage drop ≤5 mV at 100 A initially and after salt spray (IEC 60068-2-52 severity 3 / ISO 9227 NSS 480 h) and thermal cycling; current cycling 450 A/10 s × 1,000.

How this differs: Paint-cutting ground nuts are general body-electrics practice; their use on any named OEM 48 V return is not claimed.

ideaData.materialGrade: Hex nut M8 class 8 Zn + external tooth lock washer → thread-cutting serrated-flange M8 ground nut, case-hardened, Zn-Ni (≥8 µm) coated
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Mask cap before e-coat, remove at final assembly, nut + washer → no masking, thread-cutting serrated nut with torque-angle control
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Contact resistance is set by real metal-to-metal area under clamp; e-coat (~20 µm, dielectric) blocks it. A thread-cutting nut displaces coating along ~4 thread turns and the serrations penetrate the lug interface, so the current path is metal from first install. At 100 A, 50 µΩ gives 5 mV drop and 0.5 W — the ISO 21780 ground-offset budget (a few hundred mV across the system) is unaffected. Clamp load: M8 at 20 Nm with friction µ≈0.15 gives ~12 kN, sufficient to hold the gas-tight contact through thermal cycling.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: 3 masking caps (body-shop BOM), 3 external tooth lock washers, cap-removal work instruction. Add: M8 thread-cutting serrated-flange ground nut, case-hardened, Zn-Ni ≥8 µm, prevailing-torque window 4-12 Nm, tightening 20 Nm ±10 % with angle monitor. Stud: unchanged weld stud, no mask. EOL: ground voltage-drop check at 50 A ≤5 mV.
engineering.validationPlan: Joint tests (n=30 per point): initial voltage drop ≤5 mV at 100 A; after ISO 9227 NSS 480 h and IEC 60068-2-14 thermal cycling 500 × -40/+105 °C ≤8 mV; current cycling 450 A/10 s × 1,000 with ΔR ≤30 %; torque-tension and loosening (DIN 65151 transverse vibration). Vehicle: ISO 21780 ground-offset test. PPAP: fastener PPAP and body/assembly process change-points.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes cap fit/remove (~33 s labour per vehicle across 3 points) and a washer-feeding step. Nutrunner programme changes to torque-angle. Single-use nut noted in service manual. No forgotten-cap defect.
engineering.costBridge: Masking caps €0.75 → 0 (3 × €0.25); cap fit/remove labour €0.4 → 0; EOL ground rework €0.3 → €0.1; nuts and washers €0.42 → €0.60 (special nut costs more). Net ≈€1.17 per vehicle. Not included: any change of stud or e-coat.

title: Timing drive for BSG run-down without back-rock: tensioner ratchet and slap guards deleted

ideaData.title: Timing drive for BSG run-down without back-rock: tensioner ratchet and slap guards deleted
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the I6 timing drive (crank sprocket, simplex or duplex bush chain, pivoting tensioner guide, fixed guide, hydraulic tensioner) is specified to a 12 V stop-start duty spectrum. Every free engine stop ends with the crank rocking backwards 20-60° as the compressing cylinder springs the crank back; reverse rotation tightens the slack strand, drives the tensioner plunger in and vents its chamber while the oil pump is stopped, so the next start runs with a slack chain. To cover this, the tensioner carries a ratchet (rack, pawl, spring and a transport clip), and the guide faces are sized for start slap. Proposal: on the 48 V MHEV the belt starter-generator controls run-down: below ~300 rpm it applies a braking then holding torque that parks the crank 70-100° after TDC of the cylinder coming to compression with no reverse swing, then restarts in 250-350 ms at 700-900 rpm instead of a 12 V pinion start at 150-250 rpm. With back-rock eliminated and oil pressure re-established in <0.4 s, the tensioner reverts to a plain non-return-valve hydraulic plunger with a leak-down calibrated for running dynamics; the ratchet, pawl, spring and clip are deleted and the guide faces drop their slap-reinforcement. JLR's Ingenium I6 MHEV pairs a belt-integrated starter generator with the engine (sourced); the controlled run-down strategy is general practice described generically here.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Money comes from the ratchet sub-parts (rack, pawl, spring, transport pin), a simpler tensioner body casting, the deleted end-of-line tensioner pump-up/rattle audit, and lower start-rattle warranty, partly offset by BSG run-down calibration effort.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Tensioner supplier deletes one sub-assembly station (pawl/spring insertion) and the transport-pin fit; engine plant deletes the cold-start rattle audit stand at EOL. No change to chain or sprocket lines; tensioner body die gets an insert modification only.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Tensioner goes from 7 to 4 parts; no transport pin to pull at engine assembly (a common missed-step defect). Service: no ratchet reset procedure when the front cover is removed, saving a workshop step and a misbuild mode.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — engineering estimate of €2.15 net per vehicle from the cost-bridge lines
costSavingPotential.percentage: 20-26% of the affected parts' baseline cost (€9.35)
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Tensioner: ratchet rack, pawl, spring and transport pin deleted +€1.7; EOL cold-start rattle audit +€0.25; Start-rattle / chain-noise warranty accrual +€0.6; BSG run-down calibration and back-rock monitor (amortised) −€0.4; net €2.15, ±15 % estimate band → €1.83-€2.47 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €92K-€124K. Payback = (tooling + capex + validation €410000) ÷ (mid annual €108K ÷ 12) ≈ 46 months. All figures are estimates.

ideaData.riskNotes: Failure modes: BSG unavailable (48 V battery cold/low SOC) so the engine coasts down freely and rocks back; belt slip during holding. Mitigation: retain a high-viscosity plunger leak-down and fall back to 12 V pinion starts only with BSG fault flagged. Prove with OEM start-stop durability (300k starts), ISO 16750-3 vibration on the tensioner, chain elongation <0.3 %.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Range Rover / Range Rover Sport Ingenium I6 MHEV (2020-) — Belt-integrated starter generator in place of the alternator on the I6, with 48 V battery and electric supercharger (sourced).. How this differs: JLR is not stated to have changed its timing drive; using BSG-controlled run-down to delete the tensioner ratchet is our proposal, and the ratchet-vs-back-rock physics is from tensioner patents, not an OEM statement.

benchmarkAnchor.borrowedFeature: Belt-integrated starter generator in place of the alternator on the I6, with 48 V battery and electric supercharger (sourced).

ideaData.materialGrade: Tensioner body EN AC-46000 (unchanged); ratchet rack/pawl 16MnCr5 case-hardened → deleted
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Ratcheted tensioner assembly (7 parts) → plain check-valve plunger tensioner (4 parts); BSG run-down calibration
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Chain slack at restart comes from reverse rotation at stop: the last compression cylinder stores ~15-25 J and returns it as 20-60° of back-rotation, which drives the tensioner plunger in by 1-3 mm and vents its oil chamber; with the pump stopped the chamber stays empty. At a 12 V pinion start (150-250 rpm, 0.6-0.9 s to idle) the first 2-4 cam torque reversals (±25-40 Nm on an I6 cam pair) hit a slack strand: peak chain load reaches 3-4 kN vs ~1.5 kN in steady running. BSG run-down with a holding torque of 20-40 Nm at the crank (belt ratio ~2.7:1, so 8-15 Nm at the machine) removes the back-rock entirely, and a 700-900 rpm restart builds 1.5 bar gallery pressure within ~0.3 s, so the plunger is refilled before the first high-torque cam event.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete ratchet rack, pawl, pawl spring and transport pin (4 part numbers) from the tensioner drawing; plunger leak-down time re-specified from 8-12 s to 4-8 s (ISO VG 46 test oil, 100 N); check-valve ball seat unchanged. Guide faces: slap-reinforced 3.5 mm PA46 face → 2.5 mm. Engine software: BSG run-down profile with crank park window 70-100° ATDC ±10°, back-rock limit ≤2° (crank sensor counted). Tensioner body die: insert change to delete ratchet pocket.
engineering.validationPlan: OEM start-stop durability: 300,000 BSG starts on 2 engines (dyno, 20-110 °C oil), plus 30,000 forced free run-downs with BSG disabled to prove the fallback. Chain elongation acceptance <0.3 %, guide wear <0.5 mm. Rattle NVH at cold start -20 °C per OEM sound-quality spec on 3 vehicles. ISO 16750-3 random vibration on 6 tensioners. PPAP level 3 change for the tensioner; engine homologation unaffected (no emission change).
engineering.dfmImplications: Tensioner assembly part count 7 → 4; one pawl insertion and one transport-pin station removed at the supplier; engine line deletes the transport-pin pull step and its vision check. Poka-yoke is easier because there is no ratchet orientation. Workshop: no ratchet release tool.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline ratcheted tensioner ≈ €7.80; plain tensioner ≈ €6.10. EOL rattle audit fixture/time ≈ €0.35 per engine falls to ≈ €0.10 sampling. Start-rattle warranty accrual ≈ €1.20 assumed to halve. BSG run-down calibration and back-rock monitoring adds ≈ €0.40 per vehicle amortised. Not included: any fuel effect, or chain/sprocket changes (none proposed).

title: Petrol I6: fixed-timing exhaust camshaft as 48 V torque fill replaces low-end scavenging
description: [MHEV] Deletes a vane phaser (rotor, stator, lock pin, spring, central bolt valve), the exhaust OCV solenoid, one cam sensor and target, and the oil-feed machining in the head and cam journal; a plain sprocket replaces the phaser. Baseline: the petrol 3.0 L I6 carries vane phasers on both intake and exhaust camshafts. The exhaust phaser (~50° crank authority) earns its place in two regimes: (1) low-speed full load, where intake/exhaust overlap scavenges residual gas through the twin-scroll turbine to raise turbine enthalpy and cut time-to-torque, and (2) part load, where late exhaust closing gives internal EGR. Proposal: on the 48 V MHEV the low-end transient is covered electrically — the BSG (or e-supercharger where fitted) fills 150-250 Nm at the crank for the first 0.5-1.5 s — so scavenging overlap is no longer needed for response, and internal EGR is provided by intake-phaser early opening alone (intake phaser authority widened from 50° to 60°). The exhaust phaser, its oil-control valve (OCV), the cam-bearing oil feed grooves and the exhaust cam position sensor are deleted; the exhaust cam carries a plain bolted sprocket with a dowel at the calibrated fixed angle. Not proposed for

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Head line removes one OCV bore and two oil-feed drillings (≈ 14 s of spindle time); cam line drops the journal groove and cross-drilling; engine assembly removes the phaser torque-angle station on the exhaust side. ideaData.dfmDfa: Head part count −6 (phaser assembly, OCV, sensor, sensor bolt, two plugs); fewer leak paths and one connector fewer on the engine harness. Timing by dowel is poka-yoke and simplifies front-end service.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — engineering estimate of €25.2 net per vehicle from the cost-bridge lines
costSavingPotential.percentage: 70-95% of the affected parts' baseline cost (€30.5)
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines per vehicle: Exhaust vane phaser → sintered sprocket and bolt +€14.3; Exhaust OCV solenoid deleted +€6.8; Exhaust cam sensor and target wheel deleted +€3.2; Head/cam oil-feed machining and plugs +€0.8; Engine harness branch and connector +€0.7; Intake phaser rotor for 60° authority (added) −€0.6; net €25.2, ±15 % estimate band → €21.42-€28.98 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €1.07M-€1.45M. Mitigation: SOC floor reserved for torque fill, intake-only EGR calibration, external LP-EGR if needed. Prove via WLTP/RDE type approval, full-load curves at 20 % SOC, knock margin mapping on dyno.

ideaData.regulatoryContext: Euro 7 (Reg. (EU) 2024/1257) cold-start and RDE limits must be re-demonstrated after the valvetrain change.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Scavenging at 1,200-1,800 rpm uses valve overlap of 30-50° crank so that a pulse from the twin-scroll manifold pulls fresh charge through; trapped residuals fall from ~8 % to ~3 %, letting the engine run ~5-8° earlier spark and spool the turbine 0.3-0.6 s sooner. A 48 V machine adding 150-250 Nm for 1 s delivers the same time-to-90 %-torque without overlap: energy per launch ≈ 15 kW × 1 s = 15 kJ, i.e. 4 Wh of a 0.5-1 kWh pack, well inside the usable window. Internal EGR at part load (10-20 %) can be produced by early intake opening (backflow into the port) with the intake phaser alone, so exhaust timing becomes a fixed compromise set at the best WLTP-weighted angle.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: exhaust vane phaser assembly, exhaust OCV (central or remote), exhaust cam target wheel and Hall sensor, two head oil-feed drillings Ø4 mm and one journal groove 3 × 1.5 mm. Add: sintered D11 sprocket with Ø6 m6 dowel, fixed exhaust timing tolerance ±1° crank. Intake phaser authority 50° → 60° crank (rotor vane angle change only). Head casting unchanged (bosses left blind) for commonality with non-MHEV.
engineering.validationPlan: Engine dyno: full-load and transient (0-90 % torque at 1,250 rpm) mapping at 20 %, 50 %, 80 % 48 V SOC; knock margin and LSPI counts per OEM test (≥ 25 h low-speed high-load). Emissions: WLTP and RDE type-approval runs, Euro 7 cold-start at -7 °C on 3 vehicles. Valvetrain durability 600 h cyclic. Requires full engine re-homologation and PPAP for head and cam.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes one torque-angle tightening station and one OCV insertion with leak test; cam machining loses one drilling op (≈ 9 s). Fixed dowel timing removes a timing-tool alignment step. Engine harness loses one connector branch. Serviceability improves: no exhaust phaser rattle replacement.
engineering.costBridge: Exhaust phaser ≈ €18.50 replaced by sintered sprocket and bolt ≈ €4.20; OCV ≈ €6.80 deleted; cam sensor and target ≈ €3.20 deleted; head and cam oil-feed machining ≈ €1.10 → €0.30; harness branch ≈ €0.90 → €0.20; intake phaser rotor change adds ≈ €0.60. Not included: fuel/CO2 effect (assumed neutral after calibration), any LP-EGR if Euro 7 forces it.

title: Single-wall turbo-outlet downpipe: 48 V EHC heat replaces air-gap double-wall insulation
description: [MHEV] Deletes the austenitic liner (the expensive alloy), the sliding rings and two of four welds; replaces a multi-piece fabrication with one hydroformed tube. Adds a pressed heat shield. Baseline: on the petrol I6 the turbine-outlet downpipe to the close-coupled three-way catalyst is an air-gap-insulated (AGI) double-wall part — inner 0.8 mm 1.4828 austenitic liner, 2-3 mm air gap, outer 1.2 mm 1.4509 ferritic shell, two sliding support rings and four circumferential welds — chosen only to cut wall heat loss in the first 20-40 s of a cold start so the catalyst lights earlier. Proposal: where the vehicle already carries a 48 V electrically heated catalyst (EHC) disc for Euro 7 (a library idea assumed in this baseline), light-off no longer depends on exhaust-gas enthalpy arriving at the brick: the 4 kW disc pre-heats and post-heats the front face. The downpipe becomes a single-wall hydroformed 1.5 mm 1.4509 tube with a clip-on aluminised-steel heat shield where it passes the bulkhead and harnesses. The air-gap insulation patents describe double walls as a way to deliver hotter gas to the catalyst during warm-up (sourced); the EMICAT supplier states its 48 V heater shortens light-off for petrol and diesel (sourced). Mass falls ~0.6 kg; the part runs hotter on its skin, which is managed by the shield.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Exhaust supplier removes the liner forming, liner insertion and two orbital welding stations; hydroforming cell reused. Cycle per part drops from ~180 s to ~95 s. Scrap from liner rattle (a common AGI audit failure) disappears.

ideaData.materialGrade: Inner 1.4828 (X15CrNiSi20-12) 0.8 mm + outer 1.4509 1.2 mm → single wall 1.4509 (X2CrTiNb18) 1.5 mm + aluminised DX53D+AS120 shield
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Two-shell AGI fabrication with 4 MIG welds → single hydroformed tube, 2 welds, clipped shield
ideaData.regulatoryContext: Euro 7 (Reg. (EU) 2024/1257) cold-start and durability (200,000 km) requirements govern acceptance.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: In the first 30 s of a cold start the exhaust gas at ~15-25 g/s and 450-550 °C loses heat to the downpipe wall: a single 1.5 mm steel wall of ~1.6 kg absorbs ≈ 1.6 kg × 0.5 kJ/kgK × 300 K ≈ 240 kJ before it stops sinking heat, whereas an AGI liner of 0.5 kg absorbs ≈ 75 kJ. The difference (~165 kJ) is what AGI buys. A 4 kW 48 V EHC delivers 120 kJ in 30 s directly into the catalyst front face where it matters, plus pre-heat before crank, so the catalyst reaches 300 °C light-off independent of the extra pipe heat sink; tailpipe cold-start mass is then governed by EHC energy, not pipe insulation.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete part numbers: inner liner 1.4828 0.8 mm, two sliding rings 1.4828, AGI outer shell. New: single-wall 1.4509 1.5 mm hydroformed downpipe, bend radius ≥1.5 D, wall thinning ≤20 %, with two flanges; new clip-on heat shield DX53D+AS120 0.5 mm with 8 mm embossed stand-off. Weld spec: 2 MIG welds (flange-tube) with 1.4430 wire. EHC pre-heat strategy: 2 kW for 15 s pre-crank at T_cat < 100 °C.
engineering.validationPlan: Emissions: WLTP and RDE cold-start at -7 °C and 23 °C, 3 vehicles × 3 repeats; target ≤ baseline tailpipe THC/NOx cold-start mass. Durability: thermal shock 1,500 cycles 950 °C ↔ 100 °C per OEM exhaust spec, leak <1 l/min at 0.5 bar. Under-hood thermal survey at 40 °C ambient towing 3,500 kg on grade. Vibration ISO 16750-3. PPAP level 3 for the downpipe; emissions re-homologation.
engineering.dfmImplications: Supplier part count 6 → 2, welds 4 → 2, cycle ≈ 180 s → 95 s, one leak-test fixture retained. Shield clip has an anti-rotation tab (poka-yoke). Engine assembly: identical flange interfaces so no fixture changes. Service: no internal liner rattle complaints.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline AGI downpipe ≈ €38.00; single-wall tube with flanges ≈ €22.00. Sliding rings and liner welds ≈ €1.20 deleted; welding labour €1.80 → €0.90. Added heat shield and clips ≈ €4.50. Not included: EHC hardware (already in baseline), any extra EHC energy on WLTP CO2 (assumed within existing pre-heat strategy).

title: 8HP sailing auxiliary oil pump moved from 12 V onto the 48 V rail
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Saving is in the pump power stage (lower-current MOSFETs and smaller DC-link capacitors), copper in the feed cable, the 12 V fuse/relay slot, and a DC-DC loading step; partly offset by LV 148 48 V connector and isolation requirements. Baseline: an MHEV 8-speed that sails with the engine off needs line pressure to keep the shift elements filled for a sub-300 ms re-engagement; the 8HP solves short stop-start pauses with its hydraulic impulse storage (sourced), and hybrid 8HP versions add an electric oil pump (sourced). In our baseline that pump is a 12 V BLDC gerotor unit (≈ 250-350 W peak, 25-30 A at 12 V) with its own controller, a fused 6 mm² feed from the 12 V distribution, and its continuous load is drawn through the 48/12 V DC-DC. Proposal: re-wind the same gerotor pump motor for 48 V and supply it from the 48 V rail (current ≈ 7 A peak), sharing the 48 V MOSFET half-bridge family used elsewhere. Benefits: 4× lower current, 1.5 mm² feed in place of 6 mm², smaller connector, no DC-DC conversion loss (≈ 8-10 %), and the 12 V fuse/relay position is freed. Off-road relevance: in low-range crawling with auto-stop on a slope, the pump keeps the clutches filled so creep resumes immediately on restart, with an honest caveat that the off-road case still requires the engine to restart within the 48 V SOC budget. ideaData.materialGrade: Stator winding Cu grade 1 enamel Ø0.85 mm → Ø0.45 mm (more turns); MOSFETs 40 V → 80 V in TOLL package
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: 12 V BLDC pump with discrete driver on 12 V rail → 48 V BLDC pump, 80 V MOSFET bridge, 48 V branch harness
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Pump hydraulic power for sailing hold ≈ 3-5 l/min at 4-6 bar ≈ 40-50 W, with peaks of ~300 W for fast fill. At 12 V the peak phase current is ≈ 30 A; conduction loss in the bridge ∝ I²R, so at 48 V (≈ 7.5 A) bridge loss falls ~16× for the same R_DS(on), letting 80 V MOSFETs of 3-4× higher R_DS(on) and smaller die be used. Feed cable: 30 A over 3 m needs 6 mm² to hold drop <0.3 V; 7.5 A needs 1.5 mm² for <0.6 % drop. Removing the DC-DC path saves ~8-10 % conversion loss on the continuous sailing load (~5 W).
engineering.specDeltas: Pump motor: 12 V → 48 V nominal (LV 148 operating 36-52 V), winding turns ×4 at ¼ copper section. Power stage: 6 × 40 V 1 mΩ D2PAK → 6 × 80 V 4 mΩ TOLL; DC-link 3 × 470 µF/25 V → 2 × 100 µF/63 V polymer-hybrid. Harness: 6 mm² FLRY → 1.5 mm² FLRY on 48 V branch; 12 V fuse F-xx 40 A and relay deleted. Connector to 48 V-coded 4-way sealed.
engineering.validationPlan: LV 148 tests E48-01 to E48-15 (incl. overvoltage, load dump, ground shift) on 6 samples; AEC-Q101 qualification of MOSFETs; ISO 16750-4 climatic and ISO 16750-3 vibration (transmission-mounted profile). Functional: sailing re-engagement <300 ms at -20 °C and 120 °C ATF over 50,000 cycles; off-road auto-stop on 30 % grade with re-creep. PPAP level 3 for pump and harness.
engineering.dfmImplications: No change to transmission assembly fixtures (same flange and bolts). Harness has one fewer heavy-gauge crimp. 12 V fuse box loses a slot. Key-coded 48 V connector prevents mis-mating. EOL test bench adds a 48 V supply channel (shared with BSG tests).
engineering.costBridge: Baseline 12 V pump with driver ≈ €78.00 vs 48 V pump ≈ €71.00 (smaller power stage). 12 V feed, fuse and relay ≈ €3.40 vs 48 V branch ≈ €1.60. DC-DC continuous load step ≈ €1.50 credit (estimate). 48 V LV 148 connector and isolation adds ≈ €1.20. Not included: CO2 benefit of lower conversion losses.

title: Serpentine re-routed to four pulleys after 48 V air-con: dummy idler, bracket removed

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Block line skips four drill/tap ops on the compressor bosses (≈ 20 s); engine dress line loses one bracket fit and two torque-angle bolts; belt fit becomes simpler with fewer pulleys. Bracket die can be retired or kept for non-MHEV.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Front-end part count −6 (bracket, idler, 3 bolts, dust cap). Fewer belt-routing errors (a recurring EOL defect on serpentines). Service: shorter belt-change time.

How this differs: We keep a BSG belt (cheaper than a crank ISG) and remove only the vestigial A/C path and its idler; the belt geometry numbers are our engineering estimates.

ideaData.materialGrade: Bracket EN AC-46000 (deleted); belt 8PK EPDM unchanged section
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: 6-pulley serpentine with blanking idler → 4-pulley MHEV-specific layout
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Belt slip on the BSG is governed by the capstan relation T_tight/T_slack ≤ e^(μθ); with μ ≈ 0.5 effective for a PK belt and θ = 150° (2.62 rad) the ratio is ≈ 3.7, sufficient for 55-60 Nm at the BSG pulley at the planned static tension. The blanking idler only added wrap to a pulley that no longer exists and carried ~400-700 N hub load, costing ≈ 20-40 W of bearing and belt bending loss at highway speed. Shortening the belt by 400 mm reduces belt mass and the first span natural frequency rises, moving flutter above idle firing order (3rd order at 600 rpm = 30 Hz).
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: A/C/blanking bracket (EN AC-46000, 0.9 kg), idler pulley Ø70 mm with 6203 bearing, three M8 bolts, dust cap. Belt 8PK 1,850 mm → 8PK 1,450 mm. Tensioner arm length revised (+8 mm) to keep BSG wrap ≥150°. Block: four M8 boss drill/taps deleted (bosses as-cast for commonality). Front cover unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Belt slip test at full BSG boost/regen torque, -30 °C to 120 °C, slip <2 %; belt life 240,000 km equivalent on rig (OEM FEAD durability); tensioner ISO 16750-3 vibration; NVH run-up for belt flutter and whine on 3 vehicles. PPAP level 3 for belt and tensioner, level 2 for block machining change. Acceptance: no audible chirp at -30 °C first start.

title: 8HP converter without centrifugal pendulum absorber: lock-up damping shared with BSG
description: [MHEV] Deletes the pendulum flange, 8 masses, rollers and rivets; shortens converter balancing; partly offset by re-rated arc springs and BSG active-damping software. Baseline: premium 8-speed torque converters pair a twin torsional damper with a centrifugal pendulum absorber (CPA) on the turbine-side damper flange so the lock-up clutch can close early at low engine speed (ZF TwinTD early lock-up and damper/CPA combination: sourced). The CPA is a flange with 4 pendulum mass pairs on rollers in cycloidal tracks, ~1.2-1.6 kg. On an inline-six the dominant excitation is 3rd order, of lower amplitude than a 4-cylinder's 2nd order, and CPAs perform poorly at very low speed where centrifugal force is small (sourced). Proposal: for the I6 MHEV, delete the CPA and keep the twin arc-spring damper with re-rated springs (lower rate, longer travel), and assign the residual low-speed 3rd-order damping to the 48 V BSG: below ~1,300 rpm in lock-up the machine injects anti-phase torque of 10-20 Nm at the crank. Lock-up minimum speed may rise ~50-100 rpm on the BSG-unavailable fallback map. This is our proposal on our I6; whether a given 8HP application carries a CPA must be confirmed per part number.

engineering.mechanism: Torsional excitation of a 4-stroke I6 is dominated by 3rd order; at 1,100 rpm (55 Hz) its alternating torque at the flywheel is ≈ ±60-90 Nm at full load versus ≈ ±150-200 Nm 2nd order on an I4 of similar torque. A CPA tuned to order 3 cancels a share of this but its effectiveness scales with ω², so it is weakest just where early lock-up runs. A BSG at belt ratio 2.7 producing ±7 Nm at its shaft gives ±19 Nm at the crank in anti-phase — enough, with a softer arc-spring set (rate −20 %), to keep cabin 3rd-order levels within ~1-2 dB of baseline at 1,100-1,300 rpm. Energy cost: ≈ 30-60 W average circulating, mostly recovered.

title: Intake cam phaser with end-stop lock replaces mid-position lock where 48 V cranks fast
description: [MHEV] One lock pin and spring, the detent oil circuit in the rotor, the special OCV spool, and one camshaft cross-drilling are deleted; a high-volume standard end-lock phaser design is used. Baseline: a Miller-capable petrol I6 intake phaser needs a mid-position lock — a second lock pin (or staged pins), a detent hydraulic circuit and a matching OCV spool — because the engine starts poorly at either the full-retard or full-advance stop; the mid lock parks the cam at the cold-start angle and permits longer total phaser travel (sourced from phaser patents). Proposal: on the variant where the 48 V machine performs all warm and cold starts, the cranking speed rises from 150-250 rpm (12 V pinion) to 400-700 rpm. At that speed, dynamic compression with late intake closing at the retard stop is sufficient: effective compression ratio falls, but higher piston speed reduces blow-by and heat loss per cycle, so the engine fires on the first compression at end-stop retard. The phaser reverts to a single lock pin at full retard with a standard 4/3 OCV, and the camshaft loses the detent drilling. Explicit limitation: if the 12 V pinion starter is retained for cold starts below ~-10 °C, this idea does not apply and the mid lock must stay. No OEM is cited as having done this; patents establish why the mid lock exists.

engineering.mechanism: Starting at full intake retard (IVC ~100° ABDC) cuts effective compression from ~10.5:1 geometric to ~7:1; at 200 rpm the slow cycle loses ~25-35 % of trapped charge heat to cold walls and ring blow-by, so end-of-compression temperature may stay below the ~600-650 K needed for reliable first fire at -20 °C. At 500 rpm cycle time halves and blow-by mass per cycle (∝ time) roughly halves, raising compression end temperature ~40-60 K, which recovers first-cycle firing. The BSG needs ≈ 120-160 Nm at the crank to hold 500 rpm at -20 °C with 0W-20 oil.

OCV: special 5-port detent spool → standard 4/3 spool (common part). Camshaft: delete Ø3 mm detent cross-drilling and plug. Engine software: start only by BSG; crank target ≥ 400 rpm at -25 °C, else inhibit and warn (12 V fallback not used).
engineering.validationPlan: Cold-room start tests at -30, -25, -20 °C, 20 starts each on 3 engines with ageing-state 48 V batteries (start time < 1.2 s target). Euro 7 -7 °C cold-start emissions. title: Two-stage switched vane oil pump replaces map-controlled pump as sailing cuts low-load hours
description: [MHEV] Saving from replacing the proportional solenoid with an on/off solenoid, the analogue sensor with a switch, a simpler control-ring piston, and a freed ECU proportional driver. Baseline: the I6 uses a fully variable, map-controlled vane oil pump: a proportional variable-force solenoid moves the control ring, an analogue oil pressure sensor closes the loop, and the ECU holds a pressure target per speed/load/temperature cell. Its CO2 value is earned mostly at idle, low-load cruising and coast, where it can drop to 1.0-1.5 bar. Proposal: on the 48 V MHEV the engine is OFF in much of that low-load time — sailing, coast-off and stop-start remove a large share of idle and overrun hours — so the remaining gain of continuous control over a two-stage pump is small. Switch to a two-stage switched vane pump: an on/off solenoid selects low (≈ 2.0 bar) or high (≈ 4.0 bar) stage; the analogue sensor becomes a pressure switch for OBD. Published two-stage pump development reports large drive-energy savings versus fixed pumps (42.7 % NEDC, 46 % WLTC: sourced), and the simpler on/off control is documented (sourced). The CO2 delta to fully variable is estimated at ≤ 0.3 g/km on WLTP once sailing hours are removed — an estimate to be measured. Not combined with the library idea that deletes the mechanical pump for a sump e-pump; this keeps the chain-driven pump.

engineering.mechanism: Pump drive power P = Q·Δp/η. At 2,000 rpm cruise with Q ≈ 30 l/min, a fully variable pump at 2.0 bar draws ≈ 30/60000 m³/s × 2.0e5 Pa / 0.5 ≈ 200 W, versus a two-stage pump at its 2.0 bar low stage also ≈ 200 W — the two only differ at points where the variable pump goes below 2.0 bar (idle/overrun) or between stages. With sailing and stop-start removing ~25-35 % of WLTP idle/overrun time, the residual difference is ≈ 15-30 W average, i.e. ≈ 0.1-0.3 g/km CO2 on a 2.5 t SUV.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete proportional VFS (0-1.2 A PWM) and analogue oil pressure sensor (0-10 bar, 0.5-4.5 V). Add on/off 2-way solenoid (normally high stage) and pressure switch 1.2 bar. Control-ring piston: single chamber pair with stage port; spring preload set for 4.0 bar high stage. ECU: release one high-side PWM channel; diagnostic monitor changes to switch-plausibility.
engineering.validationPlan: Engine dyno: oil pressure maps at 60-150 °C; main/rod bearing durability 600 h OEM cycle with failure-to-low-stage case; WLTP CO2 A/B on 3 vehicles (±0.3 g/km acceptance). OBD demonstration per Euro 7 for the stage monitor. ISO 16750-3 vibration on solenoid. PPAP level 3 for pump; ECU variant release.
engineering.dfmImplications: No new engine fixtures; pump installation and chain drive unchanged. Two connector variants reduced to keyed 2-pin. Supplier assembly drops a sensor calibration step. Fail-safe high-stage default needs no poka-yoke beyond connector keying.

title: Boost-pressure wastegate capsule replaces electric actuator once 48 V EHC heats the catalyst
description: [MHEV] An electric actuator (motor, gears, sensor, ASIC) costs several times a pressure capsule; harness branch and heat shield are deleted; a boost-control solenoid and hoses are added back. Baseline: the petrol I6 turbo uses an electric wastegate actuator (DC motor, gear train, position sensor, harness) mounted on the compressor housing. Its decisive advantage over a pressure capsule is that it can hold the wastegate wide open at zero boost — used right after cold start to send hot gas past the turbine to the catalyst (sourced) — and that it can set any intermediate opening independent of boost (sourced). Proposal: on the MHEV with a 48 V electrically heated catalyst, cat heating is done electrically, so the open-at-zero-boost function is no longer needed for emissions. Revert to a boost-pressure capsule actuator with a PWM boost-control solenoid (normally-open wastegate when unpressurised at low boost is not available, so part-load pumping benefit of an open gate is lost: estimated +0.5-1 % fuel at light load, partly recovered by the 48 V load-point strategy). The capsule is mounted on the same compressor-housing bracket; linkage adapts. Applies to the petrol only; diesel uses VTG.

Revert to a boost-pressure capsule actuator with a PWM boost-control solenoid (normally-open wastegate when unpressurised at low boost is not available, so part-load pumping benefit of an open gate is lost: estimated +0.5-1 % fuel at light load, partly recovered by the 48 V load-point strategy). The capsule is mounted on the same compressor-housing bracket; linkage adapts. Applies to the petrol only; diesel uses VTG.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Turbo supplier swaps actuator fitting and end-of-line calibration (electric stroke learn) for capsule pre-load setting and weld of the rod clevis; engine plant adds two small hoses and a solenoid on the intake.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Electric actuator, its connector and harness branch (3 parts) removed; capsule, solenoid and 2 hoses (4 parts) added; net similar part count but cheaper. Hose ends are colour-coded and keyed to avoid cross-connection.

engineering.mechanism: Cold-start cat heating with an open wastegate raises gas temperature at the brick by ~50-100 K because ~80-90 % of flow bypasses the turbine and its 3-4 kg of cold metal. A 48 V EHC injecting 3-4 kW into the front face achieves light-off faster than that bypass. The remaining electric-actuator benefit is part-load pumping: opening the gate at low load lowers exhaust back-pressure by ~50-150 mbar, worth ≈ 0.5-1 % fuel at 30-60 km/h cruise. On WLTP that is ≈ 0.5-1.0 g/km, which the MHEV offsets partly through load-point shifting.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete electric wastegate actuator, its bracket heat shield and 3-wire harness branch. Add capsule actuator (spring pre-load set for 0.45 bar crack), PWM 3/2 boost-control solenoid 12 V, two Ø4 mm hoses PA12 with quick connectors. Wastegate lever ratio adapted for capsule stroke 10-12 mm. ECU: delete position-feedback loop; add duty-cycle boost control.
engineering.validationPlan: Emissions: WLTP, RDE (incl. 1,300 m altitude extension) and Euro 7 cold start on 3 vehicles. Boost-control stability over 0-3,000 m altitude, towing 3,500 kg 12 % grade at 40 °C. Actuator durability: 10 million cycles at 150 °C per OEM; ISO 16750-3 vibration engine-mounted profile; hose ageing to ISO 16750-5. PPAP level 3 turbo; emissions re-homologation.
engineering.dfmImplications: Capsule pre-load is set at the turbo supplier (welded clevis) so no adjustment on the engine line. Two hoses and one solenoid added on the intake side with keyed connectors. EOL stroke-learn routine for the electric actuator deleted, saving ≈ 20 s.

title: EHC heater disc and support brick canned inside the main TWC shell
description: [MHEV] Deletes one shell, two cones, two flanges, a gasket and two circumferential welds; shortens the hot-end assembly; adds a longer mat and an electrode boss in the main shell. Baseline: the 48 V electrically heated catalyst is delivered as its own module — coiled metal-foil heater disc held by insulating pins on a short metallic support catalyst (sourced construction), in its own shell with inlet cone, outlet cone and two V-band flanges — bolted upstream of the close-coupled three-way catalyst can. Proposal: integrate the heater disc and its metallic support brick into the front of the main TWC shell: one longer stuffed shell (1.4509, 1.5 mm) holds the heated disc/support brick, a 10 mm gap ring and the ceramic TWC bricks on mats; one inlet cone, one outlet cone, the electrode boss welded through the main shell. Two flanges, one gasket, one cone pair and one shell are deleted, and the heated face sits directly upstream of the coated ceramic brick, avoiding the heat loss in the flange gap. The supplier offers EMICAT at 48 V across 1-10 kW (sourced); the integration into one can is our proposal.

engineering.mechanism: Heat delivered by a 4 kW disc in the first 30 s (≈ 120 kJ) must reach the coated ceramic face; across a V-band joint with a 25-40 mm gas path and two cones, ~10-15 % of that heat goes to the extra shell, cone and flange mass (≈ 1.2 kg of steel at 0.5 kJ/kgK needs 60 kJ for 100 K). Placing the support brick 10 mm upstream of the first ceramic brick inside one shell removes that sink, so the same energy lights the TWC ~3-5 s sooner, or the same light-off is reached at ~10 % lower heater energy.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: EHC module shell, inlet/outlet cones, two V-band flanges + clamp, one graphite gasket. engineering.validationPlan: Hot vibration (900 °C, 30 g sine sweep) push-out test on 6 cans; thermal shock 1,000 cycles; electrode insulation resistance after 1,000 h humidity per IEC 60068-2-78; LV 148 E48 electrical tests on heater circuit; Euro 7 ageing (equivalent 200,000 km) and WLTP/RDE cold-start emissions on 3 vehicles. title: Single-bush torque-roll restrictor sized to low-range reaction; BSG restart shapes torque
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Deletes one bush and its press-fit, swaps a forged and machined aluminium link for an injection-moulded glass-filled polyamide link; adds a larger single bush. Baseline: the I6 + 8-speed powertrain is held by two hydro mounts and a torque-roll restrictor (dog-bone) with two voided natural-rubber bushes in a forged and machined EN AW-6082-T6 link. The restrictor rate is a compromise between (a) the 12 V stop-start restart shake — a pinion start at 150-250 rpm crosses the powertrain roll resonance (8-12 Hz) slowly, giving 1-2 mm restrictor travel and seat-rail jerk — and (b) the off-road strength case: 1st gear × 2.6:1 low range × converter stall reaction, about 6-8 kNm at the gearbox output, which the restrictor must react without bottoming. Proposal: with 48 V BSG restarts at 700-900 rpm in 250-350 ms the roll resonance is crossed in one or two cycles, and the BSG ramps its torque to cancel the first-compression pulse, so the soft low-amplitude stage of the restrictor is no longer needed. Use a single-bush restrictor: engine-side end bolted rigidly to the gearbox bracket via a forged stud eye, subframe side one larger progressive bush with snubber, in a PA66-GF50 moulded link. Off-road capability is kept by sizing the snubber to the low-range reaction case. Library holds passive hydromounts; this addresses the restrictor only.

engineering.mechanism: Restart roll impulse: a 12 V pinion start dwells 0.3-0.5 s near the 8-12 Hz roll mode so 3-5 cycles build amplitude; peak restrictor force ≈ 1.5-2.5 kN with a soft first stage of ~150 N/mm. A BSG start crosses it within ~0.1 s and its torque profile cancels ~50-70 % of the first compression pulse, so peak force falls below ~1 kN and the soft stage can be replaced by a single progressive bush. Strength case off-road: output torque 6-8 kNm reacted over a 0.45-0.55 m mount base gives ≈ 12-16 kN at the restrictor; PA66-GF50 dry-as-moulded σ ≈ 230 MPa, conditioned ≈ 160 MPa, so a 900 mm² section at peak stress ≈ 18 MPa holds a safety factor > 5 on conditioned strength.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: forged 6082-T6 link, second NR bush. New: PA66-GF50 link (heat-stabilised, black), section ≥ 900 mm², with insert-moulded steel bushing at the engine end (stud eye, M12); subframe end NR 55 Shore A bush, rate stage 1 300 N/mm to 2 mm then progressive to snubber at 6 mm; static stiffness tolerance ±15 %. Bolt torques unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Static ultimate load 2 × off-road case (≥ 30 kN) at -40, 23, 120 °C; fatigue 10⁶ cycles at ±12 kN per OEM mount spec; misuse: low-range wheel-drop test on vehicle 5 events; creep 1,000 h at 120 °C; restart NVH (seat-rail jerk, 3 vehicles); ISO 16750-3 vibration; VDA 675 elastomer ageing. title: Diesel I6 booster vacuum: camshaft exhauster deleted, 48 V brushless unit sole source
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Deletes the mechanical pump, its drive coupling, oil feed/return and head machining; the electric pump is upsized rather than added, so most of its cost was already in the baseline. Baseline: a diesel I6 has no throttled manifold, so brake-booster vacuum comes from a vane exhauster bolted to the end of a camshaft (diesels need either an engine-driven or a motor-driven vacuum source: sourced). Because the MHEV coasts and stands with the combustion process stopped, the booster additionally needs a motor-driven vacuum unit (the arrangement used on stop-start cars and hybrids: sourced), so today the vehicle carries two vacuum sources. Proposal: remove the camshaft-end exhauster and let the motor-driven unit be the only source: upgrade it from an intermittent-duty 12 V brushed design to a continuous-rated brushless vane unit on the 48 V rail, with a booster pressure sensor and one check valve. The camshaft end becomes a plain plug; the cylinder head loses its exhauster flange face and the lubrication feed for it. Off-road: booster assist stays available if the engine stalls on a steep descent or during a wading auto-stop, which a camshaft-driven exhauster cannot provide. Crank friction falls ~150-300 W at highway, because the exhauster vanes turn continuously whether or not vacuum is needed. This is our proposal; no OEM is cited.

engineering.mechanism: A booster needs ≈ 0.6-0.7 bar vacuum; a full stop from 100 km/h consumes ≈ 0.5-1 l of air at atmospheric pressure. A cam vacuum pump moves ≈ 200-300 cc/rev and absorbs 150-300 W at highway even when vacuum is full, because the vanes still run. A brushless 48 V vane pump of ≈ 25-35 l/min free air (≈ 150 W) restores 0.6 bar in a 1.0 l booster plus 0.5 l reservoir in ≈ 3-4 s and runs only on demand (duty ≈ 5-10 %), so average draw ≈ 10-15 W from the 48 V rail versus 150-300 W of crank friction.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: mechanical vacuum pump assembly, Oldham drive coupling, gasket, two M8 bolts, head pump flange face mill, oil feed Ø3 and return drilling; add cam-end plug. Electric pump: 12 V brushed intermittent (30 % duty) → 48 V brushless continuous rated, IP6K9K, ≥ 30 l/min free air; booster vacuum sensor 0-1 bar; vacuum reservoir 0.5 l added if analysis requires.
engineering.validationPlan: Brake performance per UN ECE R13-H incl. failure of the vacuum source (reserve for ≥ 2 full applications), FMVSS 135 where sold; functional safety analysis to ISO 26262 (target ASIL B decomposition with sensor monitoring). Pump durability 3,000 h on-off at -40 to 105 °C; LV 148 E48 tests; ISO 16750-3 vibration. Off-road: engine-off descent on 45 % grade. PPAP level 3; brake homologation.
engineering.dfmImplications: Engine part count −5, two machining ops fewer on the head, one coupling alignment check deleted. Electric pump uses existing body bracket. Single vacuum source simplifies hose kit (one check valve fewer). 48 V connector keyed against 12 V.
engineering.costBridge: Mechanical pump ≈ €24.00 deleted; coupling ≈ €1.20 and oil-feed machining ≈ €0.60 deleted; hose/check valve ≈ €3.20 → €1.80; electric pump upgrade intermittent 12 V → continuous 48 V brushless adds ≈ €9.50. Not included: fuel/CO2 saving from removing pump drag (≈ 0.5-1 % at highway, estimated) and any reservoir if required.

title: Converter bridging clutch: one friction disc instead of two as BSG trims slip heat
description: [MHEV] One friction plate, one separator, one set of friction faces and one spline element removed; piston and backing plate simplified; offset partly by a premium lining. Baseline: the 8-speed converter bridging clutch is a two-disc pack (four bonded friction faces), sized for (a) full engine torque plus margin when closed and (b) controlled micro-slip of 20-60 rpm at low speed to filter firing pulses — the thermal duty that usually sets the friction area. Proposal: on the MHEV, (1) launch torque is filled by the 48 V machine, so the clutch closes earlier with less slip energy, and (2) the BSG cancels part of the low-speed torque ripple, so the micro-slip window can be narrowed. Fit one friction disc with two bonded faces (carbon-fibre-filled paper lining), keeping clamp force and torque capacity through a higher-μ lining and slightly larger mean radius within the same cover. ZF's TwinTD shows the industry direction of closing the bridging clutch very early (sourced). Our change trims slip-heat sizing only; torque capacity is kept, unlike ideas that change the clutch count for capacity or downsize the torus.

engineering.mechanism: Lining temperature rise in micro-slip ∝ slip power / area: at 400 Nm and 40 rpm slip P = T·Δω ≈ 400 × 4.2 ≈ 1.7 kW continuously at low speed. Halving the slip window (20 rpm) with BSG damping and earlier lock-up halves this to ≈ 0.85 kW, so half the friction area holds the same face temperature (~180-200 °C limit for paper). Torque capacity T = n·μ·F·r_m: going from n = 4 to n = 2 faces is compensated by μ 0.12 → 0.15 (carbon-filled lining), r_m +6 % and clamp force +15 % from the piston apply pressure.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete one friction plate, one separator plate and one spline carrier ring. Lining: paper μ 0.12 → carbon-fibre-filled μ 0.15, groove pattern waffle; mean radius +6 %. Piston apply area unchanged; apply pressure +15 % via TCC valve calibration. Micro-slip calibration window 20-60 rpm → 10-25 rpm when BSG damping active. ATF unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Friction rig μ-v and anti-shudder (dμ/dv ≥ 0) at 40-140 °C to SAE J2490-style procedure, 6 samples; converter durability 500 h OEM cycle incl. towing 3,500 kg at 12 %; vehicle shudder evaluation at 50,000 km aged ATF on 3 vehicles. Torque capacity test 1.3 × max engine + BSG torque. PPAP level 3 converter.
engineering.dfmImplications: Stack 5 → 3 parts; selective shim classes reduced from 4 to 2. Bonding press loading halves. No change to the transmission line or the flexplate/converter bolting. Fewer stack-up gauging steps in the converter cell.
engineering.costBridge: Friction plates and separator ≈ €11.00 → €5.50; piston/backing simplification ≈ €4.20 → €3.60; stack shims and assembly ≈ €1.00 → €0.60; premium carbon-filled lining adds ≈ €1.80. Not included: any change in fuel use from the narrower slip window (expected positive, not claimed).

title: Crank thrust: two block-side AlSn20Cu half-washers replace flanged polymer-coated main shell
description: [MHEV] A flanged assembled bearing with coated flanges is replaced by a plain shell plus two stamped washers; cap-side thrust face machining is removed. No coating step on washers. Baseline: the I6 locates the crankshaft axially with a flanged (assembled-flange) main bearing pair at the thrust journal, both halves with polymer-coated thrust flanges — specified for 12 V stop-start, where every pinion start runs ~0.6-0.9 s of boundary lubrication on the thrust faces while the converter applies axial charge-pressure load (ballooning) to the crank. Proposal: with 48 V BSG starts, the crank reaches ~800 rpm in ~0.3 s and gallery pressure builds 2-3× sooner, so the sliding distance under boundary conditions per start falls by ~60 %. Use a plain (non-flanged) main shell pair at the thrust journal and two stamped AlSn20Cu-on-steel half-washers on the block side only, retained by anti-rotation tabs; the cap-side thrust face machining is deleted. Axial load capacity is checked against the converter ballooning and clutch-apply axial loads (an automatic has no clutch-pedal thrust case). Distinct from the library polymer-overlay main/rod shell idea, which concerns radial shells; this concerns axial location.

engineering.mechanism: Thrust wear per start ∝ axial load × sliding distance in mixed lubrication. Axial load from converter ballooning at standstill ≈ 1.0-2.0 kN on an 8-speed converter. At a pinion start, mixed lubrication lasts ~0.6-0.9 s at ~200 rpm mean (r_m ≈ 35 mm → sliding ≈ 0.5-0.7 m per start); at a BSG start ~0.25-0.35 s at ~500 rpm mean gives ≈ 0.2-0.3 m before full film. With 1.5 kN over one washer pair of ≈ 900 mm² the unit load is 1.7 MPa, below the ~5-7 MPa limit for AlSn20Cu washers under oil, and wear over 300k starts stays within a 0.1 mm endplay budget.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete flanged main bearing pair at journal 4 (part number with coated flanges). New: plain main shell pair (common with other journals) + 2 × AlSn20Cu/steel half-washers, 2.5 mm, with oil grooves and anti-rotation tabs. Block: delete cap-side thrust face turn; block-side face Ra 0.4 µm, flatness 0.01 mm unchanged. Crank endplay 0.10-0.30 mm unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Thrust wear rig with converter-pressure axial load 2 kN, 300,000 BSG starts + 30,000 pinion starts (fallback), endplay growth < 0.1 mm; engine durability 600 h OEM cycle; teardown inspection. Washer fitment vision check validation. PPAP level 3 for washer, level 2 for block change. Endplay measured on all durability engines at 0, 300 and 600 h. Teardown at end of test.
engineering.dfmImplications: Machining: one face turn deleted on block/cap set (≈ 8 s). Assembly: two washers placed in block before crank lay-in; tab orientation is poka-yoke and camera-checked. Bearing variant count −1 (plain shell common with other journals).

title: Compressor housing cast without ported shroud: 48 V fill covers the surge-prone low-flow zone
description: [MHEV] Removes one sand core and its setting, the slot machining and deburr, and reduces casting scrap from core shift; same alloy and die family. Fewer foundry rejects. Baseline: the I6 turbo compressor housing (gravity-cast AlSi7Mg0.3 T6) has a ported shroud (map-width enhancement): an annular recirculation cavity cast with a separate sand core and a machined slot over the wheel inducer. It lets the stage run left of its natural surge line at low engine speed and high boost — the low-end torque region (sourced: the shroud enlarges the low-flow map and reduces surge risk; it extends operating range). Proposal: on the 48 V MHEV, the BSG/e-boost fills torque at 1,000-1,600 rpm, so the calibration need not push the compressor to high pressure ratio at very low flow; the boost target there is reduced ~0.2-0.3 bar and the operating line moves right of the plain-housing surge line. Delete the cavity core and slot machining; cast a plain shroud housing. Bonus: ported shrouds can add inlet noise at some points. Risk: when 48 V SOC is low, low-end torque is limited by the surge line; calibration must accept that degraded mode.

engineering.mechanism: Compressor surge is set by inducer incidence at low flow: with a plain shroud, surge occurs at mass flow ≈ 25-30 % below peak efficiency flow at PR 2.5; the ported shroud bleeds tip flow and moves surge ≈ 10-20 % further left. The I6 operating line at 1,200 rpm full load needs PR ≈ 2.3-2.5 at low flow. If the 48 V machine supplies 100-150 Nm at the crank, the engine needs ~20-25 % less BMEP from boost there, PR falls to ≈ 1.9-2.1 and flow-per-PR moves right, restoring ≥ 10 % surge margin on the plain housing.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete recirculation cavity core, slot (width 4 mm, Ø over inducer) and associated deburr. Housing inlet bore and shroud contour unchanged; wall at slot zone becomes solid. Casting spec: AlSi7Mg0.3 T6, porosity class per VDG P202 unchanged. ECU: low-end boost target −0.25 bar at 1,000-1,600 rpm; surge-margin map updated; 48 V SOC reserve for torque fill.
engineering.validationPlan: Gas-stand compressor map with surge line (6 housings); vehicle tip-in/tip-out surge test at 0-2,500 m altitude; towing 3,500 kg 12 % grade at low SOC; compressor wheel HCF check (strain gauge) at surge proximity; ISO 16750-3 vibration. PPAP level 3 for housing; engine full-load curve re-confirmation.
engineering.dfmImplications: Core box and core shooter capacity freed; casting cycle −25 s; machining −18 s; fewer handling breakages of slot ribs. No fixture change at turbo assembly. Die insert swap keeps one die for both variants if needed.

title: Heated-disc light-off lets the main three-way brick use 400 cpsi, 4 mil cordierite
description: [MHEV] Standard-wall 400/4 substrate costs less and breaks less in canning; mat specification relaxes; partly offset by slightly higher washcoat loading. Less breakage scrap. Baseline: the close-coupled three-way converter on the petrol I6 uses a 600 cells-per-square-inch, 3 mil ceramic honeycomb, chosen mainly for low thermal mass and high geometric surface area so it warms quickly from exhaust heat; it costs a premium, and its fragile walls need a low-pressure mounting mat and break more often in canning. Proposal: when a 48 V heated metal-foil disc sits directly upstream (EMICAT-type construction, sourced), light-off is driven by electrical heat at the front face, so the fast-warm-up rationale for fragile walls weakens. Specify 400 cells / 4 mil standard-wall cordierite for the main brick, with washcoat +5 % to recover surface-limited conversion at high space velocity, precious-metal loading unchanged, and a standard intumescent mat at normal mount density. Note: this runs the opposite way to library ideas that raise cell density for exhaust-heated warm-up; it presumes an EHC and must be judged together with it. If the heater is deleted later, the honeycomb choice must be reopened.

title: Crank position sensor: speed-only differential Hall IC replaces direction-detecting sensor
description: [MHEV] A speed-only differential Hall crank sensor is a higher-volume, lower-price part than the speed-and-direction variant; ECU decoding simplifies. No tooling change. Baseline: the I6 for 12 V stop-start uses a direction-detecting crank sensor IC: it reports speed and direction (encoded as output pulse width) so the ECU keeps crank synchronisation through the back-rock oscillation at stop and can restart fast without re-synchronising (sourced from crank sensor IC literature). Proposal: on the 48 V MHEV the BSG controls run-down and parks the crank with no reverse rotation (≤ 2° measured by the machine's own rotor position via belt ratio), so the direction function is no longer needed for synchronisation. Fit a speed-only differential Hall IC on the same 60-2 target wheel and connector. Back-rock monitoring for diagnostics uses the BSG rotor angle. Limitation: if the BSG is unavailable, free run-down returns and the next start takes ~1 extra crank revolution to synchronise — accepted in the degraded mode. Pairs with the timing-drive idea in this batch but is a separate part decision.

engineering.mechanism: At stop, the compressing cylinder springs the crank back 20-60°; a speed-only sensor counts those reverse teeth as forward, so the ECU loses tooth position and must re-synchronise on the missing-tooth gap (up to one revolution at ~150-250 rpm, i.e. 0.25-0.4 s added restart). With BSG controlled run-down holding back-rock ≤ 2° (< 1 tooth of a 6° pitch wheel), the tooth count stays valid and restart synchronisation is immediate. The BSG rotor angle (resolver-less or sensor) divided by the belt ratio 2.7 provides an independent crank estimate to ±3° for plausibility.
engineering.specDeltas: Change crank sensor IC from speed+direction (pulse-width encoded, 45/90/180 µs) to speed-only differential Hall (45 µs fixed pulse); same housing, air gap 0.5-1.5 mm, connector and 60-2 target. ECU: remove direction decoding; add rule: ignore crank edges < 50 rpm with BSG park active; add BSG-angle plausibility check (±5° crank).
engineering.validationPlan: AEC-Q100 Grade 0 qualification (supplier existing); EMC to CISPR 25 and ISO 11452-2/-4; restart time tests 10,000 BSG stop/starts on 2 vehicles (synchronised restart ≥ 99.9 %); BSG-disabled fallback starts 1,000 cycles. Engine misfire monitor (OBD) re-confirmation. PPAP level 2 (same housing, IC change).
engineering.dfmImplications: No change to bore machining, fastener, connector or assembly torque. Variant reduction in the plant (one crank sensor part number across engines). Diagnostic tester routine updated only. Sensor tooling is untouched. Fixture and gauge unchanged.

title: Torque converter stator moulded in phenolic with insert-moulded race replaces die-cast aluminium
description: [MHEV] Moulding removes die-casting, bore/face machining, deburr and the race press-fit; phenolic part is lighter; insert-moulding adds a knurled race and moulding cell cost. Baseline: the 8-speed converter stator is a die-cast AlSi9Cu3(Fe) part, bored and faced, with a separate steel one-way-clutch outer race pressed in. Blade loading is set by stall: at converter stall the stator reacts the difference between turbine and impeller torque (torque ratio ~1.8-2.0) at high ATF temperature. Proposal: on the 48 V MHEV the machine fills launch torque, so the converter spends less time near stall and stall events are shorter and cooler. Use an injection-moulded glass-fibre phenolic (PF-GF) stator with the steel OWC outer race insert-moulded — a construction described in stator patents for weight and cost, with tighter blade gaps (~0.54 mm vs ~3 mm for aluminium castings) and better surface finish (sourced). The tighter gap partly recovers the hydraulic efficiency lost by the library's smaller-torus idea, and the two can be combined. Off-road crawl at stall remains the design case for blade strength and is validated explicitly.

engineering.mechanism: Stator reaction torque at stall T_s = T_t − T_p ≈ (TR − 1) · T_engine ≈ 0.9 × 500 Nm ≈ 450 Nm; on 21 blades at r ≈ 85 mm each blade carries ≈ 250 N distributed, giving blade-root bending stress of ~15-25 MPa for a 3 mm root — within PF-GF strength of ~80-100 MPa at 150 °C (factor ≥ 3). With 48 V torque fill, stall dwell per launch drops (engine speed needed for launch torque falls ~200-400 rpm), lowering ATF peak temperature by ~10-20 K in repeated launches, which protects the polymer.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete die-cast stator AlSi9Cu3(Fe), bore and face machining, OWC outer race press-fit. New stator PF-GF (≥ 50 % glass), heat deflection ≥ 200 °C, insert-moulded 16MnCr5 race with straight knurl; blade gap to impeller/turbine 3.0 → 0.6 mm; blade thickness +0.5 mm at root. Thrust washer faces moulded flat within 0.05 mm.
engineering.validationPlan: Spin burst ≥ 1.5 × max speed; stall-cycle durability 10,000 stalls at 150 °C ATF including low-range off-road crawl and towing 3,500 kg; ATF compatibility 1,000 h at 150 °C (mass/volume change, strength retention ≥ 70 %); race push-out torque ≥ 2 × max; converter performance curve (K-factor, TR) on dyno. PPAP level 3 converter.
engineering.dfmImplications: Supplier: one moulding cell replaces HPDC cell, two machining ops and a press — floor space and cycle down. Race is loaded robotically into the mould (presence sensed). Lower part weight (−0.3 kg) reduces converter inertia and balancing correction.
engineering.costBridge: Die-cast and machined stator ≈ €11.50 → moulded PF-GF with race ≈ €7.90; machining and deburr ≈ €1.60 deleted; race press-fit operation ≈ €0.50 deleted; knurled race and moulding-cell premium adds ≈ €0.60. title: Timing chain guides two-shot moulded in PA46, replacing PA66 face on aluminium carrier
description: [MHEV] Die-cast carrier, its machining and the face-clipping operation are replaced by one two-shot moulding per guide; PA46 is pricier per kg than PA66 but total mass and operations fall. Baseline: the I6 tensioning guide and fixed guide each comprise a die-cast AlSi9Cu3 carrier with a clipped-on PA66 sliding face — the stiff metal carrier being specified for the chain-slap impacts that occur on 12 V stop-start restarts after back-rock has vented the tensioner (reverse-rotation and slack-chain behaviour: sourced). Proposal: with 48 V BSG-controlled run-down and fast restarts, those impact loads fall towards running-load levels, so each guide can be a single-shot glass-fibre-reinforced PA46 carrier-and-face moulding (PA46-GF30 body with the unfilled sliding surface formed by a two-material shot, or an unfilled PA46 wear skin). PA46 holds stiffness and wear performance at 140-150 °C oil temperature better than PA66. This is the part-level complement to the timing-drive assembly idea in this batch (which removes the tensioner ratchet); it can be adopted alone if the BSG run-down strategy is in place.

PA46 keeps ~2× the modulus of PA66 above 120 °C, limiting face deflection to <0.3 mm.

title: 8HP rotor-vane set narrowed a fifth; 48 V sailing unit tops up hot-idle ATF
description: [MHEV] Less sintered and hardened material in rotor, cam ring and vanes; narrower pocket machining; partly offset by control software for flow sharing. Less grinding. Baseline: the 8-speed gearbox carries an engine-driven rotor-vane hydraulic supply whose displacement is set by one worst case — hot ATF (~120 °C) at idle (~600-650 rpm) feeding converter, lubrication, leakage of an aged valve body and a shift in progress. That sizing over-delivers at every higher speed, where surplus flow is relieved and its drive torque wasted. Proposal: the MHEV already carries a 48 V sailing supply unit (see the auxiliary assembly idea in this batch; hybrid 8HP versions carry an additional electric unit — sourced). Let it add 1-1.5 l/min during hot idle and slow shifts, and narrow the engine-driven rotor, vanes and cam ring axially by ~20 % (same diameters; same housing bore, with a spacer plate for commonality). engineering.mechanism: Pump flow Q = V·n·η_vol. With V ≈ 12 cc/rev at 620 rpm and η_vol ≈ 0.75 hot, Q ≈ 5.6 l/min — just above hot-idle demand of ≈ 5-5.5 l/min. Narrowing to V ≈ 9.6 cc/rev gives ≈ 4.5 l/min; the 48 V e-pump supplies the 1-1.5 l/min gap at ≈ 20-30 W. At 2,500 rpm highway the narrower pump displaces ≈ 18 instead of 22 l/min against a 8-10 bar relief: drag torque ≈ V·Δp/(2π·η_m) falls by ≈ 20 % of ~1.7 Nm, i.e. ≈ 90 W less at highway.

Housing pocket depth −3 mm, or common pocket with 3 mm spacer plate. Pressure control: e-pump hot-idle assist map at ATF > 100 °C and n < 900 rpm. Degraded mode: idle +50 rpm if e-pump unavailable.
engineering.validationPlan: Hot-idle line pressure at 130 °C ATF with aged (max-leak) valve body on 3 transmissions; shift-quality evaluation hot/cold; pump durability 1,000 h at 9 bar and 130 °C; cavitation check at -30 °C cold start. engineering.dfmImplications: Sinter press: punch change only; grinding cycle shorter (≈ −15 %). Vane length difference prevents mixing. Housing kept common with spacer, so the transmission line is unaffected. Punch-change only at the sinter press.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (general practice for scroll e-compressors): the discharge chamber in the rear head carries a separate pressed-in oil separator — a deep-drawn DC04 steel cylinder holding a sintered or knitted stainless-steel demister pad, retained by a circlip and sealed by an HNBR O-ring, with a machined bore, a circlip groove and a filtered oil-return orifice back to the back-pressure chamber. That is four loose parts, one press station and a ~40 s CNC operation on the EN AC-46000 rear head. Proposal for the 48 V MHEV compressor (33-34 cc class): form the separator as a centrifugal cyclone chamber cored directly in the HPDC rear head (Ø18-22 mm bore, 1° draft, finish-reamed only on the 8 mm sealing land), with a tangential inlet from the discharge port and a PPS-GF40 moulded vortex-finder tube (Ø7 mm, 0.9 mm wall) pressed into the reamed land; the oil collects in a cast sump pocket and returns through a 0.6 mm laser-drilled orifice. Benchmark: Sanden states its Gen2 Evo electric compressors (including a 48 V 33 cc unit in volume production) feature an integrated oil separator, and patent literature describes a vortex separator formed in the rear head of an electric compressor.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the steel separator cylinder, the stainless demister pad, the circlip and its groove, and most of the bore machining; the separating geometry moves into the die-casting where it costs only core-slide maintenance, while a 6 g PPS moulding replaces the steel and mesh.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Rear-head HPDC die gets one additional core slide (insert change, not a new die); CNC cycle drops ~30 s per head; the press-fit and circlip station becomes a simple vortex-tube press with force-displacement monitoring. Scrap from mesh-pad mis-seating and fibre contamination findings at the compressor end-of-line disappears.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Four loose parts become one (the PPS tube); the tube has an asymmetric locating collar so it can only be pressed one way (poka-yoke); no fasteners. Service is unaffected — e-compressors are replaced, not opened, in the field — and the cast sump pocket is cleaned by the existing washer.

Proof: OCR measurement per ASHRAE 41.4 across the speed map, compressor durability (OEM 1,000 h cyclic), SAE J2727-style leak, X-ray CT on first-off castings. Mitigation: minimum-speed limit in the inverter, vacuum-assisted HPDC on the rear head.
