engineering.mechanism: A cyclone separates droplets by centrifugal acceleration a = v_t²/r. With v_t ≈ 12 m/s and r ≈ 10 mm, a ≈ 14,400 m/s² (≈1,470 g). Terminal radial velocity of a droplet (Stokes) is u = d²(ρ_oil − ρ_gas)a / (18 μ); for d = 8 µm, ρ_oil ≈ 950 kg/m³, ρ_gas ≈ 65 kg/m³, μ ≈ 1.4×10⁻⁵ Pa·s this gives ≈ 3.2 m/s, so the droplet crosses a 5 mm annulus in ~1.6 ms against a residence time of ~4-6 ms. Pressure drop Δp ≈ K·ρ·v²/2 with K ≈ 30-40 gives 0.15-0.2 bar, inside the 0.3 bar budget a mesh pad typically uses when wetted. Below ~2,000 rpm inlet velocity halves and d50 rises by √2, so a minimum-speed limit protects separation.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: separator cylinder (DC04, 0.6 mm), demister pad (AISI 304 knitted mesh, ~4 g), circlip DIN 472 Ø22, HNBR O-ring 18×1.5, and the machined circlip groove. Add: PPS-GF40 (e.g. 40 % glass) vortex tube, Ø7.0/5.2 mm, length 24 mm, collar Ø11 mm with keying flat; press-fit interference 0.05-0.10 mm into reamed land H8, Ra ≤ 1.6 µm. Rear head drawing: cored cyclone bore Ø20 ±0.3 mm as-cast, 1° draft, tangential inlet slot 4×8 mm, sump pocket 3 cm³, laser-drilled return orifice Ø0.60 ±0.02 mm. HPDC with vacuum assist, porosity class per VDG P 202 level 2 in the cyclone wall.
engineering.validationPlan: OCR mapping per ASHRAE 41.4 at 1,500-8,500 rpm, three suction/discharge pressure sets, 3 samples; acceptance OCR ≤ 3 % mass at ≥ 2,000 rpm. Compressor durability 1,000 h cyclic on OEM rig, 3 samples, scroll-tip wear ≤ baseline +10 %. Thermal ageing of the PPS tube 1,000 h at 150 °C in POE/R1234yf (ASHRAE 97 sealed tube), dimensional change ≤ 0.5 %. Vibration ISO 16750-3 (engine-mounted profile). Helium leak ≤ 1×10⁻⁵ mbar·l/s. PPAP: change to rear-head casting and new component → full PPAP level 3 at the compressor supplier, OEM A/C system re-sign-off.
engineering.dfmImplications: Part count −4, one press station replaces a press + circlip station. HPDC core slide adds ~2 s to die maintenance per shot equivalent; no secondary op beyond a 6 s ream. Vortex tube keying flat prevents rotated insertion; force-displacement window catches missing or cracked tubes. No field service impact.
engineering.costBridge: Per compressor (one per vehicle): the steel separator cylinder and mesh pad (€1.35) are deleted; the PPS vortex tube adds €0.32. Machining of the separator bore falls from €0.80 to a €0.25 ream; the circlip, O-ring and press station fall from €0.38 to €0.10. HPDC core-slide upkeep adds €0.06. Not included: any efficiency change, die modification (in investment) or OEM engineering hours.

title: 48 V e-compressor motor feedthrough: PPS-moulded copper pins replace glass-to-metal hermetic terminal

Baseline (general practice, carried over from high-voltage compressor design): the three motor phases pass from the refrigerant-filled motor chamber to the inverter compartment through a glass-to-metal hermetic terminal — a steel body with three pins fused in glass, welded or caulked into the housing — plus an internal cluster-block connector. At 48 V (≤60 V DC, decisive voltage class A per ISO 6469-3/LV 148) required creepage is only ~1-2 mm (IEC 60664-1, PD2) and partial discharge is irrelevant, so the remaining requirement is refrigerant tightness at up to ~25-30 bar burst-safety on the suction-side motor chamber. engineering.mechanism: Insulation demand scales with voltage: IEC 60664-1 basic creepage at 63 V working voltage, PD2, material group IIIa is ~1.6 mm, versus ~4-8 mm and partial-discharge-free design at 800 V. The boundary therefore only has to be tight. Helium leak through a polymer seal path is governed by interface gap: a 1 µm gap over 4 mm length leaks ~10⁻⁴ mbar·l/s, while a laser micro-structure (20-40 µm undercuts) mechanically interlocks the PPS and keeps the gap closed through thermal cycling, giving ≤10⁻⁶ mbar·l/s in published insert-moulding practice. Current: 3.5 kW / (√3·~30 V line) ≈ 67 A rms per phase; a Ø2.4 mm Cu-ETP pin (4.5 mm², 0.017 µΩ·m) dissipates I²R ≈ 0.4 W over 20 mm — negligible.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete glass-to-metal terminal P/N (3-pin, 52-alloy pins, fused glass) and resistance-weld seat. New: pin Cu-ETP CW004A R250, Ø2.40 −0.02 mm, Sn 2-4 µm on the inverter end, two laser knurl bands 0.5 mm wide, depth 30 ±10 µm; carrier PPS-GF40, wall ≥ 2.5 mm between pins, creepage ≥ 3 mm; FKM O-ring 24×2.0, 75 Shore A, R1234yf/POE-compatible; housing bore Ø28 H8, Ra ≤ 0.8 µm, lead-in 15°×1 mm; two M4×10 8.8 screws, 2.8 Nm. Insert-moulding: mould 140 °C, pins preheated 120 °C.

Thermal shock 1,000 cycles −40/+125 °C (IEC 60068-2-14 Na), n = 30, then leak and burst (≥ 90 bar, 3× MOP). Refrigerant/oil compatibility 2,000 h at 125 °C in R1234yf + POE (sealed tube), swelling ≤ 5 %. Vibration ISO 16750-3 engine profile, n = 6. Insulation 500 V DC ≥ 100 MΩ. PPAP level 3 for compressor change; OEM A/C system leak-rate re-validation.

title: E-compressor inverter board: single DC-link shunt with phase reconstruction replaces three Hall current sensors
description: [MHEV] Three precision Hall sensors and their layout are replaced by one shunt and an amplifier already available inside the gate-driver IC; EOL calibration of three gain/offset pairs collapses to one. Baseline (common for 3-4 kW compressor drives carried over from HV designs): field-oriented control with three in-line coreless Hall current sensor ICs on the phase busbars, plus their filter networks and a 4-layer area to carry them. A scroll compressor is a near-constant, slowly varying load (no sub-second torque reversals, speed ramps of ~500-1,000 rpm/s), which is the textbook case for single-shunt current reconstruction: one 0.5 mΩ metal-element shunt in the DC-link return, sampled twice per PWM period at the active vectors to recover two phase currents, with minimum-pulse insertion near sector boundaries. Proposal for the 48 V MHEV compressor: delete the three Hall ICs, add one 0.5 mΩ 3 W shunt and a 40 V/µs current-sense amplifier integrated in a three-phase gate-driver IC, move sampling into the existing MCU ADC triggers, and add an overcurrent comparator on the shunt for hardware protection (faster than the Hall ICs' ~2-3 µs). At 48 V the DC-link current is ~80-90 A peak, so the shunt dissipates I²R ≈ 3-4 W at peak and ~1.5 W at typical 2 kW load; a 2512 shunt on 2 oz copper with thermal vias handles it. ideaData.title: E-compressor inverter board: single DC-link shunt with phase reconstruction replaces three Hall current sensors
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (common for 3-4 kW compressor drives carried over from HV designs): field-oriented control with three in-line coreless Hall current sensor ICs on the phase busbars, plus their filter networks and a 4-layer area to carry them. A scroll compressor is a near-constant, slowly varying load (no sub-second torque reversals, speed ramps of ~500-1,000 rpm/s), which is the textbook case for single-shunt current reconstruction: one 0.5 mΩ metal-element shunt in the DC-link return, sampled twice per PWM period at the active vectors to recover two phase currents, with minimum-pulse insertion near sector boundaries. Proposal for the 48 V MHEV compressor: delete the three Hall ICs, add one 0.5 mΩ 3 W shunt and a 40 V/µs current-sense amplifier integrated in a three-phase gate-driver IC, move sampling into the existing MCU ADC triggers, and add an overcurrent comparator on the shunt for hardware protection (faster than the Hall ICs' ~2-3 µs). At 48 V the DC-link current is ~80-90 A peak, so the shunt dissipates I²R ≈ 3-4 W at peak and ~1.5 W at typical 2 kW load; a 2512 shunt on 2 oz copper with thermal vias handles it. Benchmark: 48 V e-compressors are in series production (Sanden for Mercedes S/E-Class); the current-sensing scheme of those units is not published — single-shunt FOC is general practice in automotive pump and fan drives, and its use here is this idea's proposal.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Three precision Hall sensors and their layout are replaced by one shunt and an amplifier already available inside the gate-driver IC; EOL calibration of three gain/offset pairs collapses to one.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: SMT placements −10 to −12; board area −8-10 cm² (allows a smaller panel nest); EOL calibration step 20 s → 8 s. No new equipment; firmware change and a new board revision.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Fewer components and no orientation-sensitive Hall packages over busbars (a known placement-tolerance source); the shunt is a symmetric part. Field service unchanged — compressor is replaced as a unit.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — proven technique in pumps/fans applied to the compressor
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €2.35 per vehicle (Three Hall current-sensor ICs + filters: 2.55; Shunt + CSA-integrated gate-driver delta: -0.62; PCB area (4-layer FR4): 0.30; EOL current calibration: 0.12). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €2.00-€2.59 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €100K-€130K. One compressor per vehicle.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: acoustic noise and torque ripple from minimum-pulse insertion at low modulation index; current-reconstruction error at low speed; loss of per-phase fault detection. Proof: NVH (compressor on vehicle, ISO 5128 cabin noise), ISO 26262 FMEDA showing protection unchanged (compressor is typically QM/ASIL A), CISPR 25 class 5 EMC. Mitigation: phase-shift PWM method, retain winding-temperature model.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Mercedes-Benz S-Class / E-Class mild hybrid (Sanden 48 V e-compressor) — 48 V electric A/C compressor in series production. How this differs: No source describes that compressor's current sensing; the single-shunt scheme is generic motor-drive practice proposed here for our compressor.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: 4-layer FR4 board, 3 Hall placements + 3 filter networks → 1 shunt placement; firmware-based reconstruction; one-point EOL calibration
ideaData.regulatoryContext: EMC per UNECE R10 and CISPR 25 must be re-confirmed because PWM pattern changes alter the emission spectrum.
ideaData.focusArea: Electric A/C compressor — inverter control board
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Single-shunt reconstruction needs each active vector to last at least t_min = t_dead + t_settle + t_ADC ≈ 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 2 µs. At 20 kHz (50 µs period) this restricts the usable sector-boundary region to a few % of the hexagon, which a phase-shift PWM handles at a ripple cost of <2 % torque. Accuracy: shunt ±0.5 % with 50 ppm/K tempco, amplifier offset ±1 mV on 0.5 mΩ = ±2 A, comparable to Hall ICs (±1-2 % FS of 100 A). Loss: P = I²R = (60 A rms DC-equivalent)² × 0.5 mΩ ≈ 1.8 W, i.e. 0.06 % of 3 kW. Overcurrent trip latency: comparator ~0.5 µs vs Hall ~2-3 µs.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: 3 × coreless Hall current sensor IC (±100 A), 3 × RC filter, 3 × decoupling, busbar slots in the power stage. Add: shunt 0.5 mΩ ±1 %, 3 W, 2512 MnCu, Kelvin layout; gate driver changed to a variant with integrated CSA (gain 20 V/V, 40 V/µs) and OCP comparator; 2 oz outer copper in shunt zone with 12 thermal vias Ø0.3 mm. Firmware: two ADC triggers per period, phase-shift PWM, minimum vector 2 µs. EOL: one gain/offset calibration at 20 A and 0 A replaces three.
engineering.validationPlan: Bench: current reconstruction error ≤ 3 % rms across 800-8,500 rpm and 0-4 kW, n = 5. NVH on vehicle: cabin noise ≤ baseline +1 dB(A) at idle with compressor at 2,000 rpm. EMC CISPR 25 class 5 conducted/radiated, ISO 11452-2/-4 immunity. Electrical ISO 16750-2 / LV 148 (48 V ranges incl. 70 V overvoltage). Thermal ISO 16750-4, 1,000 h 105 °C operating. Functional safety: FMEDA update, overcurrent detection time ≤ 5 µs. PPAP: board revision → PPAP level 3 at inverter supplier; OEM software release.
engineering.dfmImplications: SMT placements −11; one fewer calibration point pair (EOL 20 s → 8 s); board nest smaller by ~9 cm² (panel utilisation +1 board per panel). No new fixtures. Fewer orientation-sensitive parts reduces AOI false calls.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: three Hall ICs at ~€0.85 (€2.55) are deleted; the shunt plus the incremental cost of a CSA-integrated gate driver add €0.62. PCB area reduction saves €0.30. EOL calibration drops from €0.20 to €0.08. Not included: firmware engineering (in validation investment) and any efficiency gain.

ideaData.title: Active roll actuator: torque estimated from motor current and bar twist deletes magnetostrictive torque sensor
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V electromechanical roll stabiliser (two per vehicle, front and rear) contains a BLDC motor, a three-stage planetary gear and an integrated non-contact torque sensor on the output — Schaeffler describes exactly this architecture, with the torque signal used to control the actuator precisely, and a patent family describes inverse-magnetostriction sensing. The roll controller, however, closes its outer loop on body roll (lateral acceleration, roll rate from the IMU, ride-height sensors) and only needs actuator torque for the inner loop. Proposal: estimate output torque as T_out = i·η(ω, T, sign)·Kt·i_q, where i ≈ 150-200 is the three-stage ratio, η is a stored efficiency map (forward and back-driven, temperature-dependent), Kt is learned at EOL; cross-check with bar torsion T_bar = k_bar·(θ_motor/i − θ_body-derived), using the known torsional stiffness of both bar halves and the motor position sensor that is already present for commutation. A Kalman observer fuses the two. Expected accuracy ±8-12 % versus ±2-3 % for the sensor — sufficient because roll-angle error is governed by the outer loop and a 10 % torque error is a ~0.1° roll error at 0.5 g. The sensor ring (magnetised shaft zone or sleeve), its coil/ASIC, internal wiring and calibration are deleted from both actuators.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes the most expensive sensing element in each actuator (magnetised shaft zone, pick-up coils and ASIC, internal harness, EOL calibration); the replacement is software running on the existing actuator MCU with sensors that are already fitted.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Deletes the shaft magnetisation station and the torque-sensor calibration rig at the actuator supplier; adds a 15-20 s friction/efficiency learn run on the existing EOL test bench. Housing machining simplified (no sensor pocket).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Per actuator −1 sensor assembly, −1 internal connector, −1 calibration step. Serviceability improves: no sensor recalibration after actuator swap; the observer re-learns friction on first drive.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — two sensors per vehicle deleted
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €19.90 per vehicle (Torque sensor element + ASIC (2 actuators): 17.00; Internal sensor harness and connector (2): 2.40; EOL torque calibration (2): 1.30; Observer software runtime / flash uplift: -0.80). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €16.9-€21.9 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €846K-€1.09M. Assumes active roll fitted to all MHEV vehicles; scale by real take-rate.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: efficiency scatter and wear over life (gear friction rises), cold-temperature viscosity changes, loss of a diverse measurement for ASIL argument. Proof: ISO 26262 safety analysis (roll control typically ASIL B-C for unintended roll torque) showing current-based plausibility is sufficient; vehicle handling ISO 3888-2, ISO 7401; actuator durability 1.5 M cycles. Mitigation: retain current and position plausibility, online friction adaptation.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Schaeffler 48 V electromechanical active roll control (volume production since 2015) — Actuator = motor + three-stage planetary + integrated non-contact torque sensor used for precise control. How this differs: We keep the architecture but replace the physical torque sensor with a model-based torque observer; no source says any OEM has done this.

ideaData.focusArea: 48 V electromechanical active roll control — sensing
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Output torque from current: T_out = i·η·Kt·i_q. With i = 180, Kt = 0.025 Nm/A, i_q = 250 A peak and η = 0.80, T_out ≈ 900 Nm — the right order for a large-SUV front actuator (~1,000-1,200 Nm). Efficiency of a three-stage planetary varies ~0.75-0.90 with load, speed and temperature, so an uncompensated estimate errs ±10 %; a 3-D map (load, speed, oil temperature) plus online friction adaptation brings it to ±6-8 %. Bar torsion check: T = k·Δθ with k ≈ 8-12 kNm/rad per half; motor position resolution 0.1° electrical ÷ 180 ≈ 0.0006° output, so torsion resolves to <1 Nm. Roll angle sensitivity: φ ≈ (M_roll − T_bars)/K_roll; 10 % torque error at 0.5 g ≈ 0.1° roll.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete per actuator: magnetised shaft zone (or sleeve), pick-up coil set and sensor ASIC, internal 4-wire harness and connector, sensor pocket machining in the housing, magnetisation station and torque calibration step. Add: efficiency map (3 × 12 × 10 points, forward/back-driven) and Kalman observer in actuator MCU software (~20 kB flash, ~5 % CPU); EOL learn routine: ±300 Nm sweep against the bench load cell to fit Kt and η offsets; drawing note: friction torque at output 5-15 Nm at 23 °C (new tolerance, previously not specified).
engineering.validationPlan: Bench: estimate vs reference load cell over −40/+85 °C, 0-1,200 Nm, n = 6 actuators, acceptance ±10 % (2σ). Durability 1.5 M roll cycles + 500 h salt/humidity per ISO 16750-4/-5, re-check accuracy at end. Vehicle: ISO 3888-2 lane change, ISO 7401 step steer, roll-angle error ≤ 0.2° vs baseline. Safety: HARA/FMEDA update, fault injection on current sensing; single-point fault metric ≥ 90 % for ASIL B. EMC CISPR 25 and ISO 11452. PPAP level 3 for actuator change; OEM chassis software release.
engineering.dfmImplications: Per actuator −3 parts and −2 stations (magnetisation, torque calibration); EOL adds a 15-20 s learn on an existing bench. Housing loses one machined pocket. No new fixtures; field swap no longer requires sensor offset coding.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (two actuators): sensor elements and ASICs €17.00 deleted; internal sensor wiring/connector €2.40 deleted; torque calibration falls from €1.60 to a €0.30 learn run; added MCU flash/runtime and EOL learn logistics €0.80. Not included: software development (in validation investment) and any warranty change.

ideaData.title: Roll actuator housing flow-formed in 16MnCr5 with integral first-stage ring-gear teeth, wade-sealed
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline (generic construction of an electromechanical roll actuator; supplier designs are not published): a cylindrical steel housing turned and bored from a seamless E355 tube, with separate ring-gear inserts for the planetary stages pressed and pinned into the bore, and end flanges joined to the tube. The actuator sits low on the axle — on the front axle close to or below the wading line of a 900 mm-wading SUV — so its seals and housing joints are part of the off-road specification. Proposal: flow-form the housing from a 16MnCr5 pre-form cup over a toothed mandrel so that the first-stage (high-speed, low-torque) ring-gear teeth are formed integrally in the bore (module ~0.8-1.0, DIN 3962 quality 9-10), and the bore for the second and third-stage rings is formed to near-net size (IT9), needing only a finish turn on bearing seats. The housing is then gas-nitrocarburised (compound layer 10-15 µm, 550-600 HV) for tooth wear resistance and corrosion protection, deleting the e-coat. The motor-end cap is laser-welded (continuous, no gasket), and the output end carries a double-lip FKM seal with an excluder lip rated for 900 mm wading (IP6K9K + IPX7 immersion). Only the high-torque final stage keeps a separate hobbed ring. Physics: first-stage ring torque is only ~motor torque × stage ratio (~1-2 Nm × ~5 ≈ 5-10 Nm), so formed teeth with lower accuracy are adequate. Benchmark: Schaeffler 48 V roll control uses a three-stage planetary in the actuator (source); this housing route is a proposal.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes one or two ring-gear inserts and their press-and-pin operations; flow-forming produces the bore and teeth in one chipless operation, cutting machining and material (no tube bore turning).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Requires a CNC flow-forming machine (at the supplier) with toothed mandrels; bore turning cycle drops ~60 %; adds nitrocarburising batch; laser end-cap weld replaces bolted/gasket joint. Material utilisation rises from ~55 % (bored tube) to ~85 %.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Per actuator −1 ring gear (sometimes −2), −2 pins, −1 gasket; planetary assembly drops into integral teeth with no angular orientation. Welded end cap means the actuator is a sealed replacement unit — consistent with current dealer practice of swapping the actuator.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €14.20 per vehicle (First-stage ring gear inserts (2): 12.00; Press-fit and pinning (2): 1.20; Housing material + bore machining (2): 4.60; Gas nitrocarburising (2): -3.00; End-cap laser weld vs gasket + screws (2): -0.60). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €12.1-€15.6 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €604K-€781K. Two actuators per vehicle; assumes active roll on all MHEV vehicles.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: formed-tooth profile accuracy and springback, nitrocarburising distortion of bearing seats, weld integrity under salt and immersion, stone impact on the low-mounted housing. Proof: gear noise on actuator rig, ISO 16750-3 vibration, ISO 16750-5 immersion, 1,000 h salt spray (ISO 9227 NSS), gravel impact per VDA 621-427, wading on vehicle. Mitigation: post-NC finish turn on seats only.

How this differs: Source does not describe the housing; integral flow-formed ring teeth and the wade-rated welded construction are this idea's proposal based on general flow-forming practice (internal splines in clutch drums).

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Tube cut, bore-turn, ring hob + case-harden, press and pin → pre-form cup, flow-form over toothed mandrel, finish-turn seats, gas nitrocarburise, laser-weld end cap

engineering.mechanism: Tooth bending stress σ_F = F_t/(b·m)·Y_F·Y_S. First stage: T_ring ≈ 8 Nm on a ~60 mm pitch diameter → F_t ≈ 270 N; with b = 10 mm, m = 0.9, Y_F·Y_S ≈ 4.5, σ_F ≈ 135 MPa, well below the ~300-350 MPa bending endurance of nitrocarburised 16MnCr5. Third stage carries ~1,000 Nm and stays a hobbed, case-hardened ring. Flow-forming wall reduction 30-50 % per pass work-hardens the material (+20-30 % yield), and rolled teeth have unbroken grain flow. Wading: a static immersion head of 0.9 m = 9 kPa; a double-lip seal with excluder holds ≥ 30 kPa, giving margin for thermal pumping when a hot actuator is quenched.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete per actuator: first-stage ring gear (20MnCr5, hobbed, case-hardened), 2 × Ø4 dowel pins, end-cap gasket and 6 screws, e-coat. New housing: 16MnCr5 pre-form cup (forged/deep-drawn), flow-formed to wall 3.5 ±0.1 mm, internal teeth m = 0.9, z = 66, DIN 3962 Q9; bearing seats finish-turned IT6, Ra 0.8; gas-nitrocarburise 570 °C, CLT 10-15 µm, post-oxidised; laser weld end cap 2 kW fibre, penetration ≥ 1.2 mm. Output seal: FKM double-lip + excluder, shaft Ra 0.2-0.4 µm.
engineering.validationPlan: Actuator rig: 1.5 M load cycles at ±1,000 Nm (OEM durability), n = 6; gear noise ≤ baseline +2 dB. ISO 16750-3 vibration (sprung-mass profile), ISO 16750-4 thermal shock incl. splash water at 110 °C → 0 °C, ISO 16750-5 / IPX7 immersion and IP6K9K. Salt spray 1,000 h ISO 9227 and VDA 233-102 cyclic, gravel VDA 621-427. Weld: metallography + helium leak on n = 30. Vehicle wading 900 mm, 10 crossings hot. PPAP level 3; new process (flow-forming) needs run-at-rate at supplier.
engineering.dfmImplications: Part count −4 per actuator; press-and-pin station deleted; ring gear orientation no longer matters. Flow-forming adds mandrel wear (re-grind every ~40k parts). Laser weld needs clamping fixture with motor already installed — sequence change. Field service: sealed swap unit.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (two actuators): first-stage ring inserts €12.00 deleted; press-and-pin €1.20 deleted; housing tube + machining drops from €9.00 to €4.40 as flow-formed; nitrocarburising adds €3.00; laser end-cap weld adds €0.60 net of the deleted gasket and screws. Not included: machine capex amortisation at the supplier (in investment) and any mass saving value.

title: 48 V rack EPS ball-screw thread: CBN hard whirling replaces thread grinding on the rack
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Machine time on the thread falls from ~7 min to ~1 min; grinding-wheel dressing and nital/burn inspection reduce; one hard-whirling centre replaces several thread grinders in capacity. Baseline: in a belt-drive (rack-parallel) EPS the motor turns a ball nut on a ball-screw thread machined into the rack shaft; after induction hardening of the thread zone to 58-62 HRC the gothic-arch ball track is ground on a thread grinder, typically the longest single operation on the rack. MAPAL reports that for a steering-rack thread, grinding takes more than seven minutes while whirling finishes it in about 60 seconds; EMUGE and Leistritz describe CBN hard whirling of hardened ball-screw threads (to ~65 HRC) to near-ground accuracy in a single pass. Proposal for the 48 V EPS of the 2.7 t SUV (rack force up to ~16-18 kN, which is why 48 V was chosen): rough-whirl the soft rack (Cf53 or 42CrMo4 QT), induction-harden the thread zone to 58-62 HRC (case 1.5-2.5 mm), then CBN hard-whirl the gothic-arch profile in one pass (~60 s), followed by a 20 s tape-superfinish to Ra ≤ 0.2 µm on the ball track. Lead accuracy target ≤ 12 µm/300 mm (ISO 3408-3 class T5-T7 equivalent) — adequate for an EPS where backlash is taken up by the preloaded nut. The rack is shared with the 800 V BEV (same EPS family), so volume covers both.

Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €8.59-€11.1 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €430K-€556K. One rack per vehicle; BEV racks would add further saving, not counted.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: white-layer formation and residual tensile stress from hard machining reducing rolling-contact fatigue life; lead error accumulation; NVH (ball-pass noise) from surface waviness. Proof: Barkhausen/X-ray residual stress (target compressive ≤ −300 MPa), ball-nut rig durability (OEM ~1 M cycles), NVH on rack test bench, steering feel on vehicle. Mitigation: tape superfinish, CBN edge prep.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Steering-rack thread production (MAPAL whirling vs grinding data) — Steering-rack thread whirled in ~60 s versus >7 min grinding (MAPAL); CBN hard whirling of hardened ball-screw threads to near-ground accuracy (EMUGE, Leistritz). How this differs: Applied to the ball-screw track of our 48 V belt-drive EPS rack with a superfinish step; whether a given EPS supplier already whirls is not known from sources.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Soft thread turning, induction hardening, CBN-wheel thread grinding (~7 min) → soft rough whirl, induction hardening, CBN hard whirling (~60 s) + tape superfinish (20 s)

ideaData.focusArea: 48 V belt-drive rack EPS — rack ball-screw gear
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Rolling-contact fatigue life of a ball track scales roughly with (C/P)³ and is sensitive to surface integrity: a tensile residual stress or white layer can cut L10 by 30-50 %, while a compressive surface stress of −300 to −600 MPa (typical after hard turning/whirling with honed CBN edges) is neutral or beneficial. Waviness drives ball-pass noise at f = n_balls × relative speed; superfinish to Ra ≤ 0.2 µm and waviness Wt ≤ 1.5 µm keeps it at ground-thread level. Productivity: whirling removes the 0.1-0.2 mm hardened stock with a multi-insert ring rotating at ~2,000 rpm around the slowly turning rack, so metal removal is continuous rather than single-point grinding with multiple passes.
engineering.specDeltas: Drawing: ball-track profile gothic arch, conformity 0.52-0.54, Ra ≤ 0.20 µm, Rz ≤ 1.5 µm, waviness Wt ≤ 1.5 µm; lead deviation ≤ 12 µm/300 mm; residual stress at surface ≤ −300 MPa (X-ray, sample 1/shift); no white layer > 1 µm (metallography 1/batch). Process: CBN inserts (e.g. 6 inserts, gothic-arch, 0.02 mm × 20° chamfer hone), cutting speed ~150-200 m/min, single pass; tape superfinish 30 µm → 9 µm film, 20 s. Delete grinding process sheet, wheel/dresser specification and nital etch 100 % inspection (replaced by eddy-current burn check sample).
engineering.validationPlan: Rack gear rig durability per OEM EPS spec (~1 M cycles at road-load spectrum + 10k parking cycles at 16 kN), n = 6, no spalling. Ball-nut NVH: rack bench, order analysis ≤ baseline +1 dB. Residual stress and white layer metallography n = 10 from run-at-rate. Corrosion (ISO 9227 NSS 240 h on bellows-protected zone). Vehicle steering-feel subjective + objective (ISO 13674-1 on-centre). PPAP level 3 (process change on a safety part, ASIL D item); UNECE R79 CoP evidence updated.
engineering.dfmImplications: Machine count for the thread operation falls ~3:1; floor space and grinding coolant system reduced. CBN inserts re-indexed every ~800-1,000 racks. Adds one superfinish station. No change to EPS assembly or service.
engineering.costBridge: Per rack (one per vehicle): thread grinding at ~€95/h for 7.2 min (€11.40) is deleted; hard whirling for ~1 min at €110/h costs €1.85; consumables fall from €1.10 (wheel, dressing) to €0.45 (CBN); superfinish adds €0.40; burn-related scrap and inspection fall from €0.60 to €0.30. Not included: induction hardening (unchanged) and supplier margin effects.

ideaData.title: Air-supply dryer: moulded PA66-GF30 cartridge with 3A molecular sieve replaces machined aluminium silica-gel dryer
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: air-suspension supply units from Wabco, AMK, Continental and Hitachi use silica-gel desiccant (source), commonly in a dryer body turned or impact-extruded from aluminium with a spring-loaded end cap, circlip and O-rings, integrated with the compressor head. Off-road use is the dryer's worst case: repeated access-height/off-road-height lifts and kneel cycles move several times the on-road air volume, often in humid or wading conditions, and the dryer is regenerated only by purge air at exhaust. Proposal (on the 48 V brushless supply unit already defined in the library, shared with the BEV): replace the machined aluminium body with an injection-moulded PA66-GF30 cartridge welded (vibration-welded) to a moulded head that carries the inlet check valve and purge orifice, and replace ~110 g silica gel with ~70 g of 3A molecular sieve beads (or a 70/30 sieve/silica layered bed). 3A sieve holds 18-21 % water by mass at low partial pressure and retains capacity above 50 °C, where silica gel loses most of its adsorption — relevant because the dryer sits next to a compressor discharging at 120-150 °C during long off-road lift sequences. Smaller bed volume shortens the cartridge by ~30 %, cutting purge-air volume per regeneration. Benchmark: WABCO supply units on Audi Q7/Q8, Bentley Bentayga and Lamborghini Urus (source) use silica-gel dryers; the moulded sieve cartridge is this idea's proposal.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: A moulded and welded polyamide body replaces a machined aluminium body with circlip and end cap; a smaller mass of higher-capacity desiccant offsets its higher price per kg; assembly steps fall.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Deletes aluminium turning (~90 s) and anodise/passivation; adds one 2-cavity injection tool and a vibration-welding station (~12 s). Desiccant fill by volumetric doser with vibration settling, then weld — a closed cartridge with no circlip.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count per dryer 7 → 3 (cartridge, head, desiccant charge) plus the existing check valve; no circlip or spring; weld is poka-yoke by asymmetric weld flange. Service: dryer remains replaceable with the supply unit, as today.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — one supply unit per vehicle
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €2.98 per vehicle (Dryer body: 2.60; Desiccant charge: -0.05; Seals, spring, end cap, circlip: 0.28; Dryer assembly labour: 0.15). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €2.53-€3.28 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €126K-€164K. Air suspension assumed standard on the luxury SUV MHEV; scale by take-rate.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: PA66 hydrolysis and creep at 120-150 °C wet air; weld burst at 20-bar closed-loop variants; sieve dusting (attrition) contaminating valves. Proof: burst ≥ 4× MOP after 1,000 h 130 °C/95 % RH ageing, ISO 16750-3 vibration with dust capture filter check, off-road duty test (500 lift cycles) with dew-point measurement, ISO 16750-5 water. Mitigation: hydrolysis-stabilised PA66-GF30, 40 µm sintered PE filter disc.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Audi Q7/Q8, Bentley Bentayga, Lamborghini Urus (WABCO air-suspension supply unit) — Integrated compressor + dryer supply unit; silica-gel desiccant used in Wabco/AMK/Continental/Hitachi dryers. How this differs: We change the dryer body to moulded PA66-GF30 and the desiccant to 3A sieve for hot, high-duty off-road lifting; dryer body construction of those units is not stated in the sources.

ideaData.materialGrade: EN AW-6082-T6 machined dryer body + silica gel → PA66-GF30 (hydrolysis-stabilised) cartridge + 3A molecular sieve beads 1.6-2.5 mm
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Turned aluminium body, circlip end cap, O-rings → injection-moulded cartridge + head, vibration welded after desiccant fill
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Equilibrium capacity at 60 °C and ~10 % RH-equivalent: silica gel ~3-5 % water by mass, 3A sieve ~15-18 %. Water load per off-road lift: raising four springs by 75 mm needs ~25-35 litres of free air; at 30 °C, 80 % RH that carries ~0.7-0.9 g water. 20 lift cycles ≈ 16 g of water before purge. Silica at 60 °C (110 g × 4 %) holds ~4.4 g; sieve (70 g × 16 %) holds ~11 g; a 70/30 layered bed handles the stated cycle with purge between lifts. Purge air volume needed scales with bed volume, so a 30 % shorter bed regenerates with ~30 % less air, sparing compressor duty — itself the off-road limit.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: EN AW-6082-T6 dryer body (turned, 2.1 mm wall), end cap, spring, DIN 472 circlip, two NBR O-rings. Add: cartridge PA66-GF30 HS (hydrolysis-stabilised), wall 2.8 mm, ribbed; head PA66-GF30 with moulded check-valve seat and Ø0.9 mm purge orifice; vibration weld 240 Hz, 1.5 mm amplitude, melt-down 0.8 ±0.2 mm; desiccant 3A sieve beads 1.6-2.5 mm, 70 ±2 g (or 50 g sieve + 25 g silica layered), 40 µm sintered PE filter discs both ends; burst ≥ 80 bar (4× 20 bar closed-loop MOP).
engineering.validationPlan: Burst/pressure cycling: 1 M cycles 0-20 bar at 110 °C, n = 6, then burst ≥ 80 bar. Hydrolysis ageing 1,000 h 130 °C saturated air, tensile retention ≥ 70 %. Dew point: supply unit rig, 500 off-road lift cycles at 35 °C/90 % RH, outlet pressure dew point ≤ −20 °C. Vibration ISO 16750-3 + particle count in valve block filter. Water: ISO 16750-5 / IP6K9K on unit, vehicle wading 900 mm. Salt ISO 9227. PPAP level 3 on supply unit; OEM air-suspension system re-validation (cold −40 °C function).
engineering.dfmImplications: Dryer part count 7 → 3; turning, anodise and circlip stations deleted; new 2-cavity tool and vibration welder (~12 s). Volumetric fill and weld form a closed, tamper-evident cartridge. Weld flange is asymmetric so head cannot be rotated. Field: same replacement unit.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (one supply unit): machined aluminium dryer body €3.80 becomes a moulded and welded PA66-GF30 cartridge at €1.20; desiccant rises from €0.45 to €0.50 (less mass, higher €/kg); O-rings, spring, end cap and circlip fall from €0.40 to €0.12; dryer assembly labour falls from €0.35 to €0.20. Not included: the value of extra off-road lift cycles, which is a capability gain.

title: 48 V heated windscreen terminals: conductive-adhesive bonded clips replace indium-solder copper-braid connectors

ideaData.title: 48 V heated windscreen terminals: conductive-adhesive bonded clips replace indium-solder copper-braid connectors
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: heated glazing is powered through connectors soldered onto printed silver busbars; the Oeko-Institut ELV Annex II review notes that lead in solder relieved glass stress and that lead-free solders give higher stresses except indium-containing ones, with connectors and solder heated locally on the glass. Lead-free glazing solder is therefore typically an indium-rich alloy (costly) applied by induction or resistance soldering, with a copper braid or stamped tab and a 4-6 mm² lead sized for 12 V heating currents. On a 48 V heated windscreen (the library already proposes a 48 V coated screen), the supply current falls fourfold: ~1.0-1.2 kW / 48 V ≈ 21-25 A shared by two terminals, versus ~80-100 A at 14 V. That changes what the joint must carry: at ~12 A per terminal, a silver-filled electrically conductive adhesive (ECA, volume resistivity ~2-5×10⁻⁴ Ω·cm) over a 40 mm² pad has a joint resistance of ~1-2 mΩ and dissipates <0.3 W — acceptable — while imposing far lower thermal stress on the glass than a soldered joint because cure is at ~120-150 °C, not ~200-230 °C local soldering. Proposal: stamped tinned CuSn6 clip with a 1.5 mm² lead and sealed 2.8 mm terminal, bonded with a one-component Ag-epoxy ECA, cured in-line by IR (or during the laminating autoclave, where sequence allows), plus a structural epoxy fillet for mechanical retention.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Indium-bearing solder preforms and induction soldering stations are deleted; at 48 V the lower current lets the terminal and lead shrink; glass breakage scrap from solder-induced stress falls.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Glazing supplier replaces induction soldering cells (~25 s per terminal, preheat) with a dispensing + clip-placement robot and an IR cure tunnel (~60 s, parallel). Breakage at soldering, a known yield loss, is reduced. Pull-test sampling continues.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Two terminals per screen; clip has a locating tab on the busbar edge (poka-yoke for position). Smaller 2.8 mm sealed terminal eases harness routing at the A-pillar/cowl. Windscreen replacement at service unchanged; aftermarket screens come with terminals fitted.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — two terminals per screen, plus yield gain
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €3.05 per vehicle (Joining material: 1.25; Connector + pigtail lead: 0.75; Joining process: 0.60; Glass breakage scrap at termination: 0.45). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €2.59-€3.36 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €130K-€168K. Assumes a 48 V heated windscreen is fitted to all MHEV vehicles; shared with BEV but BEV volume not counted.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: ECA conductivity drift under humidity/thermal cycling (silver migration, epoxy moisture uptake), creep under harness pull, rise of joint resistance causing hot spots. Proof: 85 °C/85 % RH 1,000 h, thermal shock −40/+105 °C 1,000 cycles, pull-off ≥ 100 N after ageing, joint resistance rise ≤ 20 %, thermography at 1.2 kW. Valid only at 48 V currents; not for 12 V screens.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Heated glazing practice under ELV Annex II (Oeko-Institut exemption 8 review) — Connectors soldered to printed heated glazing; lead-free solders give higher glass stress except indium-containing solders; local heating on the glass. How this differs: We exploit the 4× lower current of a 48 V screen to move from solder to conductive adhesive; no source states an OEM has done this.

ideaData.materialGrade: Indium-containing lead-free solder + Cu braid/tab, 4-6 mm² lead → Ag-filled 1K epoxy ECA + tinned CuSn6 stamped clip, 1.5 mm² lead
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Local induction/resistance soldering of connector on glass → robotic ECA dispense, clip placement, IR cure + structural fillet
ideaData.regulatoryContext: ELV Directive 2000/53/EC Annex II: the glazing-solder lead exemption has expired for new types, which is what pushes cost into indium solders; ECA is lead-free and indium-free.
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Current per terminal I = P/(2·V): 1,100 W/(2 × 48 V) ≈ 11.5 A vs ≈ 39 A at 14 V. Joint resistance of ECA: R = ρ·t/A = 3×10⁻⁶ Ω·m × 50 µm / 40×10⁻⁶ m² ≈ 3.8 µΩ bulk, plus interface ~1 mΩ; P = I²R ≈ 11.5² × 1×10⁻³ ≈ 0.13 W, versus ~1.5 W if the same joint carried 39 A — so ECA is viable at 48 V only. Glass stress: thermal mismatch stress σ ≈ E·Δα·ΔT; soldering at ΔT ≈ 180-200 K with a Cu tab (Δα ≈ 8 ppm/K vs soda-lime) gives local tensile stress of tens of MPa (crack risk); ECA cure at ΔT ≈ 100 K with a compliant epoxy layer roughly halves it.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete per screen: 2 × indium-containing solder preforms, 2 × Cu braid/tab connectors with 4 mm² leads and 6.3 mm terminals, induction soldering process sheet. Add: 2 × stamped CuSn6 R550 clips, Sn 2-3 µm, 40 mm² bond pad, 1.5 mm² FLRY-B leads, 2-way sealed 2.8 mm connector; ECA: 1K Ag-epoxy, 0.10 ±0.02 g per pad, bond line 50 ±20 µm, cure IR to 140 °C core for 8 min; structural fillet 2K epoxy. Busbar print unchanged. Acceptance: joint R ≤ 2 mΩ new, pull ≥ 150 N new.
engineering.validationPlan: Per OEM glazing spec and ISO 16750-4: damp heat 85/85 1,000 h (n = 20), thermal shock −40/+105 °C 1,000 cycles (n = 20), joint R rise ≤ 20 %, pull ≥ 100 N after ageing. Electrical: 1.3 kW continuous 1,000 h at 40 °C ambient with thermography (pad ΔT ≤ 25 K). Vibration ISO 16750-3 body profile. UNECE R43 glazing approval check (terminal does not affect optics). PPAP level 3 at glazing supplier; OEM windscreen re-release.
engineering.dfmImplications: Glazing line: induction soldering cell → dispense/place robot + IR tunnel; breakage yield improves. Clip tab gives positional poka-yoke; vision check for ECA bead. Vehicle plant: smaller connector, same operation. Service: unchanged (complete screen).
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: indium-solder preforms (€1.60) are replaced by ECA at €0.35; Cu braid connectors and 4 mm² leads (€1.20) become stamped clips with 1.5 mm² leads (€0.45); soldering station cost per screen (€0.90) becomes dispense + cure (€0.30); glass breakage scrap allocated per screen falls from €0.70 to €0.25. Not included: harness savings beyond the pigtail.

title: 48 V main coolant pump: PPS-GF40 moulded rotor can replaces deep-drawn stainless can

Mitigation: dome ribs, PPS grade with high hydrolysis resistance.

engineering.mechanism: Eddy loss in a thin conductive can: P ≈ (π² · σ · B² · f² · t² /6) · V_can for thin walls; with σ(1.4404) ≈ 1.35 MS/m, B ≈ 0.25 T harmonic content at the can, f = 200 Hz (6,000 rpm, 4-pole), t = 0.35 mm and V ≈ 1.5 cm³, plus field-harmonic contributions, loss lands at ~10-25 W — 2-4 % of a 600 W pump. PPS: σ ≈ 0, loss ≈ 0. Magnetic gap grows by 0.55 mm; with a total effective gap of ~1.2 → 1.75 mm, airgap flux falls ~10-12 % for ferrite (high reluctance magnet dominates less), recovered by +6 % magnet length or stack. Pressure: hoop stress σ = p·r/t = 0.35 MPa × 15 mm / 0.9 mm ≈ 5.8 MPa, vs PPS-GF40 long-term strength at 125 °C ~40-50 MPa.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete: can P/N (1.4404, 0.35 mm, deep-drawn), weld ring, laser-weld process sheet, locating pin. Add: can PPS-GF40, 0.9 ±0.05 mm in air-gap zone, dome 1.6 mm with 6 radial ribs, flange with 3 anti-rotation keys; EPDM O-ring 42×2.5 (peroxide-cured, glycol); rotor OD reduced by 1.1 mm (2 × 0.55 mm) or magnet length +6 %; leak test ≤ 1×10⁻³ mbar·l/s He (coolant side); burst ≥ 14 bar.
engineering.validationPlan: Pressure pulse 1 M cycles 0-3.5 bar at 120 °C in G48 50 %, n = 6, then burst ≥ 14 bar. Coolant ageing 3,000 h at 125 °C (OEM coolant spec), dimensional change ≤ 0.3 %. Pump efficiency map across 1,000-6,000 rpm: hydraulic-to-electrical efficiency ≥ baseline −1 % point. ISO 16750-3 engine vibration, ISO 16750-4 thermal shock, LV 148 electrical. Durability 10,000 h pump life test. PPAP level 3 at pump supplier.
engineering.dfmImplications: Part count −2 (weld ring, locating pin); laser-weld station and its fume extraction deleted; moulding runs 4-cavity with ~35 s cycle. O-ring assembled with a cone tool; moulded keys prevent misorientation of can to stator. Pump stays a field-replaceable unit, no service change.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: deep-drawn stainless can €2.10 becomes a €0.85 PPS moulding; the laser-weld/crimp joint at €0.60 becomes an O-ring joint at €0.25; extra magnet/stack to recover the wider gap adds €0.40. Not included: efficiency benefit (eddy loss removed) beyond restoring baseline performance.

title: 48 V PTC air heater: three weighted MOSFET stages plus PWM replace six stages
description: [MHEV] Halves power switches, gate drivers and stage current sensors; simplifies internal busbars and terminals; board area shrinks. Control resolution is kept by PWM on the smallest stage. Context: the library already proposes a 48 V 3 kW PTC air heater for the diesel I6 (replacing the fuel-fired heater), and separately clamped AA1050 fins. This idea addresses its element grouping and power stage. Baseline (a 12 V-derived heater architecture): heating rods grouped in six switched stages for power steps, each with a MOSFET (or pair), gate drive, individual stage current sensing and its own busbar tab. At 48 V each stage of a six-stage 3 kW heater carries only ~10 A, so the stage count is set by power resolution, not current. Proposal: group the rods into three stages weighted 0.5/1.0/1.5 kW (binary-like steps 0.5-3 kW), and PWM the 0.5 kW stage at 10-20 Hz with slew-rate-controlled gate drive to fill between steps; one DC-bus shunt replaces per-stage sensing (stage faults detected by current step response when each stage switches). ideaData.title: 48 V PTC air heater: three weighted MOSFET stages plus PWM replace six stages
ideaData.technicalDescription: Context: the library already proposes a 48 V 3 kW PTC air heater for the diesel I6 (replacing the fuel-fired heater), and separately clamped AA1050 fins. This idea addresses its element grouping and power stage. Baseline (a 12 V-derived heater architecture): heating rods grouped in six switched stages for power steps, each with a MOSFET (or pair), gate drive, individual stage current sensing and its own busbar tab. At 48 V each stage of a six-stage 3 kW heater carries only ~10 A, so the stage count is set by power resolution, not current. Proposal: group the rods into three stages weighted 0.5/1.0/1.5 kW (binary-like steps 0.5-3 kW), and PWM the 0.5 kW stage at 10-20 Hz with slew-rate-controlled gate drive to fill between steps; one DC-bus shunt replaces per-stage sensing (stage faults detected by current step response when each stage switches). PTC stones self-limit at their Curie point (e.g. 200-220 °C), so the reduced stage count does not change over-temperature safety; inrush (PTC cold resistance is below nominal) is bounded by staggering stage turn-on 200 ms apart. Rod busbars reduce from six to three internal groups. Benchmark: thick-film electric heaters (BorgWarner) show the industry trend to fewer, PWM-controlled heating zones with high power density; this PTC regrouping is our proposal, not a sourced design.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Halves power switches, gate drivers and stage current sensors; simplifies internal busbars and terminals; board area shrinks. Control resolution is kept by PWM on the smallest stage.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Heater supplier: PCB populated with three power stages instead of six; three busbar groups; EOL test per stage shortens. No new process; one PCB revision and a busbar stamping die change.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Fewer internal terminals (6 → 3 stage groups); simpler rod insertion pattern with grouping keyed by busbar shape. Unit remains a cartridge in the HVAC case, serviceable as today.

costSavingPotential.percentage: 12-18 % of the PTC heater electronics cost

Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €1.80-€2.33 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €90K-€117K. Diesel I6 assumed 40 % of MHEV volume; all lines are fleet averages (per-diesel figure × 0.4).

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: PWM of a 0.5 kW load at 10-20 Hz produces 48 V bus ripple (≈10 A steps) visible to other consumers and flicker-like effects; EMC; reduced power granularity at mid steps. Proof: LV 148 E48-xx bus ripple limits, CISPR 25 class 5, cabin comfort (power steps), PTC stone ageing 1,000 h. Mitigation: slew-controlled edges (≥ 20 µs), coordinate PWM phase with DC-DC.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: BorgWarner thick-film coolant heater (high-voltage electric heater) — Thick-film element screen-printed on a metal plate giving high power density and fast response. How this differs: We stay with PTC stones (cheaper at 48 V, self-limiting) but borrow the idea of few heating zones with continuous electronic control; the stage regrouping is our proposal.

ideaData.regulatoryContext: EMC per UNECE R10; the 48 V bus quality limits of LV 148 / ISO 21780 apply to the PWM ripple.
ideaData.focusArea: 48 V PTC air heater — power stage and element grouping
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Stage current I = P/V: 0.5 kW/48 V = 10.4 A, 1.5 kW/48 V = 31 A — all within one 100 V TOLL MOSFET each (R_DS(on) ~1.5 mΩ → P_cond = 31² × 1.5 mΩ ≈ 1.5 W). Power resolution: binary 0.5/1.0/1.5 gives 0.5 kW steps; PWM on the 0.5 kW stage at duty d fills continuously. PWM ripple: 10.4 A steps on a 48 V bus with ~20 mΩ source impedance → ~0.2 V, inside the ±0.5-1 V dynamic window typical of 48 V specifications. PTC self-limiting: resistance rises 2-3 decades above T_Curie, so each stone limits its own surface temperature regardless of stage grouping.
engineering.specDeltas: PCB: power switches 6 → 3 (100 V, ≤1.5 mΩ, TOLL), gate drivers 6 → 3 with slew control (dV/dt ≤ 2.5 V/µs), per-stage shunts 6 → 1 DC-bus shunt 0.25 mΩ; firmware: stage weights 0.5/1.0/1.5 kW, PWM 10-20 Hz on stage 1, stagger 200 ms on switch-on. Busbars: six stamped CuSn0.15 groups → three groups; rod count and stones unchanged. Diagnostics: stage open/short from current step at switching (resolution ±2 A).
engineering.validationPlan: Heater bench: power accuracy ±5 % at each step, n = 5; PWM ripple on 48 V bus per LV 148 / ISO 21780 dynamic limits. EMC CISPR 25 class 5 and ISO 11452-2. Thermal: 1,000 h operation at 3 kW, 40 °C inlet; PTC resistance drift ≤ 10 %. Over-temperature: blocked-airflow test, surface ≤ PTC limit. Vibration ISO 16750-3, thermal shock ISO 16750-4. Cabin warm-up test at −20 °C: time-to-comfort ≤ baseline +3 %. PPAP level 3 (PCB and busbar change).
engineering.dfmImplications: SMT placements −15 to −18; busbar stamping simplified (3 groups); EOL test steps 6 → 3 (≈ −12 s). Rod insertion pattern keyed by busbar shape. Same cartridge envelope in the HVAC case; no plant change.
engineering.costBridge: Fleet average (per diesel vehicle × 0.4): MOSFETs and drivers fall from €2.64 to €1.50; stage sensing from €0.84 to €0.18; busbars/terminals from €0.96 to €0.64; PCB area from €0.72 to €0.48; added EMC filtering for PWM €0.24. Not included: petrol vehicles (no 48 V PTC assumed) and any cabin-comfort effect.

ideaData.title: Two separate 48 V e-pumps, one supplier drive platform: shared stator die, PCB, connector
ideaData.technicalDescription: This is a sourcing and commonisation lever, not a hardware merger: unlike concepts where one motor shaft drives two hydraulic stages, both e-pumps stay independent (own location, own control, own failure mode) and only their drive kit is shared. Context: the library proposes a 48 V main water pump with split-cooling valve and a sump-mounted 48 V gerotor e-pump replacing the chain-driven lubrication pump. Specified separately, each brings its own BLDC lamination die, magnet design, winding, inverter PCB, 48 V connector and software baseline — two development, tooling and DV sets for drives of similar power (~500-700 W and ~300-500 W at cold-start viscosity peaks). Proposal: nominate one supplier drive platform — one 4-pole/6-slot M270-35A lamination, two stack lengths (22 and 30 mm), one rotor design with length variants, one control/power PCB populated for 10 A or 15 A phase current, one sealed 48 V + LIN connector family with two codings and a common flange interface — onto which each hydraulic head is fitted. Drive-part volume doubles to 100,000/yr, giving quantity breaks on laminations, magnets, PCBs and connectors, and one sensorless FOC core with two parameter sets. Benchmark: published wet-running drive construction and can trade-offs define the interface; the platform approach itself is our proposal (no OEM attribution).
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Doubles volume on every motor and electronics part, halves tooling sets (lamination die, PCB, connector, can) and halves software/validation effort for the drive; one supplier nomination gives commercial leverage.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One winding line and one PCB SMT program serve both pumps; EOL motor test shared. Pump-specific hydraulics (impeller, gerotor) bolt on at the supplier. Vehicle plant: two pumps still fitted separately but with one connector type.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part numbers for drive components fall from ~2×12 to ~14 (variants by stack length and population); connector commonised reduces harness variants and mis-plug risk (keyed variants per pump). Service: common drive subassembly as service part across both pumps.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — two drives per vehicle commonised
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €6.90 per vehicle (Coolant pump motor + electronics: 3.50; Engine-oil e-pump motor + electronics: 2.50; Connectors and harness ends: 0.60; EOL fixtures, service part numbers (amortised): 0.30). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €5.86-€7.59 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €293K-€380K. Both pumps fitted to every MHEV per the library proposals; if either is not adopted the saving does not apply.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: oil pump drive oversized (cost and inertia) or coolant pump compromised; cold-start oil viscosity torque peak (−30 °C) sets the motor; cross-platform failure exposure (one defect hits both pumps). Proof: cold-start oil-pressure build-up at −30 °C, pump durability 10,000 h each, ISO 16750-3/-4, LV 148, CISPR 25. Mitigation: two stack lengths, current-limit parameterisation.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Wet-running automotive pump practice (Energies 2025; US 9887603) — Wet-rotor pump drive construction and the can/gap-tube trade-offs that define a drive interface. How this differs: Defines one drive platform across coolant and oil e-pumps; the sources describe pump construction, not cross-pump commonisation.

ideaData.materialGrade: Common stator lamination M270-35A; common rotor magnet grade (ferrite or NdFeB per pump power)
ideaData.manufacturingProcess: Two separate pump drive designs → one drive platform with two stack lengths, one PCB with population variants, one connector
ideaData.focusArea: 48 V electric pumps — motor and electronics commonisation
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: Drive sizing: coolant pump P_hyd ≈ Q·Δp = 200 l/min × 1.2 bar ≈ 400 W, η_pump·η_motor ≈ 0.55 → ~700 W electrical peak. Oil pump at −30 °C: viscosity ~10-20× warm value raises gerotor drag torque to ~1.5-2.5 Nm at 1,500 rpm → ~300-400 W mechanical for a short peak, ~150 W warm. Both fit one 4-pole/6-slot frame with stack 30 vs 22 mm (torque ∝ stack length). Cost learning: part cost typically falls ~8-12 % per doubling of volume for laminations, PCBs and connectors (learning-curve rule of thumb, an estimate), and tooling/validation fixed costs are shared over 2× units.
engineering.specDeltas: Platform spec: stator OD 62 mm, M270-35A, 6 slots, concentrated winding, stack 22/30 mm; rotor 4-pole, magnet length per stack; PCB 4-layer, 6 × 100 V MOSFETs (populated 10 A or 15 A variants), LIN 2.2 + PWM-fallback; connector one sealed 48 V/LIN 4-way family with two codings; can/flange interface Ø48 mm (coolant) — oil variant flange identical, can optional. Software: one FOC core, two parameter sets. Deleted: second lamination die, second PCB layout, second connector family, second software baseline.
engineering.validationPlan: Drive platform DV once: LV 148 electrical, ISO 16750-2/-3/-4/-5, CISPR 25 class 5, ISO 11452, 10,000 h endurance per variant (n = 6 each). Pump-level: coolant pump hydraulic map and cavitation (NPSH) test; oil pump cold-start pressure build-up ≤ 1.5 s to 1 bar at −30 °C 0W-20, n = 6. Engine durability per OEM (piggy-back on engine fleets). PPAP level 3 for both pumps from one supplier; family PPAP for drive parts.
engineering.dfmImplications: Drive components: 24 → ~14 part numbers; one winding line, one SMT program, one EOL motor test. Connector coding poka-yoke prevents swapped pumps. Supplier must manage two hydraulic heads on a common drive line.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle (both pumps): coolant pump drive €38.00 → €34.50 and oil pump drive €34.00 → €31.50 through doubled volume and shared design (oil variant slightly oversized); connectors/harness ends €3.20 → €2.60; EOL fixtures and service part numbers €0.80 → €0.50. Not included: hydraulic heads (unchanged) and the pumps' own adoption business cases.

title: 48 V battery, DC-DC and fuse branch pre-assembled off-line as one tested floor module
description: [MHEV] Moves ~160 s of main-line work to a cheaper off-line cell, deletes one bracket, and catches joint/connector defects on the bench instead of at vehicle EOL, cutting rework. Baseline (typical final-assembly practice): the 48 V battery, the 48/12 V DC-DC converter, their brackets and the short 48 V/12 V link cables are installed individually on the main trim line — five to six operations totalling ~210 s, partly in awkward positions (under-floor or boot-floor well), with two B+ joints torqued in the car and connector mating done blind. Defects surface only at EOL electrical test, where rework in a finished vehicle is expensive. Proposal: build a 48 V energy module off-line — battery, DC-DC, one stamped carrier tying both (replacing two separate brackets), the link cables and the 48 V branch pigtail — torque its joints on a bench with a DC nutrunner, check every connector with acoustic/force mating assurance, and run a 30 s module electrical test (48 V/12 V continuity, isolation of 48 V to chassis, DC-DC wake-up over CAN). The module is delivered in sequence to the main line and installed with four bolts and two connectors in ~50 s. Physics/economics: main-line minutes cost ~1.5× off-line minutes (line balance losses, overhead, takt constraints), and in-car rework of a 48 V joint costs 10-20× bench rework. Benchmark: connector mating verification by acoustic/force signature

engineering.mechanism: Cost of a minute differs by location: main-line minute = labour + share of conveyor, takt imbalance (~10-15 % loss) and overhead ≈ €1.30; off-line cell minute ≈ €0.85. Moving 160 s saves 160/60 × (1.30) and spends 170/60 × 0.85 (bench work is slightly longer but ergonomic). Defect economics: a loose B+ joint found at vehicle EOL costs ~25-40 min diagnostic + rework (~€35-55), on the bench ~2 min. At a plausible baseline escape rate of 1.5 % to EOL, expected rework ≈ €0.70/vehicle; bench detection and CPA cut it ~70 %.
engineering.specDeltas: New carrier drawing: HX340LAD 1.5 mm stamped, 4 × M8 vehicle mounting points, battery hook-in rails and DC-DC clamp; delete DC-DC bracket and battery bracket P/Ns (DC04). Process: module cell with DC nutrunner (torque-angle window, e.g. 12 Nm ±10 %, 30-90°), CPA verification per connector, module test (48 V continuity ≤ 1 mΩ per joint, 48 V-to-chassis isolation ≥ 1 MΩ, DC-DC CAN wake). engineering.mechanism: Clamp load F = T/(K·d); with K scattering 0.15-0.25, torque-only control allows ±25 % clamp scatter and cannot see a trapped lug (torque reached at low angle). Angle after snug reflects stiffness of the joint: a correct M8 lug joint reaches 12 Nm in ~30-60° after 3 Nm snug; a trapped lug or cross-thread reaches it in <15° or >120°. Joint resistance: a properly clamped Cu lug ~20-50 µΩ; a poorly clamped one 0.5-2 mΩ, dissipating P = I²R = 250² × 1 mΩ ≈ 62 W in boost — enough to discolour and loosen the joint over time.
engineering.specDeltas: Joint spec: M8 B+ joints 12 Nm ±10 %, snug 3 Nm, final angle window 30-90°, gradient limits per joint family; flanged nuts with serrations retained. Delete: manual audit work instruction and click-wrench audit station; EOL clamp-probe test reduced to 1/50 + flagged VINs. Add: angle-capable controllers at 3 stations, 3 acoustic CPA devices, MES records per VIN per joint; reaction plan: two consecutive rejects → line stop.
engineering.validationPlan: MSA: torque-angle repeatability gauge R&R ≤ 10 % (VDA 5), attribute agreement ≥ 95 % on 300 seeded good/bad joints (trapped lug, missing washer, painted lug, cross-thread). CPA classifier: 1,000 mating events incl. seeded half-mates, miss rate ≤ 1 % with 2-of-3 sensor rule. Parallel run 3 months with audit retained; zero escapes required before audit deletion. Field: monitor 48 V joint-related warranty for 12 months.
engineering.dfmImplications: No part count change; nutrunner controller upgrade at 3 stations and three acoustic CPA devices; one inspector station deleted; EOL cycle −90 s on 98 % of vehicles. Per-joint traceability by VIN supports dealer root cause and targeted recalls instead of broad campaigns.

title: Potentiostatic micro-short screening shortens 48 V ageing to one day, deletes 48 h pack rest

ideaData.title: Potentiostatic micro-short screening shortens 48 V ageing to one day, deletes 48 h pack rest
ideaData.technicalDescription: This idea changes how long product sits waiting to reveal a micro-short, not who measures it: it is distinct from relying on supplier grading data, because the ageing period itself is shortened by a different physical measurement. Baseline: high-power lithium-ion cells for the 48 V pack (12-14 per pack) are screened for internal micro-shorts by the delta-OCV method — Keysight states the OCV decay method typically takes 3-5 days for classifying cells in manufacturing — and many pack lines then add a 24-48 h rest and voltage-spread re-check before shipment to catch assembly-induced soft shorts. Both tie up dangerous-goods inventory, racks and floor space. Proposal: (1) the cell maker adopts potentiostatic self-discharge measurement (SDM) after formation, holding each cell at fixed potential and measuring the replenishing current — research reports precise currents within a few hours at 0.25 µA resolution, and Keysight states it is typically on the order of an hour — shortening ageing from ~5 days to ~1 day; (2) at our 48 V pack line (the library proposes building these packs in-house) the 48 h rest is replaced by a 60-90 min SDM through the pack's own sense lines in a temperature-stabilised fixture, before the lid is welded. Physics: a 10-50 µA soft short in a 10 Ah cell shows as only microvolts of drift per day, but as a clear current under potentiostatic hold once the RC transient (minutes to hours) settles.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cuts supplier ageing WIP and storage (negotiated price-down), deletes the pack rest racks, handling and floor space, and catches defective cells before the lid is welded (cheaper scrap).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Pack line adds a multi-channel SDM fixture (~180-200 channels for 700k cells/yr at ~90 min) in a ±0.5 K enclosure; deletes the 48 h rest storage (≈400 packs WIP) and its DG-compliant rack area. Supplier changes ageing plan.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No product change; pack sense connector must be accessible before lid welding (it is). Result per cell stored in the battery record (useful for the EU battery passport).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — mainly logistics and floor space
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cost-bridge lines net €2.07 per vehicle (Supplier cell ageing (14 cells): 1.12; Pack 48 h rest + re-check: 0.95; Self-discharge field returns: 0.10; SDM fixture operation at pack line: -0.10). Range −15 %/+10 % for estimate uncertainty: €1.76-€2.28 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €88K-€114K. 14 cells per pack; one pack per vehicle.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: temperature sensitivity of SDM (a 0.1 K drift can mimic µA currents), false accepts of slowly developing defects that appear only after days, supplier reluctance. Proof: correlation study SDM vs 14-day OCV on ≥ 5,000 cells incl. seeded defects, gauge R&R, temperature-controlled fixture. Mitigation: keep sample OCV ageing for audit (1 %).
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Li-ion cell manufacturing — Keysight potentiostatic self-discharge measurement — Delta-OCV takes 3-5 days in manufacturing; potentiostatic SDM measures self-discharge current in about an hour. How this differs: Applied to 48 V MHEV cells at supplier and, uniquely, at our pack line to delete the pack rest-check; no OEM attribution.

ideaData.manufacturingProcess: 5-day OCV ageing at supplier + 48 h pack rest re-check → ~1-day ageing + potentiostatic SDM at supplier, 90 min SDM at pack line before lid weld
ideaData.regulatoryContext: EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 data-carrying requirements make per-cell screening results useful records; storage of Li-ion cells is a fire-protection permit topic for the plant.
ideaData.focusArea: Battery production — cell screening and pack end-of-line
ideaData.targetVehicle: Luxury SUV 48 V MHEV (3.0 L I6 petrol/diesel, 8-speed automatic, AWD)

engineering.mechanism: OCV method sensitivity: ΔV = I_sd·t / (C·dQ/dV); for a 10 Ah cell with dV/dQ ≈ 10 mV/Ah near 30-50 % SOC, a 20 µA soft short drifts 20 µA × 120 h = 2.4 mAh → 24 µV per 5 days — at the edge of resolution, which is why ageing takes days. Potentiostatic: hold V within ±1 µV, the source current settles to I_sd after the RC transient τ = R_eff·C_eff (minutes to hours); with 0.25 µA resolution the 20 µA defect is a 80σ signal. Temperature: dV/dT ≈ 0.1-0.3 mV/K; a 0.01 K/min drift creates a spurious current, hence ±0.5 K enclosure and rate control.
engineering.specDeltas: Supplier spec: ageing ≥ 24 h at 25 °C, SDM hold 60 min at 3.70 V ±1 µV, accept I_sd ≤ 15 µA (to be set by correlation), per-cell record. Pack line: SDM fixture 196 channels, enclosure 25.0 ±0.5 °C, per-cell hold 90 min via BMS sense harness before lid weld; reject threshold I_sd > 20 µA or > 3σ above lot mean. Delete: 48 h pack rest storage, voltage-spread re-check station, rest racks (DG zone).
engineering.validationPlan: Correlation: 5,000 cells measured by SDM and 14-day OCV, plus 50 seeded defect cells (nail-induced micro-short, particle contamination); target detection ≥ 99 % at ≤ 0.5 % false reject. Gauge R&R ≤ 10 % on 30 cells × 3 repeats × 3 channels. Field: 12-month tracking of 48 V battery returns for self-discharge. Supplier PCN + PPAP level 3 for process change; internal pack process FMEA and run-at-rate.
engineering.dfmImplications: Pack line: −1 station (re-check), −400 packs WIP, −~150 m² DG storage; +1 SDM enclosure. Cell handling reduced (no rest move-in/move-out). Scrap of a defective cell happens before lid welding (cell-level, not pack-level).

Not included: cell price effects beyond the ageing step; working-capital interest.

ideaData.title: Returnable UN-certified totes with short-circuit nests replace one-way DG cartons for 48 V batteries
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: 48 V lithium-ion batteries are UN 3480 dangerous goods; inbound shipments from the battery supplier commonly use one-way UN-specification corrugated cartons with foam inserts and terminal caps, one or two batteries per carton, unpacked by hand at the line and disposed of as mixed waste. ADR packing instruction P903 requires batteries to be UN 38.3 tested, protected against short circuit, secured against movement and packed in strong outer packagings (1.2 m drop performance where specification packaging applies), and — for batteries of 12 kg or more with a strong, impact-resistant casing — allows strong outer packagings, protective enclosures, pallets or other handling devices. Proposal: a returnable, design-type-tested rigid tote (HDPE/PP, 1,200 × 800 footprint, ~8-12 batteries) with moulded nests that cover the terminals (short-circuit protection without loose caps), vertical separation so terminals carry no superimposed load, and a lid strapped for transport; pooled in a closed loop with the supplier (≤ 800 km road under ADR). At the line the tote presents batteries for a lift-assist or robot pick with no unpacking. ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Line-side presentation changes to tote with direct pick; cardboard handling and waste compaction removed for this flow. Requires empty-tote return loop, inspection and cleaning at the supplier.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Nests orient the battery terminals the same way every time (poka-yoke for lift-assist gripper). Terminal caps (loose parts) deleted. Battery design unchanged.

engineering.mechanism: Cost per trip of a returnable tote = (purchase ÷ trips) + return freight + cleaning/inspection + loop management. With a ~€95 tote holding 10 batteries, 10 % annual loss and ~25 trips/yr over 5 years, depreciation is ~€0.11 per battery-trip, plus pool fee/management ~€1.00. Return freight: empties nest 3:1, so return truck cost per battery ~1/3 of outbound ≈ €0.90. Drop physics: a 10 kg battery falling 1.2 m has E = m·g·h ≈ 118 J; moulded nests with 15-20 mm crush ribs absorb this within the tote wall, as cartons with foam do today.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete per battery: UN 4G carton, PE foam inserts (2), terminal caps (2), carton label. Add: tote 1,200 × 800 × 400 mm, HDPE, 10 nests, ribbed walls, lid with strap points; UN design-type mark; RFID tag; lithium battery mark and class 9 label holders. Process: line-side pick by lift-assist with nest-aligned gripper; empties return nested 3:1; inspection checklist per trip (crack, nest damage). Contract: pool size ~6,000 totes (incl. 15 % safety stock).
engineering.validationPlan: UN design-type testing per ADR 6.1.5 for packaging group II performance: drop 1.2 m (5 orientations), stacking 24 h at 3 m equivalent, n per standard, by an accredited lab. Transport trial: 20 loaded trips with shock loggers (≤ 10 g peaks). Vibration ISO 13355 random for packaged goods. DG audit of loop (outbound/inbound empties). Internal logistics approval; no product PPAP impact.
engineering.dfmImplications: Line operations: unpack + dispose (≈ 32 s) → direct pick (≈ 12 s). Terminal caps deleted. Requires tote wash/inspect at supplier and RFID tracking. Gripper alignment improved by nests.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: one-way UN carton and foam (€6.50) and waste disposal (€0.30) are deleted; tote trip cost adds €1.10, empty return freight €0.90, cleaning and DG inspection €0.35; line unpacking labour falls from €0.40 to €0.15. Not included: tote capex depreciation beyond the trip rate, which is in the investment line.

engineering.mechanism: Expected warranty part cost per vehicle = Σ (failure probability × part cost). Baseline: 0.008 × €480 (BSG) + 0.005 × €620 (e-compressor) + 0.006 × €700 (roll actuator) = €3.84 + €3.10 + €4.20 = €11.14. Reman at 60 % of new + €25 core handling: 0.008 × €313 + 0.005 × €397 + 0.006 × €445 = €2.50 + €1.99 + €2.67 = €7.16. engineering.specDeltas: Component specifications add a design-for-reman annex: housings screwed (no adhesive-only joints), bearings press-fit with extraction grooves, PCBs connectorised (no soldered motor leads), serial DataMatrix on housing, software re-flashable via standard diagnostic. Service: new reman part numbers (suffix R) for BSG, e-compressor, roll actuator; core deposit €100-200 per unit; dealer core scan in warranty system; supplier reman EOL = new-part EOL test plan.
engineering.validationPlan: Reman qualification per unit type: n = 6 reman units through new-part EOL tests and a 500 h durability (ISO 16750-3 vibration + thermal cycling), plus NVH on vehicle (BSG belt noise, compressor cabin noise). Process audit of reman lines (VDA 6.3). Core-return KPI and reman field-return rate tracked monthly (target ≤ new-part rate). Legal review of warranty use in each market.
engineering.dfmImplications: Minor design-stage cost (screwed vs bonded joints); no vehicle-plant impact. Dealer: core handling + scan (≈ 3 min). Supplier: disassembly, cleaning, test lines. Part numbers +3 reman variants.

title: Dealer repair-not-replace for 48 V battery: BMS service bay, crash-lock reset and cell-stack exchange
description: [MHEV] Most warranty events are fixed with a board, a reset or balancing instead of a whole battery; the dangerous-goods return of a full battery is avoided in those cases. Baseline: many 48 V MHEV battery faults (BMS communication failure, wake-up failure, protection lock, crash-data lock, cell imbalance) lead to replacement of the complete battery under warranty. Independent repairers now offer diagnostics, balancing, cell repair and BMS recovery for BMW 48 V batteries instead of replacement, and services exist to reset stored crash data in BMW 48 V batteries — evidence that a large share of "battery failures" are electronics or logic states, not cell damage. Proposal: design the 48 V battery with a separate electronics bay under a gasketed service cover (BMS board, main-switch MOSFET board, fuse) that is opened without breaking the cell-stack enclosure, and give dealers an OEM-authorised procedure: (1) diagnose with the dealer tool — logic lock or crash flag after a non-deployment event → authenticated reset; (2) BMS/switch board fault → replace the board (€95 class part) and re-learn; (3) cell imbalance → guided balancing; (4) cell damage or water ingress → exchange the sealed cell stack only, keeping housing and electronics. Planning assumption: warranty claims 1.2 % of vehicles, of which ~65 % are resolved at levels 1-3. Note: the library's hot-plate-welded lid idea cover

engineering.mechanism: Expected warranty cost per vehicle = claim rate × cost per claim. Baseline: 1.2 % × (€650 battery + €120 labour + €60 DG return) = 1.2 % × €830 = €9.96. Proposed: 35 % of claims still need full or stack exchange (≈ €830) → 0.012 × 0.35 × 830 = €3.49; 65 % repaired at ≈ €180 (board €95 or reset/balancing, 0.8 h labour) → 0.012 × 0.65 × 180 = €1.40. Electrical safety at 48 V: below the 60 V DC class-B threshold, so no HV qualification, but short-circuit currents of several kA require insulated tools and the main switch open during board swap.
engineering.specDeltas: Housing: internal partition between cell compartment (welded, sealed) and electronics bay; bay cover PP-LGF30 with EPDM gasket, 4 × M5 screws with asymmetric pattern, tamper label; board-to-stack connection by press-fit header (no soldered sense wires). Software: authenticated crash-flag reset for non-deployment events, board re-learn routine, guided balancing function in dealer tool. Service parts: BMS board, switch board, gasket kit, sealed cell-stack module.
engineering.validationPlan: Sealing: IP6K9K and IPX7 (1 m, 30 min) after 5 open/close cycles with new gasket, n = 6. Battery qualification unchanged otherwise (ISO 16750 series, LV 148, UN 38.3 for the stack). Functional safety: review of reset function (no reset possible after deployment-level crash). Service trial: 20 dealers, time study, first-time-fix ≥ 90 %. UN 38.3 for cell-stack service part shipping.

title: Fleet battery-health telemetry validates smaller ageing margin: 48 V cells 10 Ah to 8.5 Ah
description: [MHEV] Replaces assumed lab-based ageing margin with measured field ageing, allowing ~15 % less cell capacity (cost and mass) without lowering end-of-life performance; warranty reserve is set on data rather than conservatism. ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V battery is sized for end-of-life power and energy after ~10-15 years with conservative ageing assumptions from cell-level lab tests (e.g. 20-25 % capacity fade and 50-100 % resistance growth), because no field data exist at launch. Proposal: instrument the launch fleet (data the BMS already computes — capacity estimate, DC resistance at fixed SOC/temperature, temperature histograms, Ah throughput, boost/regen power histograms) and upload aggregated health indicators via the existing connected-car channel; after 18-24 months of fleet data (~75-100k vehicles) fit a calendar-plus-cycle ageing model to real usage and re-size the cell for the next model-year to 8.5 Ah where the data support it, keeping the same footprint by a thinner prismatic or pouch variant from the same cell family. engineering.mechanism: Required beginning-of-life capacity C_BOL = C_need / (1 − f_fade). With an energy/power need equivalent to 6.8 Ah at end of life, a 32 % lab-assumed fade (incl. margin) requires 10 Ah; if field data show 95th-percentile fade of 20 % at 15 years, C_BOL = 6.8/0.8 = 8.5 Ah. Power: DCR growth sets boost/regen capability P = V·(V_ocv − V_min)/R; resistance growth assumed 100 % vs field-observed ~60 % lets the smaller cell (whose DCR is ~1.15× higher) still meet end-of-life power. Calendar ageing follows ~√t at given temperature/SOC; field temperature histograms (often cooler than lab 45 °C storage) are the main lever.
engineering.specDeltas: Telemetry: weekly upload of SOH_capacity, DCR_10s at 50 % SOC/25 °C normalised, temperature histogram (5 K bins), Ah throughput, boost/regen power histograms — aggregated, ~2 kB/week, opt-in per GDPR. Next model-year: cell spec 8.5 Ah (from 10 Ah), DCR ≤ 1.2 mΩ at 25 °C BOL, same can footprint (thickness −3 to −4 mm with spacer if needed); pack 14s unchanged; BMS SOC/SOH parameter set update; end-of-life requirement unchanged.
engineering.validationPlan: Field model: Weibull/√t fit on ≥ 75,000 vehicles × 18 months; 95th-percentile projection with 90 % confidence. New cell: IEC 62660-1 performance/life, IEC 62660-2 reliability, UN 38.3, calendar ageing 45/60 °C at 3 SOCs for 12 months, cycle life on MHEV profile; pack: ISO 16750 series, LV 148, cold boost −30 °C. PPAP level 3 for cell change; OEM 48 V system re-sign-off. DPIA under GDPR before data collection.
engineering.dfmImplications: No part-count change; one cell P/N swap; thinner cells may need a spacer or compression-pad change in the stack. Data pipeline uses existing connectivity; dashboards for warranty and engineering.
engineering.costBridge: Per vehicle: 14 cells at 10 Ah × 3.7 V × €0.30/Wh = €155.40 → 8.5 Ah = €132.10; warranty reserve accrual rises from €6.00 to €6.80 to reflect the slimmer margin; telemetry data handling adds €0.40. Not included: the value of mass saving (~0.8 kg), cell qualification (in investment).

title: One ISO 26262 SEooC safety case for the 48 V motor-drive core, reused four times
description: [MHEV] Safety analyses, confirmation measures and safety-test campaigns are paid once per tier instead of once per actuator; each programme pays only for assumption validation and delta work.
